Compare Sachal with Shah Latif to see both poets more clearly. Shah Latif often tells a story of a heroine on a journey. Sachal often speaks directly to the heart without a long story. Both poets praise love, sincerity, and courage, but Sachal voice is more direct and questioning. The guide on [Shah Latif themes](/blog/sindhi-shah-latif-poetry-themes.html) explains the journey image that dominates Shah Latif. Reading both guides together helps pupils answer comparison questions, such as how the two poets treat love differently. Keep the comparison short: one similarity and one difference, each with one example.

sections.h2: How to Write About Sachal in Exams
paras: A good exam answer on Sachal follows a simple order. First, name the verse and its image in one or two sentences. Second, state the message in one sentence: love, tolerance, or truth. Third, explain the image in your own words. Fourth, add one lesson for daily life. For example, a verse about the mirror of the heart can be answered as the image of looking honestly at oneself, the message of truth, and the lesson of admitting mistakes. This four-step answer is complete and easy to mark. Avoid writing a long biography when the question asks about a message. A brief line about Sachal as the poet of love is enough.

Practise with one verse at a time. Choose a short verse from your textbook, write the image, the message, and the daily lesson, and ask your teacher to check your sentences. If your teacher says your message is too general, add one concrete detail from the verse. General answers say love is good. Strong answers say this verse teaches that love removes pride, shown by the image of fire burning selfishness. That detail is what earns marks. You can find Sachal selections in your class book through the [books page](/books.html). Read them aloud slowly, and let the simple words do their deep work.
bullets: Name the verse image in one or two sentences.
State the message as love, tolerance, or truth.
Explain the image in your own words.
Add one daily-life lesson with a concrete example.
Keep biography short when the question asks about a message.

points: Sachal is the poet of love, truth, and tolerance.
Love for Sachal means action: forgiving, sharing, and refusing hatred.
Tolerance means respecting people who differ from us.
Read each short verse three times: words, image, lesson.
Exam answers need image, message, and one daily lesson.

faqs.q: Why is Sachal called Sarmast?
faqs.a: Sarmast means absorbed in love. People gave him this name because his poetry shows a heart fully absorbed in love for truth and humanity.

faqs.q: What is the main message of Sachal poetry?
faqs.a: Love all people, keep the heart free from hatred and pride, and speak the truth with kindness.

faqs.q: How is Sachal different from Shah Latif?
faqs.a: Shah Latif often teaches through heroine stories and journeys. Sachal often speaks directly to the heart with short, questioning verses.

faqs.q: Can I write about Sachal without long philosophy?
faqs.a: Yes. Explain one image, state one message, and give one daily-life example. That is enough for a strong school answer.

title: Tashreeh Method for Sindhi Poetry Passages
desc: Master Sindhi poetry tashreeh with reference, meaning, and message: a clear exam method with a model answer shape.
intro: Tashreeh is the part of the Sindhi exam where many pupils feel most nervous. A short poetry passage appears, and you must explain it clearly. The tashreeh method Sindhi poetry passages pupils need is simple: reference, meaning, and message. Reference tells where the passage comes from. Meaning explains what the poet says in your own words. Message states what the reader should learn. Many pupils lose marks because they write only a summary, or only a translation, or a long introduction with no explanation of the lines. This guide shows a step-by-step method, a model answer shape, and checking habits that turn tashreeh from a fear into a steady source of marks.

sections.h2: What Tashreeh Really Asks For
paras: Tashreeh means detailed explanation. The examiner does not ask you to repeat the passage in harder words. The examiner asks you to prove that you understood the passage. A good tashreeh answer does three things. It names the poet and the poem or Sur. It explains the meaning of the lines in simple, connected language. It states the message and shows how the lines support it. If any of these three parts is missing, the answer feels incomplete. If all three are present, even a short answer can earn good marks. Think of tashreeh as a conversation with the examiner. You are saying: here is where these lines come from, here is what they mean, and here is why they matter.

Before you write, read the passage three times. The first reading is for sound and general sense. The second reading is for hard words and images. The third reading is for the message. Underline the words you must explain. Mark the image, such as a journey, a river, or a waiting heart. Ask yourself what the poet wants the reader to feel or learn. This three-reading habit takes only two or three minutes, but it prevents the most common error: writing an answer about the wrong theme because you rushed. Pupils who plan tashreeh for two minutes write clearer answers than pupils who start writing at once.

sections.h2: Step One: Reference in Two Lines
paras: Reference, called hawala in school language, tells the source of the passage. Write it in one or two lines: the name of the poet, the name of the poem or Sur, and the context if you know it. For example, these lines are taken from a Sur in Shah Jo Risalo by Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai, where the poet describes the journey of Sasui. That single sentence gives the examiner the source and the situation. Do not write a long biography of the poet in the reference. A long biography wastes time and space. If you are unsure of the exact Sur name, write the poet name and the general theme, and move on. A short honest reference is better than a long guessed one.

Some passages in exams come from poems you studied in class, and some come from unseen passages. The reference method works for both. For a seen passage, name the poet and poem. For an unseen passage, name the theme and the kind of poetry, such as a verse about patience and journey. Do not invent a poet name or a poem name. If you do not know it, say that the passage speaks of a general theme and focus your energy on meaning and message. Examiners mark meaning and message more heavily than a perfect reference. Accuracy matters more than pretending.

diagram.caption: Use this order for every tashreeh answer in the exam.

sections.h2: Step Two: Meaning in Your Own Words
paras: Meaning is the longest part of tashreeh. Explain the passage line by line, but in connected paragraphs, not as a list of translations. Begin with the first line or beit, explain its words and image, then move to the next line and show how it continues or deepens the idea. Use your own Sindhi words, not the textbook words repeated. If the poet says that the traveller walks alone at night, you can explain that the traveller faces darkness and loneliness but keeps walking. This rephrasing shows understanding. If a line contains a muhavara or a fixed phrase, explain it as one unit, not word by word. The guide on [Sindhi muhavare](/blog/sindhi-muhavare-idioms-meaning.html) shows how to learn idioms as pictures and situations.

Explain hard words inside the meaning, not in a separate list. When you meet a difficult word, write its simple meaning in brackets or in the same sentence. For example, the word for thirst here means longing, not only need for water. This method keeps the meaning flowing. Avoid copying the textbook explanation word for word. Examiners can tell memorised answers from understood answers. A memorised answer often uses words the pupil cannot explain. An understood answer uses simple words the pupil controls. Keep your sentences short. One idea per sentence makes your meaning clear and easy to mark.

sections.h2: Step Three: Message With Evidence
paras: After the meaning, write the message in one or two sentences. The message answers the question: what does the poet want the reader to learn, feel, or do. State it directly. For example, the poet teaches that patience in hardship leads to nearness to the goal. Then support it with one detail from the passage. The detail can be an image, a verb, or a repeated word. If the passage repeats a word for walking, the repetition proves that the poet values steady effort. Without evidence, the message sounds like a guess. With evidence, it sounds like an argument. This is the difference between an average answer and a strong one.

Do not add a second, unrelated message. One clear message with evidence beats two vague messages. If the passage truly carries two ideas, such as patience and honesty, mention the second briefly and link it to the first. For example, the traveller patience is possible because of honesty of heart. That linking sentence shows mature thinking. Avoid moralising beyond the passage. If the passage is about a traveller, do not turn it into a lecture on ten other topics. Stay close to the lines. The examiner wants to see that you can read what is there, not that you can write about everything you know.

sections.h2: Model Shape and Checking Habits
paras: A model tashreeh answer has a clear shape. Paragraph one: reference in two lines. Paragraph two: meaning of the first part of the passage. Paragraph three: meaning of the second part, with images explained. Paragraph four: message with evidence and a short closing line. The whole answer fits on about one to one and a half pages. This shape works for seen and unseen passages, for Shah Latif, Sachal, and other poets. Pupils who practise this shape find that tashreeh becomes predictable. They no longer stare at the passage wondering where to start. They start with reference, move to meaning, and finish with message.

For practice, choose one poetry passage per week from your textbook. Read it three times, write the tashreeh using this shape, and ask your teacher to mark reference, meaning, and message separately. This feedback tells you which part needs work. Many pupils find that their meaning is good but their message is vague, or their reference is too long. Fix one weakness at a time. For more help with reading poetry before tashreeh, see the [beit-by-beit method](/blog/sindhi-poetry-beit-meaning-method.html) and the [Shah Latif guide](/blog/sindhi-shah-latif-poetry-themes.html). You can find poetry passages in your class book via the [books page](/books.html). With steady practice, tashreeh becomes one of your strongest exam skills.
bullets: Read the passage three times before writing.
Keep the reference to one or two honest lines.
Explain meaning in connected paragraphs, not word lists.
State the message with one detail as evidence.
Check that every paragraph stays close to the given lines.

points: Tashreeh needs three parts: reference, meaning, and message.
Read the passage three times before writing.
Explain meaning in your own connected words.
Support the message with one detail from the passage.
Keep the answer to about one to one and a half pages.

faqs.q: How long should a tashreeh answer be?
faqs.a: About one to one and a half pages: a short reference, two meaning paragraphs, and a message paragraph with evidence.

faqs.q: Should I translate the passage word by word?
faqs.a: No. Explain the meaning in connected sentences in your own words, with hard words explained inside the meaning.

faqs.q: What if the passage is unseen?
faqs.a: Use the same method. Give a theme-based reference, explain the meaning from context, and state the message with evidence.

faqs.q: Can I write more than one message?
faqs.a: Keep one main message. Mention a second idea only briefly and link it to the first, with evidence.

title: Studying Dialogue in Sindhi Drama
desc: Learn how dialogue reveals character and conflict in Sindhi drama: reading, analysing, and answering exam questions.
intro: In a Sindhi drama, characters do not tell you who they are. They show it through what they say and how they say it. The skill of studying dialogue Sindhi drama means listening to conversations the way you listen to real people: who speaks first, who interrupts, who stays polite under pressure, and who changes after a hard truth. Many pupils read a play like a story and miss its real engine. A play moves through dialogue. Each exchange adds tension, reveals a secret, or pushes a character toward a choice. This guide shows how to read dialogue, how to spot character and conflict inside it, and how to write exam answers that quote short lines and explain them well.

sections.h2: What Dialogue Does in a Play
paras: Dialogue in drama does four jobs at once. It tells the story, because characters share news and plans through speech. It reveals character, because word choice and tone show kindness, pride, fear, or honesty. It creates conflict, because characters disagree, misunderstand, or hide the truth. It controls pace, because short exchanges feel fast and tense, while long speeches feel slow and serious. When you read a play, ask which job each exchange performs. A short quarrel may create conflict. A long confession may reveal character. A quick question may move the story forward. Naming the job helps you analyse the dialogue instead of only retelling it.

Stage directions also matter. Words in brackets that describe entering, leaving, pausing, or speaking softly tell you how a line should sound. A line that reads as anger on paper may read as sadness if the stage direction says the speaker lowers the voice. Always read the stage direction before the line. If your textbook gives a short introduction to the play, read it first. It tells you the situation, the place, and the relations between characters. Without that background, a simple line such as I will go can be misunderstood. With background, you know whether going means escape, courage, or defeat.

sections.h2: Listening for Character in Speech
paras: Each character in a good play speaks differently. A kind elder speaks slowly and uses respectful words. A proud young man speaks quickly and uses sharp words. A frightened child asks short questions. A wise teacher asks questions that make others think. When you study dialogue, collect two or three short lines for each important character and ask what they prove. A line in which a character apologises proves humility. A line in which a character blames others proves pride. A line in which a character stays silent at a key moment can also prove character. Silence in drama is a choice, and it often speaks louder than words.

Watch how a character speech changes across the play. A character who begins with pride may end with humility. A character who begins with fear may end with courage. This change is called character development, and examiners value answers that notice it. To track it, compare the first speech of a character with the last speech. Ask what happened between the two speeches that caused the change. Often a conflict, a loss, or a kind act caused it. If a character does not change, say so honestly and explain why. A stubborn character who refuses to change can teach a lesson about pride just as clearly as a changing character teaches a lesson about growth.

diagram.caption: Fill one row for each key exchange before you write your answer.

sections.h2: Finding Conflict Inside Conversations
paras: Conflict in drama lives inside conversations. Two characters want different things, and their words collide. One wants to tell the truth, the other wants to hide it. One wants to leave, the other wants to stay. One wants money, the other wants honour. When you find such a clash, you have found the conflict. Mark the lines where the clash becomes clear. Often one character asks a question and the other avoids answering. Avoidance is a signal of conflict. So is repetition. When a character repeats the same sentence, it shows stubbornness or fear. When characters interrupt each other, it shows rising tension. These small signals help you explain how the play builds pressure.

The turning point of a play often appears as a single line. A confession, a refusal, a promise, or a discovery changes everything after it. In your answer, quote that line briefly and explain why it matters. Ask what would have happened if the character had said the opposite. This question shows cause and effect. For example, if a character had not confessed, the family would have kept blaming the wrong person. That sentence proves you understand the structure of the play. Do not quote long speeches. Quote a few words and explain them. Short quotations with clear explanation earn more marks than long quotations without comment.

sections.h2: Reading Dialogue Aloud and in Pairs
paras: Drama is written to be spoken, so silent reading alone is not enough. Read the play aloud, alone or with a classmate. Take one role each and read the lines with feeling. You will notice pauses, questions, and emotions that silent reading hides. A line that looked flat on paper may sound sharp when spoken. A line that looked angry may sound sad when spoken slowly. After reading aloud, discuss two questions with your partner: what does each character want in this scene, and what stops the character from getting it. Those two questions reveal the conflict of the scene. This pair method works well in class and at home, and it makes drama enjoyable rather than difficult.

When you read aloud, also notice the rhythm of exchanges. Fast exchanges with short lines create excitement or quarrel. Slow exchanges with long lines create reflection or sadness. In your answer, you can mention this rhythm in one sentence. For example, the short questions and answers in this scene show rising tension. That observation shows careful reading. Avoid acting out the whole play in an exam answer. One sentence about rhythm is enough. The main work is still character, conflict, and message. For a similar focus on character and message in stories, see the guide on [Sindhi afsana analysis](/blog/sindhi-afsana-story-analysis.html).

sections.h2: Writing a Dialogue Answer for Exams
paras: A good exam answer on drama dialogue follows a simple order. First, name the play, the scene, and the speakers in one or two sentences. Second, explain what happens in the scene in your own words. Third, analyse two or three key exchanges, each with a short quotation and an explanation of what it reveals. Fourth, state the message or the result of the scene. Keep quotations short. A quotation of five to ten words is enough. After each quotation, write one or two sentences of explanation. A quotation without explanation proves nothing. An explanation without a quotation can sound like a guess. Together they make a strong answer.

Practise with one scene at a time. Choose a scene with two characters and one clear conflict. Fill the dialogue table, then write a one-page answer using the order above. Ask your teacher to mark whether your quotations are short and your explanations are clear. If your answer only retells the story, add more explanation of character and conflict. If your answer only lists quotations, add more connection between them. You can find drama lessons in your class book through the [books page](/books.html). With practice, dialogue study becomes a habit of listening closely, which helps not only in drama but in every Sindhi lesson.
bullets: Read stage directions before the spoken line.
Collect two or three short lines per character.
Mark where characters clash, avoid, or interrupt.
Quote five to ten words, then explain them.
Track how speech changes from first scene to last.

points: Dialogue tells the story, reveals character, and creates conflict.
Read stage directions before the spoken line.
Prove each trait with a short quotation plus explanation.
Find the conflict where characters want different things.
Track how a character speech changes across the play.

faqs.q: How long should a quotation be in a drama answer?
faqs.a: Five to ten words is enough. Follow each short quotation with one or two sentences of explanation.

faqs.q: Should I retell the whole scene?
faqs.a: No. Give a short summary, then analyse two or three key exchanges with evidence and explanation.

faqs.q: What if a character stays silent?
faqs.a: Silence is also meaningful. Explain what the silence shows, such as fear, respect, guilt, or refusal.

faqs.q: How does dialogue show conflict?
faqs.a: Through clashing goals, avoided answers, repetition, and interruption. Mark those signals when you read.

title: Sindhi Folk Tales and Their Moral Lessons
desc: Enjoy Sindhi folk tales and learn their moral lessons: honesty, kindness, wisdom, and storytelling skills for pupils.
intro: Every Sindhi child has heard a folk tale from a grandparent, a teacher, or an elder at night. A clever farmer outwits a greedy landlord. A kind girl shares her bread and is rewarded. A foolish traveller learns wisdom the hard way. The study of Sindhi folk tales moral lessons is not only about enjoying old stories. It is about learning how stories teach honesty, kindness, courage, and wisdom without lecturing. Folk tales use simple characters, clear problems, and memorable endings to carry lessons that stay in the heart. This guide explains what folk tales are, how their morals work, how to retell them well, and how to write about them in school answers.

sections.h2: What Makes a Folk Tale
paras: A folk tale is a story passed from person to person, often without a known author. It belongs to the whole community. Folk tales use simple language, familiar places, and clear characters: a wise old woman, a greedy merchant, a brave child, a talking animal, or a kind neighbour. The story usually begins with a problem, such as hunger, injustice, or a journey, and ends with a result that feels fair. Good people are rewarded, greedy people lose, and foolish people learn. This clear pattern helps listeners remember the tale and its lesson. Unlike a modern afsana, a folk tale does not hide its message. The message stands in the open, like a lamp in a courtyard.

Folk tales also carry the culture of Sindh. They describe village wells, river journeys, harvests, weddings, and markets. They use muhavare, proverbs, and songs that elders know by heart. When you listen to a folk tale, you learn language as well as values. You hear how elders speak, how they joke, and how they warn. In school, folk tales appear as reading lessons, storytelling practice, and moral education. Pupils should enjoy them first and analyse them second. If you only hunt for the moral and never enjoy the story, you miss the pleasure that kept these tales alive for generations.

sections.h2: How Morals Work in Folk Tales
paras: The moral of a folk tale is the lesson the story teaches. It is rarely stated as a rule at the start. It grows from what happens to the characters. A greedy character loses wealth because of greed. A kind character gains friends because of kindness. A patient character succeeds because of patience. The reader learns by watching results, not by memorising rules. When you analyse a folk tale, ask three questions: what did the main character choose, what happened because of that choice, and what should a wise reader learn. Those three questions give you the moral in one clear sentence. For example, the tale teaches that greed destroys what honesty could have kept.

Some tales carry more than one moral. A tale about a clever farmer may teach both wisdom and hard work. A tale about a kind girl may teach both generosity and courage. Choose one main moral for your answer and mention a second briefly if it fits. Avoid forcing a moral that the story does not support. If the tale ends with a funny twist, the moral may be about wisdom rather than goodness. Read the ending carefully. The ending is where the moral becomes clear. A tale that ends with laughter may still teach that cleverness beats strength, and that is a valid moral.

diagram.alt: Finding the Moral of a Folk Tale
diagram.caption: Use these four steps for any Sindhi folk tale.

sections.h2: Familiar Tales and Their Lessons
paras: Many Sindhi folk tales share common lessons. Tales of honesty show that a lie may bring quick gain but lasting shame. Tales of kindness show that sharing brings more joy than keeping. Tales of wisdom show that thinking before acting saves trouble. Tales of courage show that a small person with a brave heart can face a large problem. When you retell a tale, name its lesson early or late, but do not preach through the whole story. Let the story do the teaching. For example, tell how the kind girl shared her bread, how the traveller blessed her, and how the village learned of her kindness. The listener will feel the lesson without a long lecture.

Tales also teach social lessons: respect elders, protect guests, care for neighbours, and keep promises. These lessons matter in village life, where people depend on one another. A tale about a guest teaches hospitality. A tale about a promise teaches trust. A tale about a neighbour teaches that a good neighbour is worth more than a distant relative. In school answers, connect the tale moral to one daily example. A pupil who keeps a promise to a classmate practises the same trust the tale praises. This connection turns an old tale into a living lesson. The guide on [Sindhi afsana analysis](/blog/sindhi-afsana-story-analysis.html) uses a similar choice-and-result method for modern stories.

sections.h2: Retelling a Folk Tale Well
paras: Retelling is a skill every pupil can learn. Begin with the setting in one or two sentences: a village, a river, a market, or a home. Introduce the main character and the problem quickly. Tell events in order, without adding new characters or side stories. Use dialogue for key moments. A short spoken line, such as I will share my bread, makes the tale lively. End with the result and the moral in one sentence each. A good retelling takes three to five minutes when spoken, or about one page when written. It should feel like a story, not like a summary of points. Practise retelling one tale to a younger sibling or a parent. If they listen with interest and can repeat the moral, your retelling worked.

Use your own words when retelling. Do not try to memorise the textbook version word for word. Memorised retellings sound stiff and break if you forget one line. Your own words keep the story flowing even if you forget a detail. Use simple Sindhi, clear sentences, and natural pauses. If the tale includes a song or a repeated line, keep that line in its original form, because repetition is part of its charm. After retelling, ask your listener what lesson they heard. Their answer tells you whether your retelling made the moral clear. If they heard a different moral, discuss it. Folk tales allow honest discussion about meaning.

sections.h2: Writing About Folk Tales in Exams
paras: A school answer on a folk tale follows a simple order. First, name the tale and its main character in one or two sentences. Second, summarise the story in five to seven sentences. Third, state the moral in one sentence with evidence from the ending. Fourth, add one lesson for daily life with a concrete example. For example, a tale about sharing can end with the lesson that sharing food in school builds friendship. This four-part answer is complete and easy to mark. Avoid writing a long summary that leaves no room for the moral. The moral is the heart of the answer, so give it a full paragraph.

For storytelling practice, choose one tale per week. Read it, retell it aloud, then write a one-page answer using the order above. Ask your teacher to mark the summary, the moral, and the daily example separately. If your moral is vague, add one detail from the ending as evidence. If your summary is too long, cut side details and keep only the main line of events. You can find folk tales in your class book through the [books page](/books.html), and solved material on the [solved notes page](/solved.html). Folk tales remind us that wisdom does not need difficult words. It needs a good story, an honest heart, and a lesson that lives in daily action.
bullets: Name the tale and its main character first.
Keep the summary to five to seven sentences.
State the moral in one sentence with ending evidence.
Add one daily-life example of the moral.
Retell in your own words, not memorised text.

points: Folk tales teach morals through character choices and results.
Find the moral by asking what the character chose and what happened.
Retell tales in your own words with short dialogue.
State the moral in one sentence with evidence from the ending.
Connect each moral to one daily-life example.

faqs.q: What is a Sindhi folk tale?
faqs.a: A story passed from person to person in the community, with simple characters, a clear problem, and an ending that teaches a moral.

faqs.q: How do I find the moral of a folk tale?
faqs.a: Look at the main character choice and its result. The moral is the lesson a wise reader learns from that result.

faqs.q: Should I memorise folk tales word by word?
faqs.a: No. Retell them in your own words, keeping only repeated lines or songs in their original form.

faqs.q: Can a folk tale have more than one moral?
faqs.a: Yes. Keep one main moral at the centre and mention a second briefly if the story supports it.

title: Writing a Précis: A Summary Method for English
desc: Learn a clear precis method to shrink any English passage to one-third length while keeping its main argument, facts, and tone intact.
intro: A precis is a short, faithful summary of a longer passage. The writing precis summary method English pupils need is not about copying sentences or dropping random lines. It is a disciplined way to read carefully, find the central argument, remove examples and repetition, and then rewrite the meaning in your own words at about one-third of the original length. This skill matters far beyond examinations. It trains you to separate what an author is really saying from what is only decoration, and it helps you revise faster, answer comprehension questions better, and write clearer essays. In this guide you will learn a step-by-step method you can use on any passage, from a textbook paragraph to a newspaper editorial. You will also see common mistakes to avoid and a simple checklist to test your finished precis before you hand it in.

sections.h2: What a Precis Is and What It Is Not
paras: A precis restates the main ideas of a passage in fewer words, in the same order, and in the same tone. If the original is serious, your precis stays serious. If the original argues for something, your precis shows that argument. You do not add your own opinion, new examples, or extra facts. You also do not copy whole sentences. The goal is to prove that you understood the passage well enough to say it again more briefly.

A precis is not a list of points, not a paraphrase of one paragraph, and not a personal reaction. It is a connected piece of writing, usually in one paragraph, written in your own words. It keeps proper nouns, key numbers, and decisive facts, but it drops illustrations, repetitions, quotations, and rhetorical flourishes. Think of it as the skeleton of the passage: everything essential remains, everything extra is gone. Pupils who treat a precis as a miniature essay, with a clear beginning, middle, and end, usually score better than those who simply compress sentences one by one.

sections.h2: Step One: Read, Underline, and Find the Main Idea
paras: Read the passage twice before you write anything. On the first reading, read for general sense and do not stop at hard words. On the second reading, underline the topic sentence of each paragraph and circle words that signal argument, such as therefore, however, because, and as a result. Ask one question of every paragraph: what is this paragraph doing for the whole passage? Is it giving a cause, an effect, an example, a contrast, or a conclusion? Write a short note in the margin in three to five words.

After the second reading, write the central idea of the whole passage in one sentence of your own. If you cannot do this, you are not ready to write. Read again. A useful test is to cover the passage and say the main idea aloud. If you can explain it to a friend in one sentence without looking, you have understood it. This one-sentence core becomes the backbone of your precis, and every other sentence you write should support it. You can find more reading strategies in our comprehension guide on [guessing vocabulary from context](/blog/english-comprehension-vocabulary-context.html) and browse solved materials on the [books page](/books.html).
bullets: First reading: grasp the overall meaning without worrying about every word.
Second reading: underline topic sentences and mark argument signals.
Margin notes: summarise each paragraph in three to five words.
One-sentence test: state the central idea aloud before writing.

sections.h2: Step Two: Cut to One-Third Without Losing Meaning
paras: Now build a rough draft from your margin notes, not from the original sentences. Write in your own words and keep the original order of ideas. Aim for about one-third of the original word count. If the passage is 300 words, your precis should be near 100 words. Remove examples unless an example is the argument itself. Remove repeated ideas, adjectives that only decorate, and long introductions. Keep names, dates, and figures that change the meaning if removed.

Use clear, plain sentences. Avoid copying phrases longer than two or three words. If you find yourself copying, close the passage and write from memory, then check back for accuracy. Keep the same tense and person as the original where possible, and keep the same level of certainty. If the author says something may happen, do not write that it will happen. This faithfulness to meaning is what examiners value most, more than fancy vocabulary.

diagram.caption: Follow these four moves in order for every precis.

sections.h2: Common Mistakes That Cost Marks
paras: The most common mistake is adding personal opinion. Phrases such as in my opinion or I think do not belong in a precis unless the original passage itself expresses that opinion. Another frequent error is keeping the examples and dropping the argument. If you describe three illustrations but never state the conclusion they support, the precis fails even if it is short. A third mistake is changing the meaning through careless synonyms. Words such as some, many, all, always, and never carry precise weight, so keep them accurate.

Length errors are also common. A precis that is half the original is too long, while one that is only a few sentences usually drops essential ideas. Count your words and check the ratio. Finally, watch your grammar. A precis is judged as a piece of writing, so spelling, punctuation, and sentence structure matter. Leave two minutes at the end to read your precis aloud and fix anything that sounds unclear or incomplete.
bullets: Do not add your own opinion or new examples.
Do not keep illustrations while dropping the conclusion.
Do not weaken words like all, always, may, and never.
Count your words and aim for roughly one-third of the original.

sections.h2: A Practice Routine You Can Repeat Weekly
paras: Choose one short passage each week, ideally 250 to 350 words, from a textbook, newspaper, or past paper. Time yourself: ten minutes to read and plan, fifteen minutes to draft, and five minutes to check. After writing, compare your precis with the original paragraph by paragraph and ask whether any key idea is missing or distorted. Keep a notebook of your precis attempts so you can see progress over time.

You can also practise with a partner. Both pupils summarise the same passage, then compare versions and discuss which one is more faithful and more concise. This discussion teaches more than solitary practice because it forces you to defend your choices. For more English writing help, see [direct and indirect speech rules](/blog/english-direct-indirect-speech-rules.html) and [active and passive voice](/blog/english-active-passive-voice-method.html), or explore the full library on the [solved books page](/solved.html).

points: A precis restates the main argument in about one-third of the original length.
Read twice, note each paragraph, and state the central idea in one sentence.
Draft from margin notes in your own words, keeping the original order and tone.
Keep names, key numbers, and decisive facts; drop examples and repetition.
Check accuracy, length, and grammar before submitting.

faqs.q: How long should a precis be?
faqs.a: About one-third of the original passage. A 300-word passage becomes roughly 100 words. Count your words and adjust by cutting decoration or restoring a missing key idea.

faqs.q: Can I copy sentences from the original?
faqs.a: Avoid copying. Write in your own words. Copying more than a short phrase suggests you have not understood the passage, and it weakens your score.

faqs.q: Should a precis include my opinion?
faqs.a: No. A precis reports what the author says, not what you think about it. Keep your own views out unless the passage itself states them.

faqs.q: What if I do not understand a word in the passage?
faqs.a: Use context clues to guess the general sense and keep reading. The main idea usually becomes clear from surrounding sentences. You can also review guessing vocabulary from context to build this skill.

title: Guessing Vocabulary from Context in English Comprehension
desc: Learn to guess unknown English words from surrounding sentences, so comprehension passages become faster and less stressful without a dictionary.
intro: Every pupil meets unknown words in a comprehension passage. The guessing vocabulary context English comprehension method turns that moment from a panic into a puzzle you can solve. Instead of stopping at the first hard word, you use the sentences around it — definitions, examples, contrasts, and cause-and-effect signals — to infer what it probably means. This skill is essential in examinations, where dictionaries are not allowed, and in real reading, where stopping for every word breaks your flow. In this guide you will learn five reliable context clues, a four-step routine for applying them, and practice habits that build vocabulary faster than memorising word lists alone. You will also learn when a guess is good enough and when you should keep reading for more evidence.

sections.h2: Why Context Works Better Than Stopping
paras: Authors rarely drop a difficult word without giving the reader some help. They define it, give an example, contrast it with its opposite, or show its result. Skilled readers notice these signals automatically. Unskilled readers stop, worry, and lose the thread of the passage. The difference is not talent; it is habit. When you train yourself to look around an unknown word before you worry about it, you keep reading and you usually guess well enough to answer the question.

Context guessing also builds long-term vocabulary. A word you work out from a real sentence is remembered better than a word you copied from a list, because you have connected it to a meaning, a situation, and a feeling. Over weeks of practice, words you once guessed become words you know. That is why teachers value this skill so highly: it makes you an independent reader rather than a reader who depends on a dictionary or a teacher for every hard word.

sections.h2: Five Context Clues to Look For
paras: First, look for a definition clue. The author may explain the word directly, using phrases such as means, is defined as, or in other words. Second, look for an example clue. Words such as for example, such as, and including introduce cases that show what the word covers. Third, look for a contrast clue. Words such as but, however, unlike, and whereas signal that the unknown word is the opposite of something nearby.

Fourth, look for a cause-and-effect clue. If a sentence says that something caused a result, the unknown word often names the cause or the result, and the other half of the sentence tells you its direction. Fifth, look for a word-part clue. Prefixes such as un, re, and pre, and suffixes such as tion, ness, and able, narrow the meaning. Combine these clues rather than relying on one. Two weak clues together often give a strong guess. For more writing support, see [writing a precis](/blog/english-precis-summary-method.html) and the [books page](/books.html).
bullets: Definition: means, is defined as, in other words.
Example: for example, such as, including.
Contrast: but, however, unlike, whereas.
Cause and effect: because, so, therefore, as a result.
Word parts: prefixes and suffixes that hint at meaning.

sections.h2: A Four-Step Routine for Any Unknown Word
paras: Step one: read the whole sentence containing the unknown word, then read the sentence before and after it. Do not guess from the word alone. Step two: ask what part of speech it is. Is it a noun, verb, adjective, or adverb? This narrows the possible meanings sharply. Step three: look for clue words listed above and make a tentative guess in simple language. Step four: test your guess by putting it back into the sentence. If the sentence still makes sense and fits the paragraph, your guess is good enough to continue.

If the sentence still sounds wrong, try another guess or keep reading. Later sentences often confirm or correct an early guess. In an examination, mark the word lightly and move on. You can return after answering easier questions. Never spend five minutes on one word while other marks wait. A good guess plus continued reading beats a perfect definition that costs you the whole passage.

diagram.alt: Guess an Unknown Word in Four Steps
diagram.caption: Use this routine every time you meet a hard word.

sections.h2: Worked Example: Guessing Without a Dictionary
paras: Consider this sentence: The river was so polluted that the villagers could no longer drink from it, and fish began to vanish. If polluted is new to you, the result clause gives the meaning away. Water you cannot drink, where fish vanish, is dirty or contaminated. You do not need an exact dictionary definition to answer a question about why the villagers were worried. Dirty water is close enough.

Now consider a contrast example: Unlike her timid brother, Ayesha was bold and spoke first in every discussion. Even if bold is unfamiliar, unlike and timid tell you it means the opposite of shy. Practise spotting these patterns in your textbook. Underline the clue word, write your guess in the margin, and check it later with a dictionary. Over time you will notice that the same clue patterns appear again and again, and guessing becomes fast and natural.

sections.h2: Building Vocabulary After You Guess
paras: Guessing is only the first step. To keep the word, record it in a vocabulary notebook with the sentence where you met it, your guess, and the dictionary meaning. Review the notebook weekly and try to use two or three new words in your own writing. A word you use in a sentence of your own is far more likely to stay in memory than a word you only read.

Read a little every day, even ten minutes of English stories, news, or textbook passages. Wide reading exposes you to the same words in different contexts, which deepens understanding. When you meet a word a second or third time, your guess becomes knowledge. For related English skills, see [conditional sentences](/blog/english-conditional-sentences-types.html) and [idioms and phrasal verbs](/blog/english-idioms-phrasal-verbs-daily.html), or browse solved notes on the [solved books page](/solved.html).

points: Use surrounding sentences to infer meaning instead of stopping at hard words.
Look for definition, example, contrast, cause-effect, and word-part clues.
Identify the part of speech before guessing.
Test every guess by putting it back into the sentence.
Record guessed words with their sentences to build lasting vocabulary.

faqs.q: What if my guess is wrong?
faqs.a: A close guess is often enough to follow the passage and answer questions. Keep reading, because later sentences may correct you. Check the exact meaning afterwards with a dictionary.

faqs.q: Should I guess or skip the word?
faqs.a: Guess, then keep reading. Skipping entirely loses information, while a tentative guess keeps you moving. Mark the word and return to it if time allows.

faqs.q: How can I get better at guessing?
faqs.a: Practise daily with short passages. Underline clue words, write margin guesses, and check them. Over weeks you will recognise clue patterns quickly.

faqs.q: Does guessing help in exams?
faqs.a: Yes. Dictionaries are not allowed in most exams, so context guessing is the only way to handle unknown words. It also saves time for the questions that carry marks.

title: Direct and Indirect Speech Rules Made Clear
desc: Master direct and indirect speech with clear tense, pronoun, and time-word shifts, plus a conversion table and short practice sentences.
intro: Direct speech reports the exact words someone said, inside quotation marks. Indirect speech reports the meaning without quoting, usually after verbs such as said and told. The direct indirect speech rules clear learners need are really a small set of shifts: pronouns change, tenses move one step back, and time and place words adjust. Once you see the pattern, conversion becomes mechanical and fast. This guide explains each shift with simple examples, gives you a conversion table to memorise, and shows how questions, commands, and requests change. You will also learn the exceptions where tense does not shift, which are the traps that cost marks in examinations. Practise the method here and you will convert sentences confidently instead of guessing.

sections.h2: Direct Speech Versus Indirect Speech
paras: In direct speech we write the speaker's exact words. For example: Ali said, I am busy today. The words inside the quotation marks are exactly what Ali said. In indirect speech we report the same idea without quoting: Ali said that he was busy that day. Notice three changes. I became he, am became was, and today became that day. These are the three families of change you must track every time.

Indirect speech usually introduces the reported clause with that after said or told. Remember the difference between said and told: we say something, but we tell someone something. So we write He said that he was tired, but He told me that he was tired. Getting this small verb choice right makes your reported speech sound natural and correct.

sections.h2: Tense Shifts: The One-Step-Back Rule
paras: When the reporting verb is in the past tense, the reported verb usually moves one step back in time. Present simple becomes past simple, present continuous becomes past continuous, present perfect becomes past perfect, and past simple becomes past perfect. For example, I play becomes he played, I am playing becomes he was playing, and I have played becomes he had played. Future forms also shift: will becomes would, and can becomes could.

There are two important exceptions. If the reported statement is a universal truth or a fact that is still true, the tense often stays the same. For example, She said that the sun rises in the east keeps present tense because it is always true. Similarly, if the reporting verb is in the present tense, such as He says or She has said, the reported tense usually does not shift. Learn these exceptions carefully because examiners love to test them.

diagram.alt: Tense Shift Table for Indirect Speech
diagram.caption: Move each tense one step back when the reporting verb is past.

sections.h2: Pronouns, Time Words, and Place Words
paras: Pronouns change according to who is speaking and who is listening. The first person in direct speech becomes the third person in indirect speech when reporting someone else's words. For example, I and my become he and his, or she and her. The second person, you, becomes the person spoken to. For example, if Sara tells Ali, You are kind, the report is Sara told Ali that he was kind. Always ask: who said it, and to whom?

Time and place words also shift because the report happens later and elsewhere. Today becomes that day, tomorrow becomes the next day, yesterday becomes the previous day, now becomes then, here becomes there, and ago becomes before. For example, I met him here yesterday becomes He said that he had met him there the previous day. Keep a short list of these shifts in your notebook and check them every time you convert a sentence.
bullets: I, my, we -> he, his, they, their depending on the speaker.
You, your -> the person spoken to.
Today, tomorrow, yesterday -> that day, the next day, the previous day.
Now, here, ago -> then, there, before.

sections.h2: Questions, Commands, and Requests
paras: Questions change differently from statements. Yes-no questions use if or whether instead of that. For example, Are you ready? becomes He asked if I was ready. Wh-questions keep their question word: Where do you live? becomes He asked where I lived. Notice that reported questions use statement word order, not question word order, and they do not end with a question mark when reported as a statement.

Commands and requests use the infinitive with to. A positive command becomes told plus to plus verb: Close the door becomes He told me to close the door. A negative command uses not to: Do not run becomes He told me not to run. Requests often use asked instead of told: Please help me becomes He asked me to help him. Practise these patterns separately, because mixing them is a common source of errors.

sections.h2: A Quick Practice Method
paras: Use a four-check routine for every conversion. First, choose said, told, or asked correctly. Second, shift pronouns. Third, shift the tense one step back unless an exception applies. Fourth, shift time and place words. Then read your sentence aloud and ask whether it still means the same as the original. If it does, you are done.

Practise with five sentences a day from your textbook, and keep a list of your errors. Most pupils find that pronoun shifts and time-word shifts improve fastest with short daily practice. For related grammar, see [active and passive voice](/blog/english-active-passive-voice-method.html) and [conditional sentences](/blog/english-conditional-sentences-types.html), or browse solved notes on the [solved books page](/solved.html).

points: Indirect speech reports meaning without quotation marks.
Tenses usually move one step back when the reporting verb is past.
Pronouns change according to speaker and listener.
Time and place words shift: today, tomorrow, here, now.
Questions use if, whether, or a wh-word with statement word order.

faqs.q: When does tense not shift in indirect speech?
faqs.a: Tense stays the same for universal truths and when the reporting verb is present, such as says or has said. It also stays when the reported fact is still true and the reporter wants to stress that.

faqs.q: What is the difference between said and told?
faqs.a: Say does not take a person as object: He said that he was tired. Tell takes a person: He told me that he was tired. Use told when you name the listener.

faqs.q: How do I report a yes-no question?
faqs.a: Use if or whether and statement word order. Are you coming? becomes He asked if I was coming. Do not keep the question mark or the question word order.

faqs.q: How do I report a command?
faqs.a: Use told plus to plus the verb. Close the window becomes He told me to close the window. For a negative command, use not to: Do not shout becomes He told me not to shout.

title: Active and Passive Voice: A Conversion Method
desc: Learn active to passive conversion with a clear object-to-subject method, tense checks, and alerts for the most common errors.
intro: In active voice, the subject does the action: The boy kicked the ball. In passive voice, the subject receives the action: The ball was kicked by the boy. The active passive voice conversion method taught here is simple: move the object to the front, use the correct form of be plus past participle, and move the subject to a by phrase or drop it. This guide walks you through that method for every tense, shows when the passive is better than the active, and warns you about the errors pupils make most often. Once you master the pattern, conversion becomes a quick mechanical task rather than a guessing game.

sections.h2: What Active and Passive Voice Mean
paras: Active voice is direct and energetic. It tells you who did what: The teacher checked the homework. Passive voice shifts attention to the action or the receiver: The homework was checked by the teacher. Both are correct, but they serve different purposes. Active voice suits stories and clear instructions. Passive voice suits reports, science descriptions, and situations where the doer is unknown, unimportant, or obvious.

In examinations, you are often asked to convert one form to the other. The key insight is that the object of the active sentence becomes the subject of the passive sentence. The verb changes to be plus past participle, and the active subject moves to the end with by, or disappears if it adds nothing. For example, Someone stole my bicycle becomes My bicycle was stolen, where someone is dropped because it carries no useful information.

sections.h2: The Three-Step Conversion Method
paras: Step one: find the object of the active sentence and move it to the front. In The dog chased the cat, the object is the cat, so the passive begins The cat. Step two: choose the correct form of be for the tense, then add the past participle of the main verb. Chased is past simple, so the passive verb is was chased. Step three: add by plus the old subject if it matters, or leave it out if it does not. The full passive is The cat was chased by the dog.

This method works for every tense if you choose the be form correctly. Present simple uses is or are, past simple uses was or were, present continuous uses is being or are being, past continuous uses was being or were being, present perfect uses has been or have been, past perfect uses had been, and future uses will be. Memorise this be ladder and conversion becomes straightforward. For more grammar practice, see [direct and indirect speech](/blog/english-direct-indirect-speech-rules.html) and [conditional sentences](/blog/english-conditional-sentences-types.html).

diagram.alt: Active to Passive in Three Steps
diagram.caption: Apply these steps in order for every tense.

sections.h2: Tense Checks: Matching Be to the Original
paras: The most common conversion error is a tense mismatch. If the active sentence is in present continuous, the passive must also be present continuous. She is writing a letter becomes A letter is being written by her, not A letter is written by her. If the active is present perfect, the passive keeps perfect meaning: They have finished the work becomes The work has been finished. Always ask what tense the active verb is before you choose the be form.

Modal verbs follow the same pattern with be plus past participle. Can, could, must, should, and will become can be, could be, must be, should be, and will be. For example, You must submit the form becomes The form must be submitted. Notice that the modal stays the same and only be plus participle is added. Practise one tense at a time until the pattern feels automatic, then mix tenses for revision.
bullets: Present simple: The teacher checks homework -> Homework is checked.
Past simple: The teacher checked homework -> Homework was checked.
Present perfect: The teacher has checked homework -> Homework has been checked.
Future: The teacher will check homework -> Homework will be checked.

sections.h2: Common Errors and How to Avoid Them
paras: One frequent error is keeping two objects or dropping the wrong one. With verbs that take two objects, such as give, send, and show, either object can become the subject. They gave Ali a prize becomes Ali was given a prize or A prize was given to Ali. Both are correct, so choose the version that sounds natural.

Another error is using the passive for intransitive verbs, which have no object. Verbs such as sleep, arrive, and go cannot be made passive because there is nothing to move to the front. A sentence like He slept cannot become a passive. A third error is adding by with an unnatural doer. The ball was kicked by someone sounds awkward; The ball was kicked is better. Drop the by-phrase when the doer is unknown, obvious, or unimportant.

sections.h2: When to Choose Passive Over Active
paras: Use passive when the receiver matters more than the doer. In science, we write The solution was heated because who heated it does not matter. In news, we write Three roads were closed because the closure matters more than who closed them. In formal reports, passive sounds objective and measured. In stories and personal writing, active usually sounds livelier and clearer.

Good writers choose voice deliberately, not by habit. If your paragraph is full of passive sentences, try converting some to active to add energy. If your report sounds too personal, convert some active sentences to passive to sound objective. For more English writing, see [writing a formal email](/blog/english-email-formal-writing.html) and [building arguments](/blog/english-debate-argument-building.html), or explore solved notes on the [books page](/books.html).

points: Passive moves the object to subject position with be plus past participle.
Match the be form to the original tense every time.
Drop the by-phrase when the doer is unknown or unimportant.
Intransitive verbs with no object cannot become passive.
Choose passive for reports and science; active for stories and energy.

faqs.q: What is the passive of She is reading a book?
faqs.a: A book is being read by her. The tense is present continuous, so the passive uses is being plus the past participle read.

faqs.q: Can every active sentence become passive?
faqs.a: No. Only sentences with an object can become passive. Intransitive verbs like sleep, arrive, and go have no object, so they have no passive form.

faqs.q: When should I drop the by-phrase?
faqs.a: Drop it when the doer is unknown, obvious, or unimportant. My bicycle was stolen is better than My bicycle was stolen by someone.

faqs.q: How do modals change in passive?
faqs.a: The modal stays the same and you add be plus past participle. Must do becomes must be done, can see becomes can be seen, and will finish becomes will be finished.

title: Conditional Sentences: Types and Uses in English
desc: Understand zero, first, second, and third conditionals with real situations, clear verb patterns, and practice examples.
intro: Conditional sentences describe what happens if something else happens. The conditional sentences types uses English learners need are four: zero, first, second, and third. Each type pairs a different if-clause with a different result clause, and each expresses a different degree of reality, from always true to impossible. This guide explains all four types through real situations pupils recognise — weather, exams, health, and daily choices — so the verb patterns feel logical rather than memorised. You will learn which tense goes in each clause, when you can swap the clauses, and which mistakes to avoid. By the end you will be able to choose the right conditional for the meaning you want.

sections.h2: What Makes a Conditional Sentence
paras: A conditional sentence has two parts: the if-clause, which states the condition, and the main clause, which states the result. For example, in If it rains, we will stay at home, the if-clause is If it rains and the result is we will stay at home. The two clauses can swap order. We will stay at home if it rains means the same thing, but note that the comma disappears when the if-clause comes second.

The verb tenses in the two clauses are linked. You cannot mix them freely. Each conditional type has its own pair of tenses, and choosing the wrong pair changes the meaning or makes the sentence incorrect. The trick is to first decide how real the condition is, then pick the type that matches that reality. Is it always true, likely in the future, unlikely or imaginary, or impossible in the past?

sections.h2: Zero and First Conditionals: Real Situations
paras: Zero conditional describes facts and habits that are always true. Both clauses use present simple. If you heat water, it boils. If the bell rings, pupils stand. Use zero conditional for scientific truths, rules, and routines. It answers the question: what always happens?

First conditional describes a likely future result. The if-clause uses present simple and the main clause uses will plus verb. If you study tonight, you will pass the test. If it rains tomorrow, we will cancel the match. Even though the meaning is future, the if-clause stays in present simple. A common mistake is writing If you will study, which is incorrect in standard conditionals. Keep will out of the if-clause.

diagram.alt: Four Conditional Types at a Glance
diagram.caption: Match the verb pair to how real the condition is.

sections.h2: Second Conditional: Imaginary Present and Future
paras: Second conditional describes imaginary, unlikely, or dream situations in the present or future. The if-clause uses past simple and the main clause uses would plus verb. If I had a bicycle, I would ride to school. If she were taller, she would join the team. The past tense here does not mean past time; it signals distance from reality. That is why we say If I were you, not If I was you, in careful English, though was is common in informal speech.

Use second conditional for advice, wishes, and hypothetical choices. If I were you, I would apologise is classic advice. If we had more books, we would read more is a wish about the present. Pupils often confuse second conditional with past time. Remember: the past verb form expresses unreality, not past time. The time is present or future, but the situation is imagined.

sections.h2: Third Conditional: Impossible Past
paras: Third conditional describes past situations that cannot be changed. The if-clause uses past perfect and the main clause uses would have plus past participle. If I had studied harder, I would have passed. If we had left earlier, we would not have missed the bus. Both clauses look back at a past that is already fixed, so the sentence expresses regret, relief, or explanation rather than a plan.

Third conditional is common in reflections and stories. It answers the question: what would have happened differently? Notice the difference from second conditional. If I studied harder, I would pass talks about a present habit and a future result. If I had studied harder, I would have passed talks about a past exam that is already over. Keep the had and have forms in the right clauses: had goes in the if-clause, would have goes in the result.
bullets: Zero: always true, present plus present.
First: likely future, present plus will.
Second: imaginary present, past plus would.
Third: impossible past, past perfect plus would have.

sections.h2: Choosing the Right Conditional in Practice
paras: Before you write, ask two questions. First, is the time present, future, or past? Second, is the condition real, possible, imaginary, or impossible? If the condition is always true, use zero. If it is likely in the future, use first. If it is imaginary now, use second. If it is impossible in the past, use third. This two-question check prevents most errors.

Practise by turning one situation into all four types. Take studying: If you study, you learn; If you study tonight, you will pass; If you studied every day, you would top the class; If you had studied last term, you would have passed. Seeing the same idea in four forms makes the pattern clear. For more grammar, see [direct and indirect speech](/blog/english-direct-indirect-speech-rules.html) and [active and passive voice](/blog/english-active-passive-voice-method.html), or find solved notes on the [solved books page](/solved.html).

points: Zero conditional: always true, present plus present.
First conditional: likely future, present plus will.
Second conditional: imaginary present, past plus would.
Third conditional: impossible past, past perfect plus would have.
Keep will and would out of the if-clause in standard conditionals.

faqs.q: Can the if-clause come second?
faqs.a: Yes. We will stay at home if it rains means the same as If it rains, we will stay at home. When the if-clause comes second, do not use a comma.

faqs.q: Why do we use past tense in second conditional?
faqs.a: The past form signals unreality, not past time. If I had money, I would help talks about an imagined present, not about yesterday.

faqs.q: What is the difference between first and second conditional?
faqs.a: First conditional is a likely future: If you study, you will pass. Second conditional is imaginary: If you studied every day, you would top the class. The first is possible; the second is a dream or unlikely case.

faqs.q: Can I use unless instead of if not?
faqs.a: Yes. Unless means if not. Unless you hurry, you will miss the bus means If you do not hurry, you will miss the bus. Do not add not after unless.

title: Idioms and Phrasal Verbs for Daily English
desc: Learn twenty high-frequency phrasal verbs and everyday idioms with dialogues you can reuse in school, home, and exam writing.
intro: Native speakers use phrasal verbs and idioms constantly, often without noticing. The idioms phrasal verbs daily English pupils need most are not rare or literary; they are the everyday expressions for starting, stopping, continuing, giving up, and getting along. This guide introduces twenty high-frequency phrasal verbs with short dialogues you can reuse, explains how phrasal verbs are built, and shows how to use idioms safely without sounding forced. You will learn the difference between separable and inseparable phrasal verbs, why literal translation fails, and how to practise a few expressions at a time so they stay in your active vocabulary.

sections.h2: What Phrasal Verbs Are and How They Work
paras: A phrasal verb is a verb plus a particle, usually a preposition or adverb, that together make a new meaning. Look up does not mean to look in an upward direction; it means to search for information. Give up does not mean to give something upward; it means to stop trying. The particle changes the verb completely, so you must learn the combination as one unit, not as two separate words.

Some phrasal verbs are separable: you can put the object between the verb and the particle. Turn off the light and Turn the light off are both correct. Others are inseparable: the object must come after the whole phrase. Look after the children is correct, but Look the children after is wrong. When you learn a new phrasal verb, always note whether it is separable and whether it takes an object. That small note prevents many errors.

sections.h2: Twenty Phrasal Verbs for Daily Use
paras: Here are twenty expressions worth mastering first: wake up, get up, put on, take off, look for, look after, turn on, turn off, pick up, drop off, set up, clean up, give up, carry on, find out, work out, run out of, catch up, slow down, and hang out. Each one appears in daily conversation. I need to find out the homework. We ran out of sugar. Please slow down and explain again. Learning these twenty gives you coverage for a large share of everyday talk.

Do not try to memorise all twenty in one sitting. Learn five at a time, use each one in two sentences of your own, and review them the next day. Group them by situation: morning routine, school, home, and free time. For example, morning routine gives wake up, get up, put on, and set off. School gives catch up, work out, find out, and hand in. Grouping by situation makes recall easier because the words are linked to a real scene.
bullets: Morning: wake up, get up, put on, set off.
School: catch up, work out, find out, hand in.
Home: clean up, turn off, look after, pick up.
Plans: give up, carry on, run out of, slow down.

sections.h2: Short Dialogues You Can Reuse
paras: Dialogue one, at home: Did you turn off the fan? Yes, I turned it off before leaving. Dialogue two, at school: I missed yesterday. Do not worry, we will help you catch up. Dialogue three, with a friend: I cannot work out this sum. Let us look at it together and find out where it went wrong. Notice how each dialogue uses the phrasal verb in a natural, short exchange. That is how you should practise: in two-line dialogues, not in isolated lists.

Try writing your own dialogues for five phrasal verbs each week. Keep them short and realistic. Act them out with a partner if you can. Speaking an expression aloud fixes it in memory far better than silent reading. For more speaking and writing practice, see [writing natural dialogue](/blog/english-dialogue-writing-natural-speech.html) and [story writing](/blog/english-story-writing-plot-structure.html).

diagram.caption: One day, many phrasal verbs in natural order.

sections.h2: Idioms: Use a Few, Use Them Well
paras: An idiom is a fixed expression whose meaning cannot be guessed from its words. A piece of cake means something easy, not a slice of cake. Break the ice means to ease awkwardness at the start of a meeting, not to smash ice. Idioms add colour, but they are risky. Used wrongly, they confuse the reader. Used too often, they make writing sound artificial.

The safe rule is to learn idioms in context and use only the ones you are sure about. Start with five reliable idioms: a piece of cake, under the weather, once in a blue moon, cost an arm and a leg, and on cloud nine. Use each one in a full sentence and check that the situation fits. In examinations, one well-placed idiom is better than five forced ones. Clarity always beats decoration.

sections.h2: How to Practise Without Mixing Meanings
paras: Keep a small notebook with three columns: phrasal verb or idiom, meaning in simple English, and a sentence of your own. Review it for five minutes a day. When you meet a new expression in reading, add it to the notebook instead of trying to memorise it on the spot. Test yourself by covering the meaning and recalling it from the sentence.

Avoid translating literally from your first language. Many phrasal verbs have no direct equivalent, and literal translation produces errors. Learn the English meaning through an English example. If you are unsure, check a learner dictionary that gives example sentences. For more English help, browse the [books page](/books.html) and the [solved books page](/solved.html).

points: A phrasal verb is a verb plus particle with a new combined meaning.
Learn whether each phrasal verb is separable or inseparable.
Master twenty daily phrasal verbs before learning rare ones.
Practise in short two-line dialogues, not isolated lists.
Use idioms sparingly and only when you are sure of the meaning.

faqs.q: What is the difference between look for and look after?
faqs.a: Look for means to search for something: I am looking for my book. Look after means to take care of someone: She looks after her younger brother.

faqs.q: Can I put the object between the verb and particle?
faqs.a: Only for separable phrasal verbs. Turn off the light and Turn the light off are both correct. For inseparable verbs like look after, the object must come after the whole phrase.

faqs.q: How many idioms should I use in an essay?
faqs.a: One or two well-placed idioms are enough. Too many idioms make writing sound forced. Clarity and correct grammar matter more than decoration.

faqs.q: Why does literal translation fail for idioms?
faqs.a: Idioms have a fixed figurative meaning that is not the sum of their words. A piece of cake means easy, not a slice of cake. Learn idioms through English examples, not word-by-word translation.

title: Story Writing in English: Plot Structure for Pupils
desc: Build better English stories with a simple plot structure: hook, problem, turning point, and resolution, plus a planning sheet.
kw: story writing English plot structure pupils
intro: Good stories are not accidents. The story writing English plot structure pupils can rely on has four clear parts: a hook that pulls the reader in, a problem that creates tension, a turning point where things change, and a resolution that satisfies the reader. This guide shows you how to build each part, how to plan a story before you write, and how to avoid the two most common faults: a story that wanders without a problem, and a story that ends suddenly without a resolution. You will also learn how to create characters readers care about, how to show rather than tell, and how to finish on time in an examination. With a simple planning sheet and a little practice, story writing becomes a skill you can repeat, not a mystery you hope for.

sections.h2: The Four Parts of a Simple Plot
paras: A hook is an opening that makes the reader want to continue. It can be a surprising event, a question, a vivid scene, or a line of dialogue. On the morning of the exam, Sara found an empty school is a hook because it raises a question: why is the school empty? A weak opening, such as One day there was a boy, gives the reader no reason to continue.

After the hook comes the problem: something goes wrong or someone wants something they cannot easily get. Then comes the turning point, the moment where the character makes a choice or discovers something that changes the direction of the story. Finally, the resolution shows the result of that choice. A complete story needs all four parts. If any part is missing, the reader feels that something is unfinished.

sections.h2: Planning Before You Write
paras: Spend five minutes planning before you write a single story sentence. Write one line for each part: hook, problem, turning point, resolution. Add two lines about your main character: what they want, and what stops them. Add one line about the setting: where and when the story happens. This seven-line plan is enough to guide a story of 200 to 300 words.

Planning saves time because it prevents mid-story confusion. Pupils who skip planning often reach the middle and realise they have no idea how the story should end, so they invent a sudden ending. Pupils who plan finish faster and write more coherent stories. Keep your plan beside your answer sheet and tick off each part as you write it. For dialogue inside stories, see [writing natural dialogue](/blog/english-dialogue-writing-natural-speech.html).

diagram.caption: Fill these four boxes before you start writing.

sections.h2: Characters Readers Care About
paras: Readers care about characters who want something and face a difficulty. Give your main character one clear want and one clear obstacle. A pupil who wants to win a race but has injured his leg is more interesting than a pupil who has no goal at all. You do not need long descriptions. Two or three well-chosen details — age, habit, fear, or kindness — are enough.

Show character through action and dialogue rather than telling the reader. Instead of writing Ali was brave, show Ali stepping forward when others stepped back. Instead of writing Sara was kind, show her sharing her lunch with a new pupil. Showing takes slightly more words but creates a far stronger impression, and it is one of the clearest differences between average and good story writing.

sections.h2: Show, Do Not Tell, and Keep the Pace Moving
paras: Showing means using senses, actions, and dialogue to let the reader experience the scene. His hands shook as he opened the envelope shows fear better than He was afraid. The classroom smelled of rain and wet books places the reader in the scene. Use one or two sensory details per scene, not a paragraph of description that stops the story.

Keep the pace moving by cutting scenes that do not advance the problem. If a paragraph could be removed without changing the story, remove it. Short sentences speed up tense moments. Longer sentences suit calm description. Vary sentence length deliberately. A story that moves steadily from hook to resolution feels satisfying, while a story that stalls in description feels slow even if the language is beautiful.
bullets: One clear want plus one clear obstacle per main character.
Show feelings through action, dialogue, and senses.
Cut any paragraph that does not move the problem forward.
Use short sentences for tension and longer ones for calm scenes.

sections.h2: Endings That Satisfy the Reader
paras: A good ending resolves the central problem and gives the reader a closing feeling. It does not need a moral lecture or a sudden twist. The character learns something, solves the problem, or accepts the outcome. Avoid endings such as And then I woke up, which cancel the whole story, and avoid endings that introduce a new problem in the last line. The reader should feel that the story is complete.

Leave three minutes at the end to check your story. Does it have all four parts? Does the turning point connect to the resolution? Is the tense consistent? Are names and spellings consistent? A short check catches the errors that cost easy marks. For more English writing, see [building arguments](/blog/english-debate-argument-building.html) and the [solved books page](/solved.html).

points: Every story needs hook, problem, turning point, and resolution.
Plan seven lines before writing: four plot parts plus character and setting.
Give the main character one want and one obstacle.
Show feelings through action, dialogue, and senses.
End by resolving the central problem, not by waking up.

faqs.q: How long should my story be?
faqs.a: Follow your exam instruction, often 200 to 300 words. Plan to fit the length: a short story needs one problem and one turning point, not three subplots.

faqs.q: What makes a good hook?
faqs.a: A surprising event, a question, a vivid scene, or a line of dialogue. A good hook raises a question the reader wants answered.

faqs.q: Should I write a moral at the end?
faqs.a: A short closing reflection is fine, but avoid a long lecture. Let the resolution show the lesson through what the character does or learns.

faqs.q: How do I avoid running out of time?
faqs.a: Plan for five minutes, write steadily, and leave three minutes to check. If you plan first, you will rarely get stuck in the middle.

title: Writing Natural Dialogue in English
desc: Make written dialogue sound real with short exchanges, varied tags, pauses, and speech habits that fit each character.
intro: Dialogue in stories and plays should sound like people talking, not like an essay read aloud. The writing natural dialogue English pupils need is built on short exchanges, varied speech tags, pauses, and small habits that fit each character. Real people interrupt, hesitate, repeat themselves, and answer questions with questions. Written dialogue should suggest that natural rhythm without copying every um and ah. This guide shows you how to punctuate dialogue correctly, how to choose tags, how to give each character a distinct voice, and how to use dialogue to move the plot forward instead of filling space. With practice, your characters will start to sound like real people.

sections.h2: What Makes Dialogue Sound Real
