You may also be asked for passport-size photographs. Requirements vary: some colleges ask for a small number, others for more, and some specify a background colour or a recent date. Get your photographs taken early so you are not rushing on admission day, and keep a few spares in your folder.
bullets: Your identity card or child registration certificate, original and copies.
A parent or guardian's identity document, if the college asks for it.
Passport-size photographs, as many as the college requires, plus spares.
Any domicile or residence proof the college lists, if applicable.

sections.h2: Academic Records: Marksheets and Certificates
paras: Your academic records are the heart of the admission file. Colleges typically ask for your latest marksheet and certificate, and sometimes for earlier records as well. Bring the originals, and carry several clear photocopies of each. If your result is recent and the certificate has not yet been issued, ask your school what interim proof the college accepts.

If you are moving between boards, the college may also ask for a migration certificate or a school leaving certificate. These take time to obtain, so apply for them as soon as you know you will move. Keep a scanned copy of every academic document in a safe place before you hand anything over, and always ask for a receipt for originals you submit.
bullets: Latest marksheet, original and several photocopies.
Latest certificate, original and copies, if issued.
School leaving or transfer certificate, if the college asks for it.
Migration certificate, if you are moving between boards.
Earlier records, if the college's list includes them.

sections.h2: Forms, Undertakings, and Category Documents
paras: Admission usually involves more than certificates. You will typically fill in an admission form, and you may be asked to sign an undertaking about attendance, conduct, or fee payment. Read every form before you sign it, and keep a copy of anything you submit. If a form asks for information you do not have, ask the college office rather than guessing. Once admitted, the [solved notes](/solved.html) can help you start your new subjects with confidence.

Some pupils apply under a particular category or quota, such as a reserved seat, a scholarship, or a sports or disability category. If that applies to you, gather the supporting documents for that category well in advance, because they often need verification or a certificate from a specific authority. Confirm exactly what the college requires for your category.
bullets: Completed admission form, filled in carefully and completely.
Undertaking or declaration forms, read before signing.
Category or quota documents, if you are applying under one.
Fee payment proof or challan, as the college requires.

diagram.alt: The Admission Folder at a Glance
diagram.caption: One folder, four sections: identity, academic records, forms, and spares — so nothing is missed at the counter.

sections.h2: The Night Before: Pack and Double-Check
paras: The night before admission, lay out everything and check it against the college's list, item by item. Put originals in one section of your folder and photocopies in another, so you can hand over copies without mixing them up. Pack extra photocopies, extra photographs, a pen, and a small amount of cash or a payment method in case a fee or a photocopy is needed on the spot.

Also check the practical details: the college's opening time, the admission counter location, and the transport you will use. Arriving early usually means a shorter queue and calmer staff. If you are unsure about anything, it is better to arrive with a question than to arrive without a document. Good planning is a habit — see [how to finish the syllabus in 30 days](/blog/how-to-finish-syllabus-in-30-days.html) for how a simple plan keeps work on track.

sections.h2: At the Counter: Stay Calm and Keep Records
paras: At the counter, listen carefully, answer honestly, and ask for clarification if a question confuses you. If the officer says a document is missing, ask whether it can be submitted later and get the answer in writing if possible. Do not argue, and do not hand over originals without a receipt.

Once admission is confirmed, note down your admission number, class, and section, and keep the receipt safely. Before you leave, ask what happens next: when classes begin, whether an orientation is scheduled, and whether any further documents are needed. A calm, organised admission day sets the tone for your first weeks at college. For what comes after the result, see [next steps after the matric science result](/blog/after-matric-science-result-college-admission-next-steps.html).

points: Always start from the college's own admission list — it is the one that matters.
Carry originals and photocopies in separate sections of one folder.
Check that names and dates match across identity and board documents.
Gather category, quota, and fee documents well in advance.
Pack spares — extra copies, extra photos, and a pen — the night before.

faqs.q: Should I bring originals or photocopies to college admission?
faqs.a: Usually both. Colleges typically want to see originals and keep photocopies. Carry several clear photocopies of each document, and always ask for a receipt for any original you hand over.

faqs.q: What if my certificate has not been issued yet?
faqs.a: Ask your school what interim proof the college accepts, such as a marksheet or a verification letter. Explain the situation to the college office honestly and confirm whether the certificate can be submitted later.

faqs.q: Do I need a migration certificate for college admission?
faqs.a: It depends on the college and the board. If you are moving between boards or joining an institution under a different board, the college may ask for one. Confirm the requirement with the college, and apply early because it takes time.

faqs.q: What if a document is missing on admission day?
faqs.a: Stay calm and ask the counter whether it can be submitted later. Get the answer in writing if possible, and submit the missing document as soon as you can. A polite question is always better than an argument.

faqs.q: How many photographs should I bring?
faqs.a: Bring at least as many as the college's list requires, plus a few spares. Photograph requirements vary, so check the college's notice for the number, size, and any background or recency rules.

title: Pre-Medical or Pre-Engineering in Class 11: How to Decide
desc: Choosing between pre-medical and pre-engineering in Class 11? Compare subjects, strengths, workload, and future paths.
intro:
Class 11 is the first time many pupils must choose a direction that genuinely shapes their future. The choice between pre-medical and pre-engineering is one of the biggest decisions of school life, and it often comes with pressure from family, friends, and teachers. Both groups are respected, both lead to real careers, and both demand hard work. The right choice is not the one that sounds most impressive — it is the one that fits your interests, your strengths, and the kind of work you want to do.

This article compares the two groups by subjects, skills, workload, and future options, and offers a calm framework for deciding. It does not tell you which group to pick, and it does not promise any career outcome. The decision is yours, and it should be made with honest information, not with pressure.

sections.h2: What Each Group Actually Studies
paras: Both groups share several subjects. Pupils in both study Urdu, English, Islamic Studies or Ethics, and Pakistan Studies, along with Mathematics in pre-engineering and a different combination in pre-medical. The defining difference is in the science core: pre-medical centres on Biology and Chemistry, while pre-engineering centres on Mathematics, Physics, and Chemistry.

That difference shapes daily life. A pre-medical pupil spends a great deal of time on living systems — cells, organs, plants, and the human body — and on memorising and understanding biological processes. A pre-engineering pupil spends more time on problem-solving: applying formulas, working through numerical problems, and building mathematical models of physical situations. Neither is easier; they are hard in different ways.

sections.h2: Pre-Medical: Who It Suits
paras: Pre-medical suits pupils who are curious about life, health, and the human body, and who enjoy careful, detailed study. It rewards patience, strong memory, and the ability to connect concepts across chapters — for example, linking cell structure to organ function to whole-body systems. Pupils who enjoy reading, making diagrams, and explaining processes in words often feel at home here.

It also suits pupils who can see themselves working with people in caring roles. The classic destinations are medicine, dentistry, pharmacy, nursing, physiotherapy, and allied health fields, along with biological and agricultural sciences. These paths are long and demanding, and they reward pupils who are motivated by helping others rather than by prestige alone.

sections.h2: Pre-Engineering: Who It Suits
paras: Pre-engineering suits pupils who enjoy mathematics, puzzles, and understanding how things work. It rewards logical thinking, comfort with numbers, and persistence through multi-step problems. Pupils who like building, fixing, designing, or taking things apart often find the group's way of thinking natural.

The classic destinations include civil, mechanical, electrical, and computer engineering, along with architecture, computing, and applied sciences. These paths reward pupils who enjoy turning ideas into working things — bridges, machines, circuits, software, and systems. Like medicine, engineering is a long road that rewards genuine interest more than fashion.

sections.h2: Workload and Study Style: An Honest Comparison
paras: Both groups are heavy. Pre-medical carries a large volume of content to learn and retain, with diagrams, terminology, and processes that must be accurate. Pre-engineering carries a large volume of practice, with numerical problems that require daily drilling to stay sharp. A pupil who dislikes memorisation will struggle in pre-medical; a pupil who dislikes daily numerical practice will struggle in pre-engineering.

The honest question is not which group is harder, but which kind of hard work you can sustain for two years. Think about the subjects where you currently do well without being forced, and about the homework you actually enjoy. That pattern is a better guide than anyone's opinion about which group is better.

diagram.caption: Both groups are demanding. The difference is the kind of hard work: content and diagrams versus problems and models.

sections.h2: A Decision Framework: Four Honest Questions
paras: Instead of asking which group is better, ask four personal questions. First, which subjects do I enjoy most, when nobody is watching? Second, where do my marks and my teachers' feedback point — not one test, but the pattern across Class 9 and 10? Third, what kind of work do I want to do every day — working with people and living systems, or working with machines, structures, and code? Fourth, am I choosing this, or am I being pushed toward it?

Discuss your answers with a teacher who knows your work, and with your parents, honestly. A teacher can tell you whether your interest in a subject is matched by the skills it requires. Your parents can tell you about practical matters such as costs and distance. But the final decision should be one you can own, because you are the one who will do the studying. Strong study habits matter in either group — see [how to get an A-plus in Sindh board exams](/blog/how-to-get-a-plus-sindh-board-exams.html).
bullets: Which science subjects do I genuinely enjoy?
What does my pattern of marks and teacher feedback show?
What kind of daily work do I want — people and living systems, or machines and code?
Am I choosing this freely, or under pressure?

sections.h2: Common Myths to Ignore
paras: Several myths surround this choice. One is that pre-medical is for toppers and pre-engineering is for the rest — false; both groups contain strong and weak pupils, and both demand excellence. Another is that one group guarantees a better future — false; both lead to respected careers, and both can lead to disappointment if chosen without interest. A third is that you can easily switch later without cost — switching is sometimes possible, but it usually means lost time and catching up on a year's syllabus, so it should not be the plan.

The most useful advice is simple: choose the group whose daily work you can sustain, and then commit to it fully. Two years of steady work in the right group beats two years of regret in the wrong one. If you want a wider view of stream choice, see our guide on [stream choice for Classes 11 and 12](/blog/class-11-12-stream-choice-science-commerce-arts.html), and browse the [books pages](/books.html) for your new subjects.

points: Pre-medical centres on Biology and Chemistry; pre-engineering centres on Mathematics, Physics, and Chemistry.
Choose by interest and strengths, not by prestige or pressure.
Pre-medical rewards memory, diagrams, and understanding living systems.
Pre-engineering rewards logic, numerical practice, and problem-solving.
Discuss the choice honestly with a teacher and your parents before deciding.

faqs.q: Which is harder: pre-medical or pre-engineering?
faqs.a: Both are demanding in different ways. Pre-medical carries a large volume of content, diagrams, and terminology to retain. Pre-engineering carries a large volume of numerical practice. The better question is which kind of hard work you can sustain for two years.

faqs.q: Can I switch groups after Class 11?
faqs.a: Switching is sometimes possible, but it usually means lost time and catching up on a year's syllabus in the new group's subjects. It should not be the plan. Choose carefully at the start, with honest advice from a teacher.

faqs.q: Does pre-medical only lead to becoming a doctor?
faqs.a: No. Pre-medical can lead to dentistry, pharmacy, nursing, physiotherapy, allied health fields, and biological and agricultural sciences, among others. Medicine is one destination, not the only one.

faqs.q: Does pre-engineering only lead to engineering?
faqs.a: No. Pre-engineering can lead to various engineering fields, architecture, computing, and applied sciences. The group's mathematics and physics foundation is useful across many technical careers.

faqs.q: What if my parents want one group and I want the other?
faqs.a: Have an honest conversation, ideally with a teacher present who knows your work. Share your interests, your marks pattern, and the kind of daily work each group involves. A decision made together, with facts, is easier to sustain than one made under pressure.

title: Science or Computer Science Group in Class 9: How to Decide
desc: Class 9 pupils choosing between the science and computer science groups can compare subjects, skills, and future options here.
kw: science computer science group class 9 decide
intro:
In Class 9, pupils in many schools must choose between the science group and the computer science group. The choice feels large, and it is — it shapes the subjects you study for two years, the skills you build, and the doors that open after matric. Yet many pupils choose on the basis of a friend's choice, a rumour about which group is easier, or pressure at home, without ever comparing the two properly.

This article compares the Class 9 science and computer science groups by subjects, skills, workload, and future options, and offers a practical way to decide. It does not declare a winner. The right group is the one that matches your interests, your strengths, and the kind of work you want to do next.

sections.h2: What the Two Groups Have in Common
paras: Both groups share a strong core. Pupils in both study Urdu, English, Islamiat or Ethics, Pakistan Studies, Mathematics, and Physics and Chemistry. The daily experience of school — the teachers, the timetable, the examination system — is largely the same. The choice is not between a hard group and an easy group; it is between two versions of a science education with different emphases.

Understanding this common core helps to calm the decision. Whichever group you choose, you will build a solid foundation in mathematics and science. The difference lies in the subjects that define each group and in the skills those subjects develop.

sections.h2: The Science Group: Biology at the Centre
paras: The science group centres on Biology alongside Physics and Chemistry. Pupils study living systems in detail — cells, plants, animals, and the human body — with diagrams, terminology, and processes that must be learned accurately. The group suits pupils who are curious about life and health, who enjoy reading and diagram work, and who can sustain careful revision over time.

The science group is the natural route toward pre-medical studies in Class 11, and it keeps the door open to health and life-science careers. It also keeps general science options open, because the mathematics and physics foundation remains strong. Pupils who already dream of medicine, nursing, pharmacy, or biological sciences usually find this group the natural fit.

sections.h2: The Computer Science Group: Computing at the Centre
paras: The computer science group replaces Biology with Computer Science. Pupils study how computers work, how data is stored and processed, and how to think in steps — the logical thinking behind programs and systems. The group suits pupils who enjoy computers, puzzles, and building things, and who like the feeling of making something work.

The computer science group is the natural route toward pre-engineering or computer science studies in Class 11, and it keeps the door open to computing, engineering, and technology careers. Pupils who enjoy using computers, who tinker with devices, or who are curious about how apps and systems work usually find this group the natural fit. A first taste of the subject's thinking style is in our guide to [flowcharts and algorithms basics](/blog/computer-flowcharts-algorithms-basics.html).

sections.h2: Skills Each Group Builds
paras: The science group builds careful observation, diagram and labelling skills, precise vocabulary, and the ability to explain living processes in order. These are the skills of the health and life sciences, and they reward patience and thorough revision.

The computer science group builds logical step-by-step thinking, comfort with systems and data, and the habit of testing and fixing errors. These are the skills of computing and engineering, and they reward persistence through trial and error. Neither set of skills is better; they are different, and they suit different minds. Think about which kind of task you enjoy: drawing and explaining a system, or building and debugging one.

diagram.alt: Science Group vs Computer Science Group
diagram.caption: Both groups share mathematics, physics, and chemistry. The defining subject — Biology or Computer Science — shapes the skills each builds.

sections.h2: Workload: An Honest Look
paras: Both groups are demanding. The science group's Biology carries a large amount of content to learn and retain, with diagrams that must be practised until they are accurate. The computer science group's computing content requires regular practice too — concepts that are not practised fade quickly, and practical work rewards pupils who sit down and try things rather than only reading about them.

The honest question is the same as for any stream choice: which kind of hard work can you sustain for two years? If you enjoy reading, drawing, and revising, the science group's workload may feel natural. If you enjoy experimenting, solving, and working with computers, the computer science group's workload may feel natural. Choose the work you can keep doing, not the work that sounds easiest.

sections.h2: How to Decide: Three Practical Steps
paras: First, look at your own record. Which subjects have you enjoyed and done well in during Classes 6 to 8 — life-science topics, or computer and logic topics? A pattern across several years is more reliable than a single test. Second, talk to a teacher who knows your work, and ask which group's daily demands match your strengths. Third, think about the future honestly: do you picture yourself in health or life sciences, or in computing and technology? You do not need a final career plan, but a general direction helps.

Finally, discuss the choice with your parents with facts on the table. Share what each group studies, what it leads toward, and why you lean one way. A decision made with information and agreement is far easier to sustain than one made under pressure. For a wider view of stream choice later on, see our guide on [stream choice for Classes 11 and 12](/blog/class-11-12-stream-choice-science-commerce-arts.html), and explore the [solved notes](/solved.html) for the subjects that interest you.
bullets: Review your pattern of interest and marks across Classes 6 to 8.
Ask a teacher which group's daily work matches your strengths.
Picture your general direction: life and health, or computing and technology.
Decide with your parents, using facts rather than rumours.

points: Both groups share Urdu, English, Islamiat, Pakistan Studies, Mathematics, Physics, and Chemistry.
The science group centres on Biology; the computer science group centres on Computer Science.
Science builds diagram, vocabulary, and process skills; computing builds logic and systems skills.
Choose by sustained interest and strengths, not by rumours about which group is easier.
Discuss the choice with a teacher and your parents, using facts.

faqs.q: Which group is easier: science or computer science?
faqs.a: Neither is generally easier. The science group's Biology carries a large amount of content and diagrams to retain, while the computer science group requires regular practice of concepts and practical work. Choose the kind of hard work you can sustain.

faqs.q: If I choose the computer science group, can I still go into medicine later?
faqs.a: In general, medical paths require Biology, so pupils aiming for medicine usually choose the science group. If medicine is your goal, discuss the requirements honestly with a teacher before choosing your Class 9 group.

faqs.q: If I choose the science group, can I still study computing later?
faqs.a: The science group keeps a strong mathematics and physics foundation, and many pupils develop computing interests alongside it. However, the computer science group gives a head start in computing. Discuss your goals with a teacher if you are torn.

faqs.q: Can I change groups after Class 9?
faqs.a: Changing groups later is sometimes possible but usually means catching up on a year's syllabus in the new group's defining subject. It should not be the plan. Choose carefully at the start.

faqs.q: What should I do if my friends all choose the other group?
faqs.a: Choose for yourself. Friends change classes, but your group shapes your subjects, skills, and future options for two years. A good friend will respect a decision made with honest thought.

title: Private vs Regular Candidates: What Is the Difference?
desc: Private and regular candidates sit the same exams but enrol differently. Learn how each route generally works.
kw: private vs regular candidates difference board
intro:
When board examination time approaches, pupils often hear two terms: regular candidate and private candidate. They sound like two different kinds of examination, but in most cases they describe two different routes to the same examination. Both kinds of candidates sit board papers, follow the board's rules, and receive board results. What differs is how they enrol, how they prepare, and what support surrounds them.

This article explains how private and regular candidacy generally differ in enrolment and examinations. Rules vary by board, class, and year, so always confirm the current requirements with your school or the board's official notification. This is a general guide, not the board's own rulebook.

sections.h2: What a Regular Candidate Is
paras: A regular candidate is a pupil who is enrolled in a recognised school or college and appears in the board examination through that institution. The school handles the admission and registration process, keeps the pupil's record, and usually provides teaching, attendance, and internal assessment. The pupil studies within the school's timetable and appears in the examination under the school's name.

For most pupils, this is the normal route. The school's structure — daily classes, homework, tests, and teacher guidance — carries a large part of the preparation. A regular candidate's main responsibility is to attend, study, and follow the school's process for forms, fees, and roll number slips.

sections.h2: What a Private Candidate Is
paras: A private candidate is a pupil who applies to the board directly, rather than through a school, under the board's private-candidacy rules. This route exists for pupils who are not enrolled in a regular institution — for example, pupils who studied at home, who left school, or who need to reappear in subjects after a gap. The board sets the eligibility conditions, and not every class or subject may be open to private candidates.

A private candidate takes on more responsibility. Without a school's daily structure, the pupil must organise their own study, track the board's announcements, and manage the application process personally. That independence suits some pupils and overwhelms others, so it should be chosen with open eyes.

sections.h2: Enrolment: The Key Difference
paras: The central difference is enrolment. A regular candidate's enrolment runs through the school: the school submits the admission forms, collects the fee, and issues the roll number slip. A private candidate's enrolment runs through the board's own private-candidate process: the pupil applies directly, submits the required documents, and receives the roll number slip from the board's prescribed channel.

Because the channels differ, the details differ too — the forms, the fee, the deadlines, and the documents required. Confirm the current process with your school or the board's official notification, whichever route applies to you. Never assume that the regular route's dates and fees apply to the private route, or the reverse.

sections.h2: Examinations: Mostly the Same Papers
paras: Once enrolled, private and regular candidates generally sit the same board papers under the same rules. The examination centres, the date sheet, and the marking are the board's, not the school's. The result is a board result either way, and the marksheet and certificate carry the board's authority.

There can be practical differences, such as the examination centre assigned or the handling of practical work, depending on the board's rules. If you are a private candidate, confirm these details early so there are no surprises on examination day. If you are a regular candidate, your school will normally guide you through them.

diagram.caption: Two routes to the same board examination: the difference is enrolment and support, not the papers themselves.

sections.h2: Which Route Suits Which Pupil?
paras: The regular route suits pupils who are in school and want the structure of daily classes, teacher guidance, and a school community. For most pupils, it is the simpler and safer route, because the school carries the administrative load and the pupil can focus on studying.

The private route suits pupils who are not in a regular institution and who can organise their own study and administration. It can be the right choice for a pupil who left school, who needs to reappear after a gap, or who is studying independently for genuine reasons. It demands self-discipline: without a timetable imposed from outside, the pupil must build their own. Pupils considering this route should speak honestly with a teacher or a trusted adult about whether they can sustain it.
bullets: Regular: best for pupils enrolled in school who want structure and guidance.
Private: for pupils not in a regular institution who can organise their own study.
Both: sit the same board papers and receive a board result.
Always confirm eligibility and the current process with the board's notification.

sections.h2: Practical Advice for Either Route
paras: Whichever route you take, the fundamentals are the same. Know your registration and roll details, track the board's announcements, keep copies of every form and receipt, and follow a steady study plan. If you are a regular candidate, stay in touch with your school office about forms and slips. If you are a private candidate, check the board's announcements regularly and keep a personal file of every document.

For study support, the [books pages](/books.html) and [solved notes](/solved.html) on this site can help with revision, and guides like [how to finish the syllabus in 30 days](/blog/how-to-finish-syllabus-in-30-days.html) and [how to avoid common exam mistakes](/blog/how-to-avoid-common-exam-mistakes.html) are useful for pupils on either route. The examination rewards preparation, not the route by which you arrived.

points: Regular candidates appear through a school; private candidates apply directly to the board.
Both routes generally lead to the same board papers and a board result.
The regular route offers school structure; the private route demands self-organisation.
Eligibility, forms, fees, and deadlines differ — confirm the current rules with the board.
Whichever route you take, track announcements and keep copies of every document.

faqs.q: Is a private candidate's result as valid as a regular candidate's?
faqs.a: In general, yes. Both sit board papers under the board's rules and receive a board result. What differs is the route of enrolment, not the authority of the result. Confirm any specific conditions with the board's official notification.

faqs.q: Can anyone appear as a private candidate?
faqs.a: No. Boards set eligibility conditions for private candidacy, and not every class or subject may be open to private candidates. Confirm the current eligibility rules with your school or the board's official notification before planning around this route.

faqs.q: Do private candidates sit different papers?
faqs.a: In general, private and regular candidates sit the same board papers under the same rules. Practical details such as centres and practical work may differ, so confirm them early with the board's official notification.

faqs.q: Can a regular pupil switch to private candidacy?
faqs.a: That depends on the board's current rules and your circumstances. Speak to your school and confirm the board's rules before making any change, because switching routes can affect enrolment, practical work, and deadlines.

faqs.q: What is the biggest challenge for private candidates?
faqs.a: Self-organisation. Without a school's daily timetable, teacher guidance, and announcement tracking, the pupil must manage study, administration, and deadlines personally. A steady personal routine and careful record-keeping make the route workable.

title: BIEK Pre-Engineering Result 2026: What 6,310 Passes Really Mean
desc: BIEK announced the 2026 Pre-Engineering Part-I result on 2 October: 6,310 of 14,683 pupils cleared all six papers. Here is what the numbers mean and what to do next.
intro: The BIEK pre-engineering result 2026 analysis starts with one honest number: of the 14,683 pupils who appeared in the Intermediate Part-I Science Pre-Engineering annual examination, 6,310 passed all six papers. The Board of Intermediate Education Karachi (BIEK) announced the result on 2 October 2026, on the directions of Chairman Faqir Muhammad Lakho, and Controller of Examinations Zarina Rashid released the figures. About 43% cleared all six papers, which means a large share of candidates are now dealing with at least one paper still to clear. That is not a reason to panic. It is a reason to read the result carefully, understand exactly which papers are cleared and which are not, and make a calm plan with your school and your teachers. This article explains the numbers, the partial-pass picture, and the sensible next steps.

sections.h2: What the headline numbers actually say
paras: The result announcement gave a full chain of figures, and each one means something different. A total of 15,044 candidates registered for the examination, and 14,683 appeared. The gap between registered and appeared is normal in board examinations, and it simply tells us how many pupils sat the papers. The most important figure for pupils is the next one: 6,310 candidates passed all six papers.

Presenting the figure as about 43% of those who appeared helps put it in perspective. Roughly four in ten candidates cleared every paper in this sitting, while 8,373 did not clear all six. Those 8,373 pupils are not in one single group, though. Some passed five papers, some passed one, and their next steps are different. The first job after any result is therefore to find your own exact position, not to compare yourself with the headline percentage.

diagram.alt: From registration to your next step
diagram.caption: The official figures for the BIEK Pre-Engineering Part-I result, and the step that follows them.

sections.h2: The partial-pass picture
paras: The board also published how many pupils passed five, four, three, two or one paper, and this breakdown is more useful than the headline alone. It shows that partial success is common, not unusual, and that most pupils who did not clear all six papers still have real progress to build on.

Read the breakdown as a map of where pupils stand. A pupil who passed five papers has one paper to deal with. A pupil who passed three papers has a different job: three papers secured, three still open. Your study plan should match your own row in this table, not somebody else's.
bullets: 79 candidates passed five papers
747 candidates passed four papers
1,827 candidates passed three papers
1,864 candidates passed two papers
1,783 candidates passed one paper

sections.h2: Why clearing all six papers matters
paras: Intermediate Part-I is the first year of the two-year Intermediate programme. The papers you clear in Part-I stay cleared, and the papers you do not clear remain open until the board's rules allow you to reappear in them. That is why the phrase 'passed all six papers' carries weight: it means the whole first-year set is finished in one sitting.

Clearing all six papers also keeps your path into Part-II straightforward. If one or more papers are still open, your school and teachers can help you plan how Part-II study and the pending papers fit together. This is a planning conversation, not a punishment, and it is one that thousands of pupils have every year. The earlier you have it, the calmer the year ahead becomes.

sections.h2: If you did not clear all six papers
paras: Start with verification. Confirm your result from the official gazette or the official online result, and write down exactly which papers you cleared and which you did not. Do not rely on a forwarded message or a screenshot from an unofficial page. Your own list of cleared and pending papers is the foundation of everything that follows.

Then take that list to your school or your subject teacher. They can explain how reappearing works under the board's current rules, including eligibility and timing, and help you arrange a study plan that covers the pending papers without neglecting Part-II work. Keep the plan realistic: a small number of pending papers with steady daily study beats a grand plan that collapses in a week. Always confirm reappearance rules, fees and deadlines through the board's official notification rather than through rumours.
bullets: Confirm your own result from the official gazette or official online slip
Write down cleared papers and pending papers separately
Discuss reappearance rules with your school or teacher
Build a daily study plan for pending papers alongside Part-II work
Check the board's official notification for dates, fees and eligibility

sections.h2: How to read the result without rumours
paras: One fact about this result deserves special attention. The BIEK gazette lists roll numbers and marks only. It does not name toppers or position holders. Never pay a third-party 'result service' for information the board publishes itself, and never forward an unverified list to classmates. A few minutes of checking the official source saves days of confusion. title: BISE Larkana Class 9 Result 2026: Districts, Portal and Next Steps
desc: BISE Larkana released the SSC Part-I (Class 9) 2026 result in October 2026 with a 5:00 PM go-live. Check the five districts covered, how to check by roll number, and what to do next.
intro: The BISE Larkana class 9 result 2026 districts question is the first one many families ask, because the board covers a wide area of northern Sindh. The Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education Larkana announced the SSC Part-I (9th class) Annual Examination 2026 result in October 2026, and the official press release said results go live at 5:00 PM. Pupils check with their roll number on the official board web portal, while schools can download the consolidated institutional gazette. This article explains which districts the board covers, how the roll-number check works, what the school gazette is for, and what a Class 9 pupil should do after seeing the result.

sections.h2: What was released
paras: The release was the SSC Part-I Annual Examination 2026 result, which is the Class 9 board result for schools under BISE Larkana. The board announced it in October 2026, and its official press release said results go live at 5:00 PM. That go-live time matters on result day, because the portal may not show anything before the announced time, and heavy traffic in the first hour can make pages load slowly.

If the portal is slow on result day, the calm response is to wait and retry rather than to trust an unofficial page. The official result is the one on the board's own portal, and the school gazette is the second official source. Everything else is somebody's copy, and copies can carry mistakes.

sections.h2: The five districts BISE Larkana covers
paras: BISE Larkana covers five districts: Larkana, Kamber Shahdadkot, Shikarpur, Jacobabad and Kashmore. If your school is in any of these districts, your Class 9 result comes from BISE Larkana, and the board's portal and gazette are the right places to check it. Pupils sometimes check the wrong board's website on result day, so confirming the district list first saves a lot of wasted effort.

The district list also explains why the school gazette matters so much. With five districts of schools to serve, the gazette lets each school see all of its own pupils' results in one consolidated document, instead of checking roll numbers one by one.

diagram.alt: BISE Larkana: five districts, one board
diagram.caption: The five districts whose Class 9 results come from BISE Larkana.

sections.h2: How to check your result by roll number
paras: Checking by roll number is straightforward, but it helps to have the slip in hand before you start. Keep your roll-number slip or admit card nearby, type the roll number exactly as printed, and check the name and father's name on the result before believing any number on the screen. A single mistyped digit can show someone else's result or no result at all.

If the portal does not show your result, work through the simple checks first: recheck the roll number, retry after some time because result-day traffic overloads board sites, and then try the gazette route through your school. Do not hand your roll number to a third-party 'result service'. The board publishes the result itself, and your school can help you if the portal keeps failing.

diagram.caption: The official route, from roll number to confirmed result.

sections.h2: What the school gazette is for
paras: The consolidated institutional gazette is the document schools download, and it lists the results of the school's pupils together. It is especially useful when the online portal is slow, when a pupil has lost a roll-number slip, or when a school needs to verify results for a whole class at once. Teachers use it to confirm results, prepare Class 10 admissions, and advise pupils about their next steps.

For pupils, the gazette is also a useful second check. If your online result and the gazette entry disagree, the school should be the one to sort it out, because the school deals with the board directly. Keep a copy or a photograph of your own gazette entry once it is confirmed, so you have it for admission and record purposes.

sections.h2: What to do after seeing your Class 9 result
paras: Class 9 is the first half of Matric, so the result is a checkpoint rather than a finish line. The useful response is to look at the subject-wise picture: which subjects are strong, which need work, and where marks were lost through understanding gaps rather than careless mistakes. That honest reading shapes the whole Class 10 year, because Class 10 builds directly on Class 9 foundations in subjects such as mathematics, science and English.

If you are unhappy with a result, discuss it with your teacher before taking any step. Boards offer scrutiny or rechecking, but the process, fees and deadlines must be confirmed through the board's official notification. Do not let a disappointing result sit unexamined, and do not let a good result turn into complacency either. The Class 9 to Class 10 jump rewards pupils who start steady work early, and our guide to [what comes after the Larkana Class 9 result](/blog/bise-larkana-class-9-result-2026-next-steps.html) walks through the next steps in more detail.
bullets: Review the result subject by subject, not just as a total
Note which subjects need concept work and which need exam technique
Talk to your teacher about any paper you want rechecked, and confirm the official scrutiny process
Start Class 10 preparation early, especially in subjects that build on Class 9
