faqs.a: Write the subject, your full name, class and section, roll number, and school name, plus the session year and teacher's name if your school asks for them. Keep it neat and centred, with a simple ruled border, and leave the page free of experiment work.

faqs.q: How do I set out the index of a practical notebook?
faqs.a: Rule columns for experiment number, experiment title, date performed, and page number, with enough rows for the whole year. Fill in each row on the day of the experiment and check the index against the notebook before submission.

faqs.q: Should each experiment start on a fresh page?
faqs.a: Yes, starting each experiment on a fresh page keeps the notebook easy to mark and the index accurate. It also prevents a long experiment from running into the next one and confusing the page numbers.

faqs.q: How should I correct a mistake in my notebook?
faqs.a: Cross it out with a single neat line and continue writing. Avoid heavy scribbling and correction fluid, which examiners dislike, and never tear out a page, since a missing page raises questions about missing work.

title: Recording Physics Practical Observations in Tables
desc: Record physics practical readings in clean, headed tables with units and repeat values, so your observations are easy to check, compare, and turn into results.
intro: In a physics practical, the observation table is the evidence for everything that follows, because every calculation, graph, and conclusion is built on the readings it contains. A table that is headed clearly, filled in honestly, and easy to read lets the examiner check your work quickly and trust your result, while a cramped or careless table casts doubt on the whole experiment. Good tables are not about beautiful handwriting alone; they are about planning the columns before you measure, recording units every time, and repeating readings so that odd results stand out. This guide shows how to set out physics observation tables that are clear, honest, and ready for calculation.

sections.h2: Plan the Table Before You Measure
paras: Draw the observation table before you take a single reading, because a table planned in advance stops you from forgetting a column halfway through the experiment. Look at the quantities you will vary and the quantities you will measure, and give each one its own column, with the quantity, its symbol, and its unit written in the heading, for example length in centimetres or time in seconds. Leave a column for repeat readings of the same measurement, since physics practicals usually require two or three readings for each setting, and add a final column for the mean if your teacher asks for one. Planning the table first also shows you whether you have enough rows for all the settings you plan to test.

Rule the table with a ruler and leave enough width in each column for the numbers you expect, including decimal places, so entries do not spill into neighbouring columns. Write the headings once, neatly, and do not rewrite them for every row, since repeated headings waste space and invite errors. If the experiment needs a separate table for a different part, such as a second set of readings, draw it as a new table with its own heading rather than squeezing it into the first one. A table planned before measuring is faster to fill in during the experiment, when your attention should be on measuring carefully, not on deciding what to write where.

sections.h2: Headings, Units, and Decimal Places
paras: Every column heading in a physics table must show the quantity and its unit, because a number without a unit cannot be checked or used in a calculation. Write the unit in the heading once, for the whole column, rather than repeating it after every number, which clutters the table and makes comparison harder. Use the unit your teacher or apparatus uses, and keep it consistent through the whole table; mixing centimetres and metres in one column is a common source of calculation errors. If you convert a unit during the experiment, note the conversion clearly so the examiner can follow it.

Record readings to a sensible number of decimal places, matching the precision of your measuring instrument, and keep the same decimal places down each column. A ruler marked in millimetres justifies readings to one decimal place in centimetres, while guessing extra digits beyond what the instrument shows is false precision, not accuracy. Write numbers plainly, with decimal points clearly placed, and avoid writing a digit over another one when correcting an entry; cross it out with a single line and write the new value beside it. Consistent units and decimal places make the table look professional and make the calculation that follows far less error-prone. For more study material, see the [solved notes](/solved.html) and the [book collection](/books.html).

sections.h2: Repeat Readings and Taking the Mean
paras: Repeat readings are the simplest way to catch mistakes in a physics practical, because a single reading can be wrong without you noticing, while three readings that disagree point straight to a problem. Take each reading independently, resetting the apparatus or your eye position between repeats where possible, rather than copying the first value three times, which defeats the purpose. Record every repeat in its own column, even if one looks odd, because hiding an awkward reading is dishonest and examiners notice gaps in a table. If a repeat is clearly wrong, for example because you misread the scale, note it briefly and repeat the measurement properly.

When the repeats agree closely, calculate the mean by adding them and dividing by the number of readings, and write the mean in its own column to the same decimal places as the readings. The mean is the value you carry into calculations and graphs, since it smooths out small random variations in measuring. If the repeats differ widely, do not just average them and move on: check the apparatus, your technique, and whether something changed between readings, and record what you found. Explaining a spread of readings honestly is far better than presenting a tidy mean built on hidden data, and it shows the examiner that you understand measurement, not just arithmetic.

diagram.alt: What Makes a Good Observation Table
diagram.caption: Five qualities of a physics observation table the examiner can trust.

sections.h2: Recording Observations During the Experiment
paras: Record readings directly into the notebook table as you take them, never on loose paper to be copied later, because copying introduces errors and loses the link between reading and setting. Read the instrument at eye level where parallax matters, such as with a metre rule or a liquid column, and record the value before moving on to the next setting. If you must estimate between scale divisions, do so consistently and note that the last digit is estimated, rather than pretending the instrument is more precise than it is. Working steadily, one setting at a time, also prevents the common mistake of recording a reading against the wrong row.

Keep the table tidy as you go by writing numbers in the centre of each cell and leaving no cell blank without explanation. A blank cell looks like a forgotten reading, so if a reading could not be taken, write a short note such as apparatus fault and record what you did about it. At the end of the readings, scan the table for patterns: values should usually change smoothly as the varied quantity changes, and a sudden jump often means a misread scale or a wrong row. Catching that jump during the experiment, when you can remeasure, is worth far more than a neat table of unchecked numbers.

sections.h2: From Table to Calculation and Result
paras: A good observation table leads naturally into the calculation, because the examiner can see exactly which numbers were used and where they came from. Show one worked calculation step by step, using the mean values from the table, and state the formula you used before substituting numbers with units. Do not present only a final answer, since the working is what earns marks and what lets an error be traced to a single step rather than blamed on the whole experiment. If a calculation is repeated for several rows, show the first one fully and then present the rest in a results table with the same care as the observations.

Finish by comparing your result with what you expected and commenting briefly on the agreement, without overstating it. If the result is close to the expected pattern, say so and note the small scatter in the readings; if it differs, suggest a specific reason from your observations rather than a vague excuse. The result section should refer back to the table, for example by naming the range of readings used, so the whole write-up hangs together as one argument. When the table, calculation, and conclusion agree with each other, the examiner can follow your thinking from measurement to result without guessing. More practical guides are on the [blog](/blog/) and the [home page](/).

points: Draw and head the table before taking any readings.
Put the quantity, symbol, and unit in every column heading.
Take two or three independent repeat readings for each setting.
Record readings directly in the notebook, never via loose paper.
Show one full worked calculation from the table's mean values.

faqs.q: Why do physics tables need repeat readings?
faqs.a: Repeat readings reveal mistakes and random variation that a single reading hides. If repeats agree closely, their mean is a more reliable value for calculations and graphs than any one reading alone.

faqs.q: Where should units go in an observation table?
faqs.a: Put the unit in the column heading once, for the whole column, such as length in centimetres. Do not repeat the unit after every number, and never mix two units in the same column.

faqs.q: How many decimal places should I use in a table?
faqs.a: Match the precision of your instrument and keep the same decimal places down each column. Do not invent extra digits beyond what the instrument can actually show.

faqs.q: What should I do with a reading that looks wrong?
faqs.a: Record it honestly, check the apparatus and your technique, and repeat the measurement properly. Note briefly what happened rather than hiding the odd reading, since examiners notice gaps.

faqs.q: Should calculations use single readings or means?
faqs.a: Use the mean of the repeat readings for each setting, and show one full worked calculation with the formula, substitution with units, and the result.

title: Writing Up a Chemistry Titration Practical
desc: Write a clear titration practical from apparatus to calculation: set out your readings honestly, work through the mean titre, and state what the result shows.
intro: A titration write-up is one of the most structured practicals you will produce, because it follows a fixed path from apparatus and method through a table of readings to a calculation based on the mean titre. Examiners look for honesty in the readings, clarity in the table, and working that can be followed step by step, rather than a perfect result alone. Many pupils lose marks not because their titration technique was poor but because the write-up hides how the result was reached. This guide walks through each part of a titration write-up in order, so your notebook shows careful work from the first rinse to the final conclusion.

sections.h2: Aim, Apparatus, and Preparation
paras: Begin every titration write-up with a short, clear aim stating what the titration is meant to find out, for example the concentration of an unknown solution using a standard solution of known concentration. Follow the aim with a list of the apparatus actually used, naming each item once, such as burette, pipette, conical flask, and indicator, and mention the solutions by name and concentration where they are known. Listing apparatus accurately matters, because the examiner checks that the method described could actually have been carried out with the equipment named. Do not copy a generic apparatus list from a textbook if your laboratory used different items.

Record the preparation steps that affect the result, such as rinsing the burette with the solution it will contain and the pipette with the solution it will measure, since rinsing with water instead would dilute the solutions and change the titre. Note the indicator used and the colour change you watched for, because the end point of a titration is defined by that change and a vague description makes the readings hard to judge. Write this section before the readings table so the examiner understands the conditions under which the numbers were obtained. A short, accurate preparation section shows that you understand why each step matters, not just what the steps were.

sections.h2: Method: Writing the Procedure Clearly
paras: Write the procedure as a numbered sequence of steps in the order you performed them, using clear, short sentences that another pupil could follow. Start with measuring a fixed volume of one solution into the conical flask with the pipette, adding a few drops of indicator, and filling the burette, then describe adding the second solution slowly with constant swirling. Explain how you approached the end point: fast at first, then drop by drop with swirling, stopping at the first permanent colour change that lasts on swirling. Mention reading the burette at eye level at the bottom of the meniscus where appropriate, and recording the reading before refilling for the next titration.

Keep the method factual and personal, describing what you did rather than copying textbook instructions word for word, and include any detail your teacher gave for this particular titration. If you carried out a rough titration first to find the approximate end point, say so, because a rough titration is good practice and examiners expect to see it mentioned. Avoid vague phrases such as the experiment was done, and avoid claiming steps you did not perform, since the method must match the readings that follow. A method written this way proves the readings are yours and gives the examiner confidence in the whole write-up. For more study help, visit the [solved notes](/solved.html) and the [book collection](/books.html).

sections.h2: The Titration Readings Table
paras: The readings table is the heart of a titration write-up, and it must show every titration you performed, including the rough one, with initial and final burette readings and the titre for each. Draw columns for titration number, initial burette reading, final burette reading, and titre used, with all volumes in cubic centimetres to two decimal places as burette readings require. Label the rough titration clearly as rough, and do not include it in the mean, since its purpose was only to find the approximate end point. Fill in the table during the practical, reading by reading, rather than reconstructing it afterwards from memory.

Check each titre as you go by subtracting the initial reading from the final reading, and watch for titres that differ sharply from the others, which usually mean a missed end point or a misread burette. If a titre is clearly an outlier, repeat the titration and record the new result honestly rather than altering the old figure to match. The table should make it obvious which titres were used for the mean and which were not, so mark the chosen ones or state the selection in a note beneath the table. An honest, complete table with one or two concordant titres is worth far more than a suspiciously perfect set of identical values.

diagram.caption: The order of a complete titration write-up from preparation to result.

sections.h2: Finding the Mean Titre
paras: The mean titre is the average of the concordant titres, meaning the titres that agree closely with each other, and it is the value carried into the calculation. Choose the titres that agree within a small range, usually a few tenths of a cubic centimetre, and state which titration numbers you used, so the examiner can check your choice against the table. Add the chosen titres and divide by how many there are, showing the working in full, and give the mean to two decimal places like the burette readings. If only two titres agree and a third differs, use the agreeing pair and say why the third was left out, rather than averaging all three and hiding the difference.

Never invent a titre to make the mean come out neatly, and never adjust a reading after the event to force agreement, because examiners recognise patterns that are too perfect to be real. If your titres do not agree well, say so honestly and repeat the titration if time allows, since an extra accurate titration is better than a doubtful mean. Where time does not allow a repeat, use the closest agreeing titres and note the spread in your conclusion, so the examiner sees that you understood the problem. The mean titre is a small calculation, but it is where honesty and accuracy meet, and it sets the tone for the final result.

sections.h2: Calculation, Result, and Conclusion
paras: Work through the calculation step by step from the mean titre, showing the formula or mole relationship used, the substitution of numbers with units, and each stage of the working. State the quantities you are using, such as the volume and concentration of the known solution, before you use them, so the examiner can follow the logic without guessing. Give the final result with the correct unit, such as moles per cubic decimetre for a concentration, and to a sensible number of significant figures that matches your data. A calculation shown in full earns marks for method even if an arithmetic slip creeps in, while a bare final answer earns nothing if it is wrong.

Finish with a short conclusion that states what the titration found and whether the result is reliable, based on how closely the titres agreed. Mention one or two specific sources of error, such as overshooting the end point or misreading the burette, and link them to the spread of your readings rather than listing generic faults. Do not claim a precision your data does not support, and do not present the result as exact if the titres varied noticeably. A conclusion that matches the evidence in the table brings the whole write-up together and leaves the examiner with a clear, honest picture of your work. More guides are available on the [blog](/blog/) and the [home page](/).

points: State a clear aim and list only the apparatus actually used.
Record rinsing, indicator, and end-point colour change in the method.
Show every titration in the table, including the rough one.
Take the mean from concordant titres only, and show the working.
Show the full calculation and conclude honestly about reliability.

faqs.q: What is a rough titration and why do it first?
faqs.a: A rough titration is a quick first run to find the approximate end point. It tells you roughly how much solution is needed, so the accurate titrations that follow can be done slowly and carefully near the end point.

faqs.q: Which titres should I use for the mean titre?
faqs.a: Use the titres that agree closely with each other, usually within a few tenths of a cubic centimetre, and state which titration numbers you chose. Leave out the rough titration and any clear outlier, and say why.

faqs.q: How many decimal places do burette readings need?
faqs.a: Burette readings are recorded to two decimal places in cubic centimetres, and the mean titre is given to two decimal places as well. This matches the precision of the burette scale.

faqs.q: What if my titres do not agree well?
faqs.a: Repeat the titration if time allows and record the new result honestly. If you cannot repeat it, use the closest agreeing titres, show your working, and note the spread honestly in your conclusion.

title: Drawing Specimen Diagrams for Biology Practicals
desc: Draw clear biology specimen diagrams with correct size, clean labels, and a scale note, so your drawing shows what you actually observed under the microscope.
intro: A biology specimen diagram is not a work of art and it is not a copy from a textbook; it is a record of what you actually saw when you looked at the specimen. Examiners mark diagrams for accuracy, proportion, clear labelling, and honest observation, so a simple drawing that matches the specimen scores far better than a beautiful one that invents details you never saw. Learning a few drawing rules, such as correct size, single-line outlines, and straight label lines, will improve every biology practical you do. This guide covers how to observe, draw, label, and check a specimen diagram that the examiner can trust.

sections.h2: Observe First, Draw Second
paras: Spend time looking at the specimen before you pick up your pencil, because a diagram drawn from a quick glance is usually wrong in proportion and missing key features. Note the overall shape first, then the main parts and how they relate to each other, and finally the smaller details that make this specimen recognisable. If you are using a microscope, move the slide gently to see the whole specimen, and adjust the focus until the edges are sharp before you start drawing. Pupils who rush to draw often produce a diagram of what they expected to see rather than what was actually in front of them, and examiners spot that quickly.

Make a few light sketch marks to plan the size and position of the drawing on the page before committing to firm lines, since a diagram that runs off the page or ends up tiny in a corner is hard to label. Decide what magnification you are drawing at in general terms, and keep the proportions of the parts true to the specimen: a part that is twice as long as another in the specimen should be twice as long in your drawing. If a feature is unclear, look again rather than guessing, and if it truly cannot be seen, leave it out rather than inventing it. Honest observation is the foundation of every mark a specimen diagram earns.

sections.h2: Size, Outline, and Clean Lines
paras: Draw the specimen large enough to label clearly, usually filling a good part of the page, because a tiny diagram cannot show detail and its label lines become tangled. Use a sharp pencil and draw outlines with single, clear lines rather than sketchy, broken strokes, and avoid shading or colouring unless your teacher specifically asks for it, since shading can hide the structures the examiner needs to see. Keep the outline smooth and continuous where the specimen's edge is smooth, and show a broken or uneven edge only where the specimen really has one. Clean lines signal careful observation, while a fuzzy outline suggests the pupil was unsure what they were looking at.

Do not draw a border around the diagram or add decorative frames, and keep the drawing area free of writing except for the title and labels. If you make a mistake, erase it cleanly and redraw the line rather than drawing over it, since double lines confuse the examiner about which edge is real. Draw only the specimen itself, not the microscope, slide, or background, unless the task asks for the field of view, and centre the drawing so there is room for labels on both sides. A large, clean, uncluttered drawing is easier to label, easier to mark, and a fairer record of your observation. For more study resources, see the [solved notes](/solved.html) and the [book collection](/books.html).

sections.h2: Labelling: Straight Lines and Correct Names
paras: Label a specimen diagram with straight, horizontal label lines drawn with a ruler, each line touching the structure it names at one end and carrying the label at the other, without crossing other label lines. Write labels in a neat row outside the drawing, using the correct biological names for the structures, and check the spelling of each term before you finish, since a misspelt label can lose the mark for that structure. Label only the structures you can actually identify and that the task asks for; labelling every tiny detail you are unsure about risks more errors than it gains marks. If two labels would cross, rearrange the labels or the drawing position rather than accepting crossed lines.

Keep label lines evenly spaced so the labels do not crowd together, and use both sides of the drawing when there are many labels rather than squeezing them all on one side. Do not use arrows with curved or slanting lines, and do not write labels inside the drawing where they cover the structures. After labelling, read each label back to its structure along the line and ask whether the line really points to the right part, because a label pointing to the wrong structure is a common and avoidable error. A diagram with a few accurate, well-placed labels always beats a diagram crowded with hopeful guesses.

diagram.alt: Parts of a Good Specimen Diagram
diagram.caption: The features examiners look for in a biology specimen diagram.

sections.h2: Magnification and Scale Notes
paras: Add a magnification or scale note to your diagram whenever the task asks for one or your teacher expects it, because the note tells the examiner how large the drawing is compared with the real specimen. If you drew from a microscope, state the magnification you used, such as the objective and eyepiece combination, and if you drew a large specimen by eye, note that the drawing is not to scale or give an approximate size where you measured it. Do not invent a magnification figure: if you are unsure what magnification you used, check with your teacher or state the drawing size honestly rather than guessing a number that looks impressive.

A scale note also helps you check your own proportions, since thinking about how much larger the drawing is than the specimen forces you to compare the parts with each other. When a diagram is drawn at a stated magnification, the examiner can judge whether the proportions are plausible, which is part of the accuracy mark. Write the magnification or scale note beneath the title, where it is easy to find, and keep it short and factual. Even a simple note such as drawing not to scale, where that is true, is better than no note at all, because it shows you thought about size rather than ignoring it.

sections.h2: Checking Your Diagram Before Submission
paras: Check every specimen diagram against the specimen itself before you close the notebook, while you can still correct errors from observation rather than from memory. Compare the shape, the relative sizes of the parts, and the number of visible structures with what you drew, and add or remove a feature only if the specimen confirms it. Read through the labels once more for spelling and for correct pointing, and check that the title names the specimen and the view, such as a cross section or a whole specimen, where that matters. A two-minute check at the end of the practical catches most of the errors that cost marks.

Also check the practical rules of the page: the diagram should be on the correct page for the experiment, dated, and matched by the index entry, so the examiner finds it without searching. If your teacher reviews diagrams in class, listen to their comments on other pupils' work as well as your own, since the same faults, such as tiny drawings or crossed label lines, appear again and again. Practise drawing the same type of specimen more than once across the year, and each attempt will be faster and more accurate. Good diagram skills are built by repeated, checked observation, not by a single perfect drawing. More practical guides are on the [blog](/blog/) and the [home page](/).

points: Observe the specimen fully before starting to draw.
Draw large, with single clear pencil lines and true proportions.
Label with straight ruled lines that do not cross.
Use correct, correctly spelt biological names for labels.
Add an honest magnification or scale note beneath the title.

faqs.q: Should I shade or colour a biology specimen diagram?
faqs.a: Usually not, unless your teacher asks for it. Shading can hide the structures the examiner needs to see, so a clean pencil outline with clear labels is normally the best choice.

faqs.q: How large should a specimen diagram be?
faqs.a: Large enough to label clearly, usually filling a good part of the page. A tiny diagram cannot show detail and its label lines become tangled and hard to read.

faqs.q: What if I cannot see a structure clearly?
faqs.a: Look again and adjust the focus or position first. If it truly cannot be seen, leave it out rather than inventing it, since examiners mark honest observation over guessed detail.

faqs.q: Why do label lines need to be straight and ruled?
faqs.a: Straight ruled lines make it clear which label belongs to which structure and prevent lines from crossing. Crossed or slanting lines confuse the examiner and can cost the mark for that label.

title: Keeping a Computer Lab Journal That Examiners Trust
desc: Keep a computer lab journal examiners trust: dated entries, working code, real output, and short reflections that prove the work is genuinely yours.
intro: A computer lab journal is different from other practical notebooks, because the work happens on a screen and the examiner cannot watch you type. The journal is the proof that you did the work yourself, understood it, and tested it, so it must show the problem, the code, the output, and your own thinking about what happened. A journal that contains only copied code with no dates, outputs, or reflections looks suspicious even when the work is genuine, while a journal with dated entries and honest notes about errors is trusted at a glance. This guide shows how to keep a computer lab journal that proves real, regular work.

sections.h2: Dated Entries in Lab Order
paras: Date every lab journal entry and keep the entries in the order the work was done, because dates and sequence are the simplest proof that the journal was built up over the term rather than written in a rush at the end. Start each entry with the date, the lab session number if your school uses one, and the title or problem statement of the task, written in your own words. If a task took more than one session, give each session its own dated entry and note that it continues the previous work, so the examiner can follow the progress. A journal with regular dates spread across the term immediately looks more credible than one with identical handwriting and no dates at all.

Write entries in the lab or on the same day, while you remember what you tried, what failed, and what you changed, since a journal reconstructed weeks later loses exactly the details that make it believable. If you must finish an entry later, say so honestly and work from the saved program file rather than from memory alone. Keep the journal's index or contents list up to date in the same way as a science notebook, listing each program or task with its date and page number. Dated, ordered entries turn a pile of code printouts into a record of learning that an examiner can follow from the first program to the last.

sections.h2: Problem, Logic, and Code
paras: Each journal entry should begin with the problem in plain language, then a short note on the logic or steps you will use, and only then the code itself, because the examiner wants to see thinking, not just typing. Write the problem as a task to solve, for example to find the largest of three numbers entered by the user, and follow it with the steps in order, such as read the numbers, compare them, and print the largest. This short plan, sometimes called an algorithm, shows that you designed the program before writing it, and it makes the code far easier to read. Pupils who skip the plan often produce code that works by accident and cannot be explained in a viva.

Write the code neatly, with consistent indentation and clear variable names, exactly as it ran in the lab, and do not tidy it up afterwards into a version that was never tested. If you handwrite the journal, copy the code carefully from the working program, checking brackets and spelling character by character, since a single wrong character can change the meaning. If you paste printed code, attach it neatly and still write the problem and logic by hand, so the entry is clearly your own work. Code that matches its stated logic, with names that make sense, is the core of a trustworthy computer journal. For more study material, see the [solved notes](/solved.html) and the [book collection](/books.html).

sections.h2: Real Output and Test Cases
paras: Record the actual output of each program, copied from the screen or pasted as a printout, together with the input values you used to test it, because output is the evidence that the program ran. Show at least two test cases where the task allows it, such as a normal input and a boundary or unusual input, and write the expected result beside the actual result so the examiner can see whether they matched. If the output was wrong on the first run, record that too, with a note on what you changed, rather than presenting only the final correct run as if it worked first time. Honest testing history is one of the strongest signs of genuine lab work.

Do not invent output, and do not copy output from another pupil's program, since output that does not match the code is easy to spot and destroys trust in the whole journal. If a program produced an error message, record the error and the fix in your own words, because debugging is real programming work and examiners respect a journal that shows it. Keep outputs attached in order, aligned with their entries, and label each one with the program title and date so a loose printout cannot be mistaken for another entry's output. A journal where every program has matching input, code, and output is a journal the examiner can believe.

diagram.caption: The parts of one complete computer lab journal entry.

sections.h2: Reflection: What You Learned
paras: End each entry with a short reflection of two or three sentences on what the program taught you, what went wrong, and what you would do differently, because reflection turns a code listing into evidence of learning. A reflection might note that a loop condition caused an extra repetition, that a variable name confused you, or that testing with a zero input revealed a fault you had not expected. Write it in your own words, even if it is simple, since a genuine short reflection is far more convincing than a polished paragraph copied from a textbook. Examiners read reflections to judge understanding, and a journal without them reads like a typing exercise.

Reflection also helps you revise, because reading back over your own notes on errors reminds you of the traps to avoid in the next program and in the viva. If the same error appears in several entries, note the pattern and the rule you will use to avoid it, such as checking loop boundaries before running the program. Keep reflections brief and specific to the entry, not general statements about computers being useful, which add nothing. Over a term, these short notes build into a personal record of progress that no copied journal can imitate, and they give you ready answers when the examiner asks what you learned.

sections.h2: Keeping the Journal Safe and Complete
paras: Keep the program files themselves safe alongside the journal, with clear file names matching the journal entries, so any program can be found and checked if the examiner asks. Save your work at the end of every lab session, and keep a backup copy where your school allows it, such as on a school drive or a personal storage device, because a lost file near submission time cannot be recreated honestly. If a file is lost despite this, tell your teacher straight away and rewrite the program yourself, noting the rewrite in the journal, rather than copying another pupil's file to fill the gap. Honesty about a lost file preserves trust; a copied file destroys it.

Before submission, check the journal from front to back: every entry dated, every program with code and output, every reflection written, and the contents list matching the pages. Ask your teacher to review the journal once during the term if they offer it, and correct any gaps while there is still time to do the work properly. Remove loose sheets that do not belong to any entry, and make sure printouts are firmly attached so pages do not fall out during marking. A complete, ordered, backed-up journal needs no last-minute panic, and it presents a term of real work in the best possible light. More guides are on the [blog](/blog/) and the [home page](/).

points: Date every entry and keep entries in lab order.
Write the problem and logic steps before the code.
Record real output with the inputs used to test it.
End each entry with a short, honest reflection.
Keep program files safe with names matching the journal.

faqs.q: What should one computer lab journal entry contain?
faqs.a: A date and title, the problem in your own words, short logic steps, the code exactly as it ran, real output with test inputs, and a short reflection on what you learned.

faqs.q: How many test cases should I show for a program?
faqs.a: Show at least two where the task allows it, such as a normal input and a boundary or unusual input. Write the expected result beside the actual result so the examiner can see whether they matched.

faqs.q: Should I record errors and failed runs in my journal?
faqs.a: Yes, record the error and the fix in your own words. Debugging is real programming work, and an honest testing history is one of the strongest signs that the journal is genuine.

faqs.q: Can I paste printed code and output into my journal?
faqs.a: Yes, if your school allows it, but attach printouts neatly in order and still write the problem, logic, and reflection by hand. The handwritten parts show the entry is your own work and understanding.

title: Preparing for Practical Viva Questions with Confidence
desc: Prepare for practical viva questions with short, confident spoken answers: practise explaining apparatus, method, and results in your own words before the day.
intro: A practical viva is a short spoken test in which the examiner asks you about the experiments in your notebook, the apparatus you used, and the results you obtained, and it rewards pupils who can explain their own work clearly. Many pupils know the experiments well on paper but struggle in the viva because they have never practised saying the answers out loud, so simple questions feel harder than they are. The good news is that viva questions follow predictable patterns, and a few weeks of short spoken practice can turn nervous silence into calm, confident answers. This guide shows what examiners ask, how to frame short answers, and how to rehearse so the viva feels familiar on the day.

sections.h2: What Examiners Ask in a Viva
paras: Viva questions usually start from your own notebook, with the examiner opening a page and asking what the experiment was about, why you used a particular apparatus, or what your result showed. Expect questions about the aim of an experiment, the principle behind it, the steps of the method, and the meaning of a graph, table, or diagram on that page. Examiners also ask general questions about the subject, such as naming an instrument and its use, or explaining a term that appears in your write-up, to check that you understand the work rather than merely copying it. Questions are normally short and direct, and they expect short, direct answers, not long speeches.

The examiner is also checking honesty, so questions often test whether the notebook really is your work, for example by asking you to explain a step in your own words or to point to a reading in your table. If you cannot explain a page of your own notebook, the examiner will doubt the whole entry, however neat it looks. That is why viva preparation starts with reading your own notebook, not with memorising new material from a textbook. Know every experiment by its aim, method, and result, and be ready to talk about any page the examiner opens. For more study help, see the [solved notes](/solved.html) and the [book collection](/books.html).

sections.h2: Building Short, Spoken Answers
paras: A good viva answer is short, structured, and in your own words, usually two or three sentences that answer the question directly and then stop. Start with the direct answer, then add one supporting detail, such as the reason or an example from your experiment, and avoid drifting into unrelated material to fill silence. For example, if asked why a burette is rinsed, a strong answer names the reason, that rinsing with the solution prevents dilution, and stops there, rather than describing the whole titration. Short answers are easier to remember, easier to say under pressure, and easier for the examiner to mark.

Practise turning written notes into spoken sentences, because an answer that reads well on paper can sound tangled when spoken for the first time. Read a question aloud, answer it without looking at the notebook, and then check whether you missed a key point or added something wrong. Keep a small list of the terms you tend to forget, such as instrument names or unit names, and repeat them until they come naturally. Avoid memorising long paragraphs word for word, since a forgotten word can derail a memorised answer, while an answer built from understanding can be recovered even if you pause. Understanding plus brevity is the combination examiners reward.

sections.h2: Practising Aloud with a Partner
paras: Practise viva questions aloud with a classmate, family member, or teacher, because silent revision does not train your voice, timing, or confidence. Take turns as examiner and pupil: one person opens the notebook at random, asks a question about that page, and listens to the answer without interrupting, then gives one point to improve. Keep each practice round short, perhaps ten minutes, and cover different experiments each time so no page stays unfamiliar. Speaking to a real person, even a friendly one, teaches you to handle the pause before answering and the feeling of being watched, which are the parts of a viva that cause most nervousness.

After each answer, ask your partner one follow-up question, such as why you chose that method or what would happen if a step were skipped, since examiners often follow a first answer with a deeper one. If you do not know an answer, practise saying so honestly and offering what you do know, for example that you are unsure of the term but can describe the step, rather than guessing wildly or going silent. Record the questions you struggled with and revisit those experiments the same day, so practice directly repairs weak spots. A few short partner sessions across the final weeks build far more confidence than a single long cramming session the night before.

diagram.alt: How to Answer a Viva Question
diagram.caption: A calm routine for answering any short viva question.

sections.h2: Handling Nerves and Difficult Questions
paras: Nerves in a viva are normal, and examiners expect them, so do not let a shaky start convince you the viva is going badly. Slow down deliberately, breathe before answering, and speak at a steady pace, since rushing makes answers harder to follow and increases mistakes. If you mishear a question, it is perfectly acceptable to ask the examiner to repeat it, and if you start an answer badly, pause and restart the sentence rather than struggling on. Examiners judge the knowledge in your answers, not a perfect performance, and a pupil who recovers calmly from a stumble often scores better than one who panics silently.

For a question you truly cannot answer, honesty is the best strategy: say that you are not sure, offer the closest related fact you do know, and do not invent a confident-sounding answer that is wrong. Examiners respect an honest gap far more than a confident fabrication, and a wrong guess can lead to further questions that expose the guess. If a question is about an experiment you did not perform well, describe what you did and what you learned from it rather than pretending it went perfectly. Calm honesty, steady pace, and short answers will carry you through the hardest parts of any viva.

sections.h2: A Final Viva Checklist
paras: In the last days before the viva, work through a simple checklist so nothing is left to chance on the day. Read every experiment in your notebook once, noting its aim, method, and result, and mark any page you cannot explain so you can revise it specifically. Practise naming the apparatus and instruments from your experiments, stating what each one measures and how it is read, since apparatus questions are among the most common. Prepare short answers for the most likely questions, such as the purpose of repeat readings, the meaning of a graph's slope, or the reason for a precaution you recorded, and rehearse them aloud at least once.

On the day itself, arrive early, keep your notebook tidy and in order, and greet the examiner politely before the questions begin. Listen carefully to each question, answer in your own words, and keep your hands free of notes, since reading answers from a slip is not allowed and looks dishonest. Remember that the viva is a conversation about work you already did, not a new examination of unseen material, so trust the preparation you have done. Walk in knowing your notebook, speak plainly, and let your own work speak for itself. More practical guides are on the [blog](/blog/) and the [home page](/).

points: Expect questions drawn from your own notebook pages.
Give short, direct answers in your own words, then stop.
Practise aloud with a partner in short, regular rounds.
Ask for a question to be repeated rather than guessing wildly.
Be honest about gaps and offer what you do know.

faqs.q: What kinds of questions come up in a practical viva?
faqs.a: Most questions come from your own notebook: the aim of an experiment, why an apparatus was used, the steps of the method, and what a table, graph, or diagram shows. General questions about instrument names and subject terms are also common.

faqs.q: How long should a viva answer be?
faqs.a: Two or three sentences are usually enough: the direct answer plus one supporting detail, such as a reason or an example from your experiment. Long, drifting answers are harder to say under pressure and harder for the examiner to mark.

faqs.q: What should I do if I do not know a viva answer?
faqs.a: Say honestly that you are not sure, and offer the closest related fact you do know. Examiners respect an honest gap far more than a confident guess, and guessing can lead to follow-up questions that expose the guess.

faqs.q: Is it acceptable to ask the examiner to repeat a question?
faqs.a: Yes, asking for a question to be repeated is perfectly acceptable and much better than answering a question you misheard. Pause, listen again, and then give your short answer.

title: Writing Precautions and Sources of Error in Practicals
desc: Write honest precautions and sources of error that strengthen a practical: name what could affect your readings and what you did to reduce each risk.
intro: Precautions and sources of error are the sections where a practical write-up shows real scientific thinking, because they prove you understood what could go wrong and what you did about it. Pupils often treat these sections as an afterthought, copying the same generic lines into every experiment, but examiners can tell the difference between a copied list and a thoughtful one at a glance. A strong precautions section names specific risks for this experiment and the exact steps taken against them, while a strong errors section honestly explains why the result may differ from the ideal. This guide shows how to write both sections so they strengthen, rather than weaken, your practical.

sections.h2: Precautions: What They Are For
paras: A precaution is a step taken before or during an experiment to prevent an error, protect the apparatus or the pupil, or keep the conditions fair, and it belongs in the write-up only if it was actually followed. Write each precaution as a specific action, such as reading the burette at eye level or keeping the distance constant between readings, rather than a vague instruction such as being careful. The examiner wants to see that you knew which parts of this experiment were sensitive and that you acted on that knowledge, not that you can recite a list of good intentions. Three or four specific, relevant precautions are worth far more than ten generic ones copied from another experiment.

Choose precautions by thinking through the method step by step and asking where a small change would alter the result, and write the precaution beside the risk it controls. For a measurement experiment, the risks are usually reading errors, inconsistent conditions, or apparatus faults, so precautions about eye position, repeat readings, and checking zero errors fit naturally. For a chemistry experiment, risks include contamination, incorrect volumes, and missed end points, so precautions about rinsing, careful measuring, and slow addition near the end point matter. When each precaution is tied to a real risk in your method, the section reads as understanding, not decoration.

sections.h2: Writing Precautions That Match Your Experiment
paras: Match every precaution to the experiment you actually performed by naming the apparatus, quantity, or step it concerns, and avoid precautions that could not apply to your method. A precaution about avoiding parallax means little in an experiment with no scale reading, while a precaution about keeping the temperature constant is meaningless if temperature was never measured. Read your method again after drafting the precautions and check that each one could have been followed during your experiment, and delete any that fail that test. Examiners notice mismatched precautions quickly, and a single irrelevant precaution casts doubt on the rest of the section.

Phrase precautions in the past tense as actions you took, such as the readings were taken at eye level, rather than as orders to a future reader, since the write-up records work already done. Keep the language simple and direct, one precaution per line or sentence, so the examiner can count and check them easily. If your teacher gave a particular precaution for the experiment, include it and say why it mattered, rather than replacing it with a generic alternative. A precautions section that matches the method, names real risks, and describes real actions is a quiet but powerful sign of a careful experimenter. For more study material, see the [solved notes](/solved.html) and the [book collection](/books.html).

sections.h2: Sources of Error: Being Honest About Limits
paras: Sources of error are the factors that may have made your readings or result differ from the true or ideal value, and writing them honestly shows that you understand measurement rather than merely reporting numbers. Divide them in your mind into random errors, such as small variations when reading a scale, and systematic errors, such as an instrument that reads slightly high every time, and name the ones that plausibly affected your experiment. Link each source of error to something in your data where possible, for example noting that a spread in repeat readings suggests reading variation, rather than listing faults with no connection to your results. An errors section grounded in your own data reads as genuine analysis.

Be specific about the likely size and direction of an error where you can, such as noting that a fast final addition may have overshot the end point and made a titre slightly large, rather than saying only that human error occurred. Avoid blaming everything on vague human error, faulty apparatus, or carelessness, since these phrases explain nothing and examiners discount them. If an error was noticed and corrected during the experiment, say so, and if an error could not be corrected, say how it limits confidence in the result. Honesty about limits does not lose marks; it earns them, because it shows the examiner you can judge your own work critically.

diagram.caption: How the two sections differ and what each one should contain.

sections.h2: Common Weaknesses to Avoid
paras: The most common weakness in these sections is copying the same generic list into every experiment, with phrases such as the experiment was done carefully or all precautions were taken, which tell the examiner nothing. Another weakness is listing precautions that contradict the method, such as claiming repeat readings were taken when the table shows only one reading, which undermines trust in the whole write-up. A third weakness is the opposite extreme: listing so many possible errors that the result appears worthless, including faults that could not have affected this experiment at all. All three weaknesses come from writing these sections without looking back at the method and the data, and all three are easy to avoid by checking each line against them.

Also avoid blaming other people or the equipment without evidence, since a claim that the apparatus was faulty needs a specific observation, such as a burette that leaked, to be believable. Avoid repeating the same precaution in different words to fill space, and avoid ending the section with a sweeping claim that the result was fully accurate despite the errors just listed. Read the two sections together after drafting them and ask whether they agree with each other and with the rest of the write-up: precautions claimed should match the method, and errors admitted should match the spread in the readings. When the sections agree with the evidence, they strengthen the entire practical.

sections.h2: Checking the Two Sections Together
paras: Before submission, check the precautions and errors sections as a pair, since they should tell a consistent story about the experiment. A precaution that was followed should not reappear as an uncontrolled error, and an error that is admitted should not have an obvious precaution that you claim to have taken but clearly did not. If you find such a contradiction, correct the section that is wrong rather than leaving both standing, because examiners read these sections together and contradictions stand out. Also check that the sections are proportionate: a short, well-controlled experiment needs only a few lines, while a longer experiment with several sensitive steps may need more.

Finally, read the sections aloud and ask whether a stranger could understand, from them alone, what was risky about this experiment and how far the result can be trusted. If the answer is yes, the sections are doing their job, and they will lift the mark of the whole write-up. Keep a personal list of the precautions and errors that recur in your subject, such as parallax, zero error, and end-point overshoot, and learn what each one means so you can use them correctly rather than copying them blindly. Over the year, these two short sections will teach you more about experimental thinking than any other part of the notebook. More guides are on the [blog](/blog/) and the [home page](/).

points: Write precautions as specific actions actually taken, not vague intentions.
Match every precaution to a real risk in your method.
Name sources of error linked to your own readings.
Avoid generic phrases such as human error with no detail.
Check that precautions, errors, method, and data agree with each other.

faqs.q: How many precautions should I write for one experiment?
faqs.a: Three or four specific, relevant precautions are usually enough. Quality matters more than quantity, and a long generic list copied from another experiment weakens the section rather than strengthening it.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a precaution and a source of error?
faqs.a: A precaution is a step taken to prevent an error, such as reading a scale at eye level. A source of error is a factor that may still have affected the result, such as variation when reading the scale, judged after seeing the data.

faqs.q: Should I admit errors if my result looks good?
faqs.a: Yes, every real measurement has limits, and admitting them honestly earns marks. Name the plausible errors, link them to your readings, and say how far they limit confidence in the result.

faqs.q: Why should I avoid writing human error as a source of error?
faqs.a: Because it explains nothing: it does not say what went wrong, how it affected the readings, or how large the effect was. Name the specific fault, such as overshooting an end point or misreading a scale, instead.

title: Plotting Graphs from Lab Data Correctly
desc: Plot lab graphs correctly: choose sensible scales, label axes with units, draw a best-fit line, and read gradients and intercepts with confidence.
intro: A graph turns a table of lab readings into a picture that reveals patterns, checks whether a relationship is straight or curved, and lets you read values that were never directly measured. Examiners mark graphs for sensible scales, labelled axes, accurate plotting, and a well-drawn best-fit line, so a careless graph can lose marks even when the underlying readings are good. Many pupils rush the graph after spending care on the table, but the graph deserves the same patience, because it is often the part of the practical that carries the final result. This guide covers choosing scales, plotting points, drawing lines, and reading gradients and intercepts correctly.

sections.h2: Choosing Axes and Scales
paras: Start by deciding which quantity goes on each axis: the quantity you changed, the independent variable, goes on the horizontal axis, and the quantity you measured, the dependent variable, goes on the vertical axis. Label each axis with the quantity and its unit, for example length in centimetres, and write the labels clearly along the axes, not squeezed into a corner. Choose a scale that spreads the plotted points over most of the graph paper, because a graph squeezed into one corner wastes the paper and makes reading values inaccurate. A good scale uses simple steps, such as one, two, or five units per large square, so that points can be plotted and read without awkward arithmetic.

Avoid scales that are difficult to use, such as three or seven units per square, since they invite plotting errors and make the graph hard for the examiner to check. Work out the range of each quantity from your table, then pick a scale that fits that range comfortably across the page, leaving a small margin at the edges. Mark the scale numbers at regular intervals along each axis, evenly spaced, and do not change the step size partway along an axis. If a quantity does not start near zero, you may start the axis at a sensible value above zero, but say so clearly and keep the intervals even, so the graph is honest about what it shows.

sections.h2: Plotting Points Accurately
paras: Plot each point from your table as a small, neat cross or dot, placed exactly where the two values meet, and check each point against the table as you plot it. Work through the table row by row, and after plotting, look back over the points to see whether they form a sensible pattern, since a point far from the pattern usually means a plotting error or a misread value. If you find such a point, check the table value and the scale before assuming the experiment went wrong, because most stray points are plotting mistakes rather than experimental ones. Plot in pencil so a wrong point can be erased cleanly, and do not join the points dot to dot unless the task specifically asks for it.

Keep the plotted points visible after drawing any line, so the examiner can see that the line was fitted to the points rather than drawn first and the points invented around it. Use a sharp pencil for points, since thick blobs hide the exact position and make checking impossible, and make the crosses small but clear. Label the graph with a title stating what is plotted against what, and write it above the graph where it is easy to find. Accurate plotting is slow work, but it is the foundation of everything the graph is used for, from checking a relationship to reading a gradient. For more study material, see the [solved notes](/solved.html) and the [book collection](/books.html).

sections.h2: Drawing a Best-Fit Line
paras: When the points suggest a straight-line relationship, draw a single straight best-fit line with a ruler, positioned so that the points are spread evenly on both sides of it, rather than joining the points one by one. A best-fit line represents the overall trend of the data, smoothing out the small random scatter in individual readings, so it will not pass through every point, and that is correct. Aim for roughly equal numbers of points above and below the line, and give extra weight to points that follow the trend closely rather than forcing the line through an obvious outlier. Draw the line thin and straight, extending it only as far as the plotted data unless you are asked to extend it for a reading.

If the points form a curve rather than a straight line, draw a smooth curve through the general trend instead, using a steady hand and keeping the curve smooth rather than wobbly through every point. Do not draw a zigzag line that visits every point in turn, since that treats random scatter as real pattern and destroys the purpose of the graph. After drawing the line, step back and check it: does it follow the overall direction of the points, and would a small shift improve the balance? A well-drawn line is the difference between a graph that merely displays data and a graph that can be used to find a result.

diagram.alt: What Makes a Good Lab Graph
diagram.caption: Five qualities of a graph the examiner can read and trust.

sections.h2: Reading Gradients from a Graph
paras: The gradient of a straight-line graph tells you how fast one quantity changes with the other, and it is found by choosing two points on the best-fit line, far apart, and dividing the vertical change by the horizontal change. Choose points on the line itself, not plotted data points, and mark them clearly on the graph, for example with a triangle showing the two changes, so the examiner can check your working. Read the coordinates of those points carefully from the axes, using the scale, and show the subtraction for both changes before dividing, including the unit of the gradient, which comes from dividing the vertical unit by the horizontal unit. A gradient worked from points close together is inaccurate, so always use a large triangle spanning much of the line.

Show the gradient calculation beside the graph or beneath it, step by step, with the two points named and the arithmetic visible, rather than presenting only a final number. If the gradient has a physical meaning in your experiment, such as a speed or a constant, state that meaning and the unit together, so the result is more than an abstract number. Check the sign of the gradient: a line rising left to right has a positive gradient, while a falling line has a negative one, and a wrong sign usually means the changes were subtracted in the wrong order. A careful gradient, with its triangle marked on the graph, is one of the most reliable marks in a practical.

sections.h2: Intercepts and Reading Values from a Graph
paras: The intercept is where the best-fit line crosses an axis, and it is read directly from the graph by extending the line to the axis if necessary, using a ruler and a dashed extension where the line goes beyond the data. Read the intercept value from the scale at the crossing point, and state which axis it belongs to, since the vertical intercept and the horizontal intercept are different values with different meanings. Intercepts often have a physical meaning, such as a starting value before the experiment began, so state that meaning where your experiment gives it one, and give the unit. An intercept read from a carelessly extended line is unreliable, so extend the line steadily and check that it follows the same direction as the fitted part.

Graphs are also used to read values between or beyond the measured points, by finding a value on one axis, moving to the line, and reading across to the other axis, a process that works best within the range of the data. Reading between measured points is usually reliable when the relationship is smooth, while reading far beyond the data is risky, since the relationship may change outside the measured range, so note that caution in your conclusion where it applies. Always mark the reading lines lightly on the graph or describe the values used, so the examiner can verify the reading rather than trusting a bare number. A graph used this carefully turns raw readings into a result the examiner can follow and believe. More guides are on the [blog](/blog/) and the [home page](/).

points: Put the changed quantity on the horizontal axis and the measured one on the vertical axis.
Choose simple scales that spread points over most of the page.
Plot small, neat points and check each one against the table.
Draw one best-fit line balancing the points, not a dot-to-dot zigzag.
Find gradients from a large triangle on the line, and mark it on the graph.

faqs.q: Which quantity goes on which axis of a lab graph?
faqs.a: The quantity you changed goes on the horizontal axis, and the quantity you measured goes on the vertical axis. Label each axis with the quantity and its unit.

faqs.q: How do I choose a good graph scale?
faqs.a: Pick simple steps, such as one, two, or five units per large square, that spread your points over most of the page. Avoid awkward steps such as three or seven units per square, which invite plotting errors.

faqs.q: Should a best-fit line pass through every plotted point?
faqs.a: No, a best-fit line shows the overall trend and smooths out small random scatter, so it will not pass through every point. Position it so points are spread evenly on both sides of it.

faqs.q: How do I find a gradient accurately?
faqs.a: Choose two points on the best-fit line far apart, mark a large triangle on the graph, and divide the vertical change by the horizontal change. Show both changes and the unit in your working.

faqs.q: Can I read values beyond my measured data from a graph?
faqs.a: Reading between measured points is usually reliable for a smooth relationship, but reading far beyond the data is risky because the relationship may change. Note that caution in your conclusion where it applies.

title: Lab Safety Rules Every Pupil Must Follow
desc: Follow essential lab safety rules for chemicals, glassware, and flames, and know what to do first if something spills, breaks, or catches fire.
kw: lab safety rules pupils must follow
intro: Laboratory safety rules exist because school laboratories contain real hazards: chemicals that can burn or stain, glassware that can break into sharp pieces, and flames that can catch clothing or hair alight. Most lab accidents are preventable, and they usually happen when a simple rule is ignored, such as running in the lab, tasting a chemical, or heating a closed container. Knowing the rules is not enough; you must follow them every time, even when the experiment seems simple, because habits formed in easy practicals protect you in harder ones. This guide covers the essential safety rules for chemicals, glassware, and flames, and what to do first when something goes wrong.

sections.h2: General Behaviour in the Laboratory
paras: Enter the laboratory calmly, go to your assigned place, and listen to the teacher's instructions before touching any apparatus or chemical, since many accidents happen in the first minutes when pupils handle equipment before the method is explained. Do not run, push, or play around in the lab, and keep bags and coats away from benches and walkways where they cause trips or knock apparatus over. Wear the eye protection your teacher provides whenever it is required, and tie back long hair and tuck in loose clothing or sleeves before starting work, because hair and cloth catch fire far more easily than pupils expect. If you are unsure about any instruction, ask before acting rather than guessing, since a question asked early prevents an accident later.

Keep your bench tidy throughout the practical, with only the apparatus and materials for the current step in front of you, and put stoppers back on bottles immediately after use so chemicals cannot be knocked over or mixed up. Never eat, drink, or chew in the laboratory, and never taste or smell a chemical directly to identify it, since even familiar-looking substances can be harmful. Wash your hands at the end of the practical and after handling any chemical, and report any accident, spill, or breakage to the teacher at once, however small it seems. A calm, tidy, attentive pupil is the safest person in any laboratory.

sections.h2: Chemicals: Handling and Spills
paras: Handle chemicals exactly as your teacher instructs, using the amounts and concentrations given, and never mix chemicals together to see what happens, since unexpected reactions can produce heat, gas, or splashes. Read the label on every bottle before you use it, checking the name and any hazard warning, and take only what you need, returning nothing to a stock bottle once it has been poured out, because returned chemical may be contaminated. Carry bottles with one hand under the base and the other around the neck or side, keeping them low over the bench, and pour slowly with the label facing your hand so drips do not hide the name. If a chemical contacts your skin or eyes, tell the teacher immediately and follow their instructions, which usually include washing with plenty of water.

If a chemical spills, do not try to clean it up on your own with paper towels or by wiping it towards yourself; step back, warn pupils nearby, and tell the teacher straight away, since the right response depends on the chemical spilled. Keep the spill contained by not walking through it, and do not pour water on a spill unless the teacher tells you to, because water makes some spills worse. Learn where the safety equipment in your laboratory is, such as the eye wash, the first aid box, and the spill kit, before you need it, by asking your teacher to point them out at the start of the year. Knowing what to do first, which is to tell the teacher and step back, turns a frightening spill into a managed incident. For more study material, see the [solved notes](/solved.html) and the [book collection](/books.html).

sections.h2: Glassware: Breakage and Sharp Edges
paras: Treat all glassware as fragile, even thick-looking beakers and flasks, and place it gently on the bench rather than sliding or dropping it into place. Check glassware before use for chips or cracks, especially around rims and joints, and hand any damaged piece to the teacher instead of using it, since a cracked vessel can break under heat or pressure. Carry glassware with both hands where it is large, keep it away from the edge of the bench, and never use a glass item as a hammer, stirrer, or lever unless it is designed for that purpose. Hot glass looks exactly like cold glass, so never pick up glassware that has been heated without checking with your teacher or using the proper holder.

If glass breaks, stop work, warn pupils nearby, and tell the teacher immediately, and do not pick up broken pieces with your bare hands, since even tiny shards cut easily. Your teacher will show you the safe way to clear breakage, usually with a brush and dustpan into a special container, not the ordinary bin, and the area should be checked for small pieces before work resumes. If you cut yourself, however small the cut seems, tell the teacher at once so it can be cleaned and covered properly, and do not continue handling chemicals with an uncovered cut. Respect for glassware, and a calm response to breakage, prevents most laboratory cuts entirely.

diagram.alt: What to Do First in a Lab Incident
diagram.caption: The first steps when something spills, breaks, or catches fire.

sections.h2: Flames, Heating, and Hot Equipment
paras: Treat every flame as a burn risk, light burners only as your teacher instructs, and never leave a lit burner unattended or point a heated test tube towards yourself or another pupil. When heating a liquid in a test tube, warm it gently, move the tube through the flame rather than holding it in one spot, and angle the mouth away from everyone, since heated liquid can bubble up suddenly and spit out. Never heat a closed container, because trapped gas or vapour builds pressure and can burst the container, and never look directly into a vessel you are heating. Turn burners off as soon as heating is finished, and check that the flame is truly out before moving on.

Handle hot equipment only with the proper holders, tongs, or heat-resistant mats, and place hot items on a heat-resistant surface, never directly on a bench or near paper. Remember that metal and glass stay hot long after heating, so warn others if an item is hot and wait for it to cool before putting it away. If clothing catches fire, the rule is to stop, drop, and roll, and to call for the teacher immediately, rather than running, which fans the flames. If a small fire starts in a container, do not try to fight it yourself with water unless your teacher directs you; step back, tell the teacher, and let them use the correct extinguisher or cover. Calm, prompt reporting is the safest response to any fire.

sections.h2: Safety as a Habit, Not a List
paras: Safety rules only protect you when they become habits, followed without thinking in every practical, not rules remembered for a test and forgotten in the lab. Build a personal start-of-practical routine: hair tied back, sleeves secure, eye protection on where required, bench tidy, and instructions heard before touching anything, and run through it every time until it is automatic. During the practical, keep checking your own behaviour: are you pouring slowly, is the burner off when not needed, is the glassware away from the edge? These small self-checks take seconds and prevent most accidents, and they are exactly the habits examiners and teachers notice when they judge a pupil's laboratory manner.

Finally, take responsibility for the safety of others as well as yourself, by warning a classmate who is about to make a mistake, reporting hazards you spot, and never distracting someone who is handling a flame or a chemical. If you see a spill, a cracked flask, or a burner left on, tell the teacher even if it is not your bench, because a hazard ignored becomes someone's accident. Laboratories are safe places when everyone follows the same rules, and your own steady example helps the whole class stay safe. A pupil who works safely every time is a pupil teachers trust with harder, more interesting practical work. More guides are on the [blog](/blog/) and the [home page](/).

points: Listen to instructions before touching any apparatus or chemical.
Wear eye protection where required and tie back hair and loose clothing.
Never taste, smell directly, eat, or drink in the laboratory.
Report every spill, breakage, or accident to the teacher at once.
Never heat a closed container or point a heated tube at anyone.

faqs.q: What should I do first if a chemical spills?
faqs.a: Step back, warn pupils nearby, and tell the teacher immediately. Do not try to clean it up alone and do not pour water on it unless the teacher tells you to, since the right response depends on the chemical.

faqs.q: What should I do if glassware breaks?
faqs.a: Stop work, warn others, and tell the teacher at once. Do not pick up broken pieces with bare hands; your teacher will clear them safely with a brush and dustpan into a special container.

faqs.q: Why must long hair be tied back in the laboratory?
faqs.a: Because hair catches fire easily and can dip into chemicals or flames when you lean over a bench. Tying it back and tucking in loose sleeves removes a common and preventable burn risk.

faqs.q: Can I look into a test tube while heating it?
faqs.a: No, never look into a vessel you are heating, and always angle the mouth away from yourself and others. Heated liquid can bubble up suddenly and spit out of the tube.

title: A One-Week Revision Plan for Practical Notebooks and Viva
desc: Use your final week wisely: split seven days between notebook review, diagram practice, and viva rehearsal so you walk in calm, organised, and ready.
kw: one week revision plan practical notebooks viva
intro: The final week before a practical examination is too short to learn everything from scratch, but it is plenty of time to turn a year's notebook work into confident performance, if it is used in the right order. Pupils who spend the whole week only reading notes arrive with tidy memories but shaky hands, while pupils who spend it only redoing experiments arrive tired and unsure of the theory. The best final week splits the time three ways: reviewing the notebook, practising diagrams and graphs, and rehearsing spoken viva answers, with rest built in so the exam day starts fresh. This plan shows how to divide seven days so each part gets its share without panic.

sections.h2: Day One and Two: Review the Notebook
paras: Spend the first two days reading through your practical notebook from front to back, one experiment at a time, and for each one, cover the result and ask yourself what the aim was, what method was used, and what the result showed. Write a one-line summary for each experiment in a separate revision sheet, in your own words, so that by the end of day two you have a short, personal index of the whole year that you can reread in minutes. Mark any experiment you cannot summarise, any table you cannot explain, and any diagram whose labels you cannot name, and put those pages at the top of your list for the rest of the week. This review is not about memorising the notebook word for word; it is about finding the weak pages while there is still time to fix them.

While reviewing, also check the notebook itself for presentation problems that can still be corrected, such as a missing index entry, an unsigned page, or a table without units, and fix them now rather than discovering them on exam morning. If a page is genuinely incomplete because an experiment was missed, tell your teacher honestly and ask what to do, rather than copying another pupil's work to fill the gap. A notebook reviewed this carefully becomes familiar ground: on exam day, when the examiner opens any page, you will already know what is on it. Two steady days of review, with short breaks and no late-night cramming, build the foundation for everything that follows.

sections.h2: Day Three and Four: Diagrams and Graphs Practice
paras: Use days three and four for hands-on practice, redrawing the diagrams and graphs from your notebook without copying them, and checking each attempt against the original. Choose the diagrams you found hardest during review, such as a specimen drawing with many labels or a graph with a gradient to find, and practise each one until you can draw it cleanly in a reasonable time. Time yourself loosely, since exam practicals have limits, but do not rush at the cost of accuracy: a diagram drawn steadily with correct labels beats a hurried one with crossed lines. After each practice drawing, compare it with the notebook version and note one thing to improve, such as larger size, straighter label lines, or a clearer title.

Practise graphs the same way, by taking a table from your notebook, choosing a fresh scale, plotting the points, and drawing the best-fit line, then reading a gradient or intercept from it.
