faqs.a: No. Marks show readiness, but your interest matters too, because a year of studying a disliked subject is a heavy cost. Choose where strong marks and genuine interest overlap.

faqs.q: What should I ask my college about Part-II admission?
faqs.a: Ask how Part-I marks affect admission, which combinations your marks support, what the timeline and documents are, and what support exists for strengthening a weak subject.

faqs.q: My Part-I result is still pending. How do I prepare?
faqs.a: Prepare your question lists now and keep strengthening your Part-I foundations, so that when your result arrives you can act within days. BIEK Pre-Engineering Part-I is out since 2 October 2026, while other Part-I groups remain pending.

title: Didn't Clear All Six Papers? Your BIEK Pre-Engineering Recovery Plan
desc: Cleared some BIEK Pre-Engineering papers but not all six? Plan your recovery by papers passed, understand the ungraded rule and use scrutiny wisely.
kw: BIEK pre-engineering recovery plan papers passed
intro: If your BIEK Pre-Engineering Part-I result, announced on 2 October 2026, shows fewer than six papers passed, you are far from alone, and you are far from finished. Out of 14,683 students who appeared, 6,310 passed all six papers, which means 8,373 students did not clear all six, spread across every possible count: 79 passed five papers, 747 passed four, 1,827 passed three, 1,864 passed two, and 1,783 passed one. Each of those groups faces a different recovery task, and the biggest mistake is treating them all as the same failure. This article builds your recovery plan from your own papers-passed count, explains the ungraded rule that may sit behind your result, and shows how scrutiny fits, or does not fit, into your next steps. Recovery is not a single road; it is a set of roads, and your count tells you which one is yours.

sections.h2: First, Read Your Result for What It Actually Says
paras: Recovery starts with an honest reading of your result, and the gazette is the best place to do it, because it groups candidates by papers passed and lists marks paper by paper. Find your entry, note your papers-passed group, and write down, for each paper, whether you passed it and what mark you received. That simple list is your recovery map: the papers on it that you passed are finished business, and the papers on it that you did not pass are the whole of your remaining task. Students who skip this step often carry a vague sense of failure into their recovery, studying everything a little and nothing properly, while students who make the list study only what remains, with full energy.

Separate two different kinds of remaining papers as you list them, because they need different responses. A paper you narrowly missed, where your mark sits close to the pass line, usually needs revision and practice rather than relearning, and it is the quickest win in your recovery. A paper where your mark is far below the line, or where you scored under 40 percent and therefore fall under the ungraded rule, needs rebuilding from the foundations, and it deserves the largest share of your study time. Be honest about which kind each paper is, and ask a teacher to check your sorting if you are unsure, because a recovery plan built on a misdiagnosis wastes the very weeks it is meant to save. Use your college's help and the board's own record to confirm your entry, and the [solved notes](/solved.html) can support your rebuilding work. The earlier guide on [reading a gazette](/blog/biek-pre-engineering-gazette-how-to-read-2026.html) explains the gazette's layout in general.

sections.h2: Planning by Papers Passed: From Five Down to One
paras: Your papers-passed count sets the scale of your recovery, and each count deserves its own plan. If you passed five papers, your task is narrow and focused: one paper stands between you and a complete result, so give that paper daily attention, practise its past papers intensively, and treat its examination as a single-paper campaign rather than a whole-year repeat. If you passed four papers, two papers remain, and your plan should split your time between them by weakness, giving the weaker paper more hours while keeping the stronger one warm with regular practice. In both cases, protect your passed papers by not neglecting them entirely in conversation, but do not waste study hours relearning what you have already passed.

If you passed three papers or fewer, your recovery is larger, and it needs a longer view and a steadier rhythm. With three papers passed, three remain, and the sensible approach is to rebuild them one at a time in order of difficulty, starting with the paper you came closest to passing, so that early progress builds confidence for the harder rebuilds. With two or one papers passed, the honest assessment is that your foundations need broad rebuilding, and you should discuss with your teachers whether your recovery runs alongside Part-II preparation, or whether a different sequence suits your situation better, since that decision depends on your college and your board's eligibility rules. Whatever your count, the principle is the same: the fewer papers you passed, the more your plan should emphasise foundations over shortcuts, and the more it should lean on teachers rather than on solitary struggle.

diagram.alt: Your Recovery Plan by Papers Passed
diagram.caption: Each papers-passed count faces a different task; start from your own count.

sections.h2: The Ungraded Rule: Under 40 Percent Means Reappear
paras: Behind many recovery plans sits the new grading rule that BIEK applies under the IBCC and Sindh Universities and Boards Department decision: a candidate who scores under 40 percent in any paper is graded as ungraded in that paper, which means the paper is not passed, and the candidate reappears in that paper subject to eligibility. This rule changes how you should read a low mark, because a mark in the thirties is not a narrow miss to be nudged over the line by rechecking, but a paper to be genuinely relearned and reappeared in. Students who misunderstand the rule sometimes spend their recovery window chasing a checking error in a paper that actually needs rebuilding, and they lose the time that rebuilding required.

If one or more of your papers falls under the ungraded rule, make those papers the centre of your plan, and be realistic about what rebuilding them takes. Return to the textbook chapters behind the paper, work through them with a teacher's guidance, and practise until you can solve typical questions without help, because a reappearance that repeats the same preparation usually repeats the same result. Check your eligibility for reappearing with your college, since reappearance is subject to eligibility and the conditions are the board's, not yours to assume. The guide to the [new grading system and the ungraded rule](/blog/biek-new-grading-system-ungraded-40-percent.html) explains the rule's background, and your teachers can confirm how it applies to your specific papers.

sections.h2: Scrutiny: What Rs 1,000 Per Paper Buys — and What It Does Not
paras: Scrutiny is the option students reach for first and understand least, so it deserves a plain explanation. BIEK's scrutiny fee is Rs 1,000 per paper, and no scrutiny deadline was published on BIEK's pages at the time of checking, which means you must confirm the current position with your college or the board rather than assuming a date. Scrutiny, like rechecking elsewhere, is a checking process: it verifies that your paper was handled correctly, and it does not re-mark your answers or rescue a paper whose answers were weak. It fits the student who has a specific reason to suspect a handling error in a particular paper, and it fits that student only.

Before paying Rs 1,000 for any paper, ask yourself whether you have such a reason. Did your mark in that paper fall far below your performance in class tests and your own sense of the examination? Did a teacher who knows your work find the mark surprising? Is there a specific anomaly, such as a paper whose total looks inconsistent with its parts? If you can answer yes with specifics, scrutiny may be worth the fee for that paper. If your honest answer is that the paper simply went badly, the fee is better spent on nothing at all, and the time is better spent rebuilding the paper for reappearance. Scrutiny and recovery are not alternatives; scrutiny checks the past result, while recovery builds the next one, and most students with papers to clear need the second far more than the first. For the Sindh process in detail, see [scrutiny and rechecking in Sindh](/blog/board-result-scrutiny-rechecking-sindh-how-to-apply.html).

sections.h2: Your Recovery Timetable Without Invented Dates
paras: A recovery plan needs a timetable, but this article will not invent one for you, because reappearance dates and second sittings depend on board eligibility and board announcements that this article does not presume. What you can timetable today is the preparation, and preparation timetabled well is what makes any future date workable. Divide your remaining papers into weekly blocks, giving each paper a set number of study days per week in proportion to its weakness, and end each week with a self-test on the papers you studied. Keep a simple log of what you covered and what you still cannot do, because that log becomes the evidence you show a teacher when you ask for help, and it keeps your recovery honest when motivation dips.

Alongside preparation, keep two administrative tasks on your list: confirming your eligibility for reappearance with your college, and confirming the current scrutiny position, including its fee and any deadline the board has since published, before you spend money on it. Both confirmations cost a single visit or message each, and both prevent the two costliest recovery mistakes, which are preparing for a sitting you are not eligible for, and paying for a process whose window has closed. Recovery is not glamorous work, and it rarely feels as good as a fresh start, but students who do it properly, paper by paper and week by week, routinely turn a partial result into a complete one. Your count tells you where you stand; your plan decides where you finish, and the plan starts with the next study session, not with the next announcement.

points: 8,373 of 14,683 candidates did not clear all six papers: 79 passed five, 747 four, 1,827 three, 1,864 two, 1,783 one.
Your papers-passed count sets your recovery scale, from a single-paper campaign to broad rebuilding.
Under 40 percent in any paper means ungraded, and the candidate reappears subject to eligibility.
BIEK scrutiny costs Rs 1,000 per paper, and no scrutiny deadline was published at check time.
Scrutiny checks handling errors; it does not re-mark weak answers, so rebuilding remains the core of recovery.

faqs.q: How many BIEK Pre-Engineering students did not clear all six papers?
faqs.a: 8,373 of the 14,683 who appeared: 79 passed five papers, 747 passed four, 1,827 passed three, 1,864 passed two, and 1,783 passed one paper.

faqs.q: What does ungraded mean under the new grading rule?
faqs.a: Scoring under 40 percent in any paper means the paper is graded as ungraded, not passed, and the candidate reappears in that paper subject to eligibility.

faqs.q: What does BIEK scrutiny cost, and is there a deadline?
faqs.a: The scrutiny fee is Rs 1,000 per paper. No scrutiny deadline was published on BIEK's pages at the time of checking, so confirm the current position with your college or the board.

faqs.q: Should I apply for scrutiny or focus on rebuilding my papers?
faqs.a: Scrutiny only fits a paper where you have a specific reason to suspect a handling error. For most papers that simply went badly, rebuilding for reappearance is the useful path.

faqs.q: Can I reappear in my remaining papers?
faqs.a: Reappearance is subject to eligibility under the board's rules. Confirm your eligibility and the available sittings with your college before planning around a particular date.

title: Karachi Board 11th Class Result 2026 Announced — BIEK HSC Part-I Pre-Medical, Commerce, Arts & More
desc: BIEK Karachi announced the remaining HSC Part-I 2026 results on 26 October 2026. Check by roll number, gazette and app, with group-wise pass percentages.
kw: Karachi board 11th class result 2026, BIEK HSC Part-I result 2026 announced, BIEK 1st year result 2026 check by roll number
intro: First-year students in Karachi have their results. The Board of Intermediate Education Karachi (BIEK) announced the Intermediate Part-I (Class XI / 1st Year) Annual Examination 2026 results for all remaining groups on Monday, 26 October 2026, on the instructions of BIEK Chairman Faqir Muhammad Lakho. The announcement, recorded in BIEK Press Release No. BIEK/PR/152/2026 dated 26 October 2026, covers Science Pre-Medical, Science General, Commerce (Regular and Private), Humanities/Arts (Regular and Private), Special Candidates (Arts Regular) and Home Economics. It completes the Karachi first-year picture for 2026: the Science Pre-Engineering group had already been announced separately earlier in October, on 2 October 2026, so this post is only about the groups declared on 26 October. This guide explains how to check your result by seat (roll) number on the board website and app, how to use the official gazette, what each group's pass percentage was, what the new 'Ungraded' rule means if you scored below 40 per cent in a paper, and what to do next.

sections.h2: The announcement: which groups were declared on 26 October 2026
paras: BIEK does not release all of its intermediate groups on a single day. For the HSC Part-I Annual Examination 2026, the Science Pre-Engineering group came first, on 2 October 2026. The 26 October 2026 announcement covers everything else: Science Pre-Medical, Science General, Commerce Regular, Commerce Private, Humanities/Arts Regular, Humanities/Arts Private, Special Candidates (Arts Regular) and Home Economics. If your group is Pre-Engineering, your result was already out weeks ago — do not wait for a second announcement for that group.

The results are published as gazette lists in which candidates are grouped by how many papers they passed, with the marks for each paper shown beside the seat number. That format matters for first-year students: unlike a simple pass-or-fail list, the gazette tells you exactly which papers you cleared and which ones still need work. Keep your seat number slip ready before you start searching, because every checking method — the website, the app and the gazette — is built around that number. The online copy of your result is provisional; the board's own record, issued through the board and your college, is the official one.

Students and parents should be careful about one common confusion. BIEK is Karachi's intermediate board, while the Board of Secondary Education Karachi (BSEK) handles Karachi's matric (SSC) examinations. A first-year result belongs to BIEK, not BSEK. Our guide to the [difference between BSEK and BIEK](/blog/bsek-biek-difference-which-board-handles-what.html) explains which board handles what, and the [books catalogue](/books.html) and [solved notes library](/solved.html) can help with the next class once you know your result.

sections.h2: How to check your Karachi 11th class result online
paras: The most direct way to see your result is the board's own website. On announcement day the site gets heavy traffic, so if a page does not load on the first try, wait a few minutes and try again rather than submitting the same search repeatedly. The steps below follow the method described in the announcement reports.

Before you begin, make sure you are looking at the HSC Part-I Annual 2026 result for your own group. Selecting the wrong group — for example, Commerce when you sat Pre-Medical — will simply return no record, even though your result has been announced. Double-check the group name on your admit card before searching.
bullets: Step 1: Open the official BIEK website at www.biek.edu.pk and go to the result section.
Step 2: Select HSC Part-I Annual Examination 2026 and then your group (for example, Science Pre-Medical or Commerce Regular).
Step 3: Enter your seat (roll) number exactly as printed on your admit card.
Step 4: Submit the search and wait for your detailed result to appear.
Step 5: Check your name, seat number and subject-wise marks, then save a screenshot or print the page for your records.

diagram.alt: How to check the BIEK 11th class result online
diagram.caption: Five steps: open biek.edu.pk, pick HSC Part-I 2026 and your group, enter your seat number.

sections.h2: Check by gazette and the official BIEK app
paras: The second method is the official result gazette: the complete PDF list of candidates' results published on the board website. For the Commerce Regular group, the board released a 172-page gazette containing the seat numbers and marks of candidates who passed one or more examination papers. Download the gazette PDF for your group, open it, and use your reader's search function — Ctrl+F on a computer, or the search option in a mobile PDF app — to find your seat number. The gazette is slower than the portal for a single student, but it is the best fallback when the website is busy, and it serves as the official record of the announcement.

BIEK also provides its results through its official Android app, available on the Google Play Store by searching for 'BIEK'. The app route uses the same seat-number search as the website. This guide uses only the checking methods confirmed in the announcement reports — the board website, the official app and the gazette. Do not pay for, or trust, result codes circulating on unofficial pages unless BIEK itself publishes one for this result. For help reading a gazette against an online result, see our guide on the [difference between a gazette and an online result](/blog/board-result-gazette-vs-online-result-difference.html).

sections.h2: Key statistics: pass percentages group by group
paras: Across the eight groups announced on 26 October 2026, 91,575 candidates appeared and 41,501 passed all of their papers, an overall pass rate of 45.32 per cent. The pass percentage here means candidates who cleared every paper of their group — six papers for Science and Arts groups, seven for Commerce and Home Economics — as reported from the board's figures. A candidate who passed some papers but not all of them is listed in the gazette under the number of papers passed, not counted in the 'passed all papers' total.

Science Pre-Medical saw 24,544 candidates appear out of 25,157 registered, with 11,966 passing all six papers — a pass rate of 48.75 per cent. Science General recorded 15,036 passes out of 30,386 who appeared, at 49.48 per cent, the highest rate among the large groups. Commerce Regular, the largest single group after Science General, had 22,693 appear and 9,332 pass all papers (41.12 per cent), while Commerce Private recorded 628 passes out of 1,413 who appeared (44.44 per cent).

Humanities (Arts) Regular recorded 3,748 passes out of 10,678 who appeared (35.10 per cent), and Humanities (Arts) Private recorded 692 passes out of 1,623 (42.64 per cent). Special Candidates (Arts Regular) had the highest pass rate of the announcement at 59.79 per cent (58 out of 97), while Home Economics recorded the lowest at 29.08 per cent (41 out of 141). These are group averages, not individual verdicts: a student who passed four of six papers is much closer to completing first year than the headline percentage suggests, because only the remaining papers need to be retaken.

sections.h2: The new grading rule: what 'Ungraded' means
paras: This year's Intermediate Part-I results use a new grading system introduced following decisions by the Inter Boards Coordination Commission (IBCC) and the Sindh government's Universities and Boards Department. Under it, a candidate who scores below 40 per cent in any paper is declared 'Ungraded' in that paper. An Ungraded paper is not counted as passed, even if the candidate's overall total looks comfortable.

The practical consequence is straightforward: you must reappear in any paper in which you were declared Ungraded, provided you meet the other eligibility conditions for taking that examination. Science groups' optional subjects in this cycle were checked through E-Assessment (OMR) and E-Marking, according to the announcement reports. If a paper shows as Ungraded on your result, do not assume it will be adjusted later — watch BIEK's official announcements for the improvement and supplementary examination schedule and form submission dates, and prepare for that paper as a separate examination.

sections.h2: What to do next: scrutiny, reappearing and 12th class
paras: First, verify your details. Compare your name, seat number and subject-wise marks against your admit card, and report any mismatch to your college and the board promptly — corrections become harder once the official record is finalised. Keep a saved copy of your online result, but remember it is provisional until the board's official record is issued.

If you believe a paper was not marked correctly, BIEK's scrutiny and rechecking route is separate from simply checking the result. Apply only through BIEK's official scrutiny notice for this examination, and confirm the fee and deadline in that notice before applying — this post does not state a fee or deadline because none was verified for this announcement. Our guide to [scrutiny and rechecking in Sindh](/blog/board-result-scrutiny-rechecking-sindh-how-to-apply.html) explains how the process works in general, but the board's own notice for HSC Part-I 2026 is the authority for your application.

If you have Ungraded papers, start preparing for those papers now rather than waiting for the supplementary schedule to be published. First-year marks feed into your composite intermediate total, so a strong 12th-class performance, combined with cleared first-year papers, still leaves you well placed for university and entry-test admissions. Students who cleared everything should turn their full attention to 12th class, where the Part-II result carries the decisive weight.

diagram.alt: Your action plan after the BIEK 11th class result
diagram.caption: Check details now, then scrutiny, reappearing in Ungraded papers, or 12th class preparation.

points: BIEK Karachi announced the remaining HSC Part-I (11th class) 2026 groups on 26 October 2026; Pre-Engineering had already been announced on 2 October 2026.
Check online at www.biek.edu.pk or the official BIEK app by seat number, or search your group's official gazette PDF.
Overall pass rate for the 26 October groups: 45.32% (41,501 of 91,575 appeared passed all papers); Pre-Medical 48.75%, Science General 49.48%, Commerce Regular 41.12%.
Below 40% in any paper means 'Ungraded' in that paper — it must be retaken, even if other papers were passed.
Apply for scrutiny only through BIEK's official notice for this examination; confirm the fee and deadline there.

faqs.q: When was the Karachi board 11th class result 2026 announced?
faqs.a: The remaining HSC Part-I (11th class) groups — Pre-Medical, Science General, Commerce, Arts, Special Candidates and Home Economics — were announced on Monday, 26 October 2026, under BIEK Press Release No. BIEK/PR/152/2026. The Science Pre-Engineering group had been announced separately on 2 October 2026.

faqs.q: How can I check my BIEK 11th class result by roll number?
faqs.a: Open www.biek.edu.pk, go to the result section, select HSC Part-I Annual Examination 2026 and your group, then enter your seat (roll) number exactly as printed on your admit card. You can also use the official BIEK Android app, or search your group's gazette PDF for your seat number.

faqs.q: What was the pass percentage for BIEK Pre-Medical and Commerce Regular?
faqs.a: Pre-Medical recorded 48.75% (11,966 passed all papers out of 24,544 who appeared) and Commerce Regular recorded 41.12% (9,332 out of 22,693). Science General was 49.48% and Arts Regular was 35.10%. The overall rate across the 26 October groups was 45.32%.

faqs.q: What does 'Ungraded' mean in the BIEK 11th class result?
faqs.a: Under the new grading system, a candidate scoring below 40% in any paper is declared 'Ungraded' in that paper, and that paper is not counted as passed. The candidate must reappear in that paper, subject to the board's other eligibility conditions.

faqs.q: Where is the BIEK 11th class result gazette?

title: Karachi Board 9th Class Result 2026 Announced — BSEK Science Group, Check by Roll Number & Statistics
desc: BSEK Karachi announced the Class 9 Science Group result 2026 on 28 October 2026, with a 69.56% pass rate. Check by roll number on bsek.edu.pk from 5:30 PM.

intro: Class 9 students in Karachi have their Science Group result. The Board of Secondary Education Karachi (BSEK) announced the result of the SSC Part-I (Class IX) Science Group (Regular) First Annual Examinations 2026 on Wednesday, 28 October 2026. The result was made available on the board's official website, www.bsek.edu.pk, from 5:30 PM on the same day. Board Chairman Professor Musharraf Ali Rajput congratulated the students who passed all their papers and said transparency remained among the board's top priorities, according to the announcement reports. The overall pass percentage is 69.56 per cent: 123,757 candidates passed all papers out of 177,923 who appeared. This guide explains exactly what was announced, how to check your result by roll number, how to read a result that shows passes in only some papers, what the new 40 per cent passing rule means, and what to do next — whether you passed everything, passed some papers, or need to plan for the next examination.

sections.h2: The announcement: BSEK Class 9 Science Group, 28 October 2026
paras: This announcement is for one group only: the Class 9 Science Group (Regular) of the SSC Part-I First Annual Examinations 2026, under the Board of Secondary Education Karachi. It is not the General Group result, which was announced separately in September, and it is not an intermediate result. That distinction matters in Karachi, because two different boards handle the two levels: BSEK handles secondary (matric) examinations, while the Board of Intermediate Education Karachi (BIEK) handles intermediate examinations. Our guide to the [difference between BSEK and BIEK](/blog/bsek-biek-difference-which-board-handles-what.html) explains which board handles what, so you do not end up searching the wrong board's website.

The announcement was reported on 28 October 2026 by ProPakistani, HUM English, Pakistan Observer and Education in Karachi, all citing the board's press release issued on 28 October 2026 and the figures shared by Controller of Examinations Ahmed Khan Chhutto. The result went live on the board website at 5:30 PM, so students checking earlier in the day would not have found it. If you tried before that time and saw nothing, that was a timing issue, not a problem with your roll number. The online result is the board's published result for this group; keep your admit card and roll number slip ready, because every checking method is built around that number.

Students should also be careful about a second confusion: Karachi's Class 11 (intermediate) results were announced by BIEK on 26 October 2026, just two days earlier. That is a different board, a different class and a different result. If you are in Class 9, this post — the BSEK Science Group result of 28 October — is the one that applies to you.

sections.h2: How to check your BSEK 9th class Science result online
paras: The confirmed checking method for this result is the board's official website. On announcement evening the site receives very heavy traffic, so if a page does not load on the first try, wait a few minutes and try again rather than submitting the same search repeatedly. Use only the official website for your result: unofficial pages may copy old results, show the wrong group, or ask for personal details the board does not need.

Before you begin, confirm you are looking at the right examination: SSC Part-I (Class IX) Annual 2026, Science Group. Selecting the General Group, or a Class 10 result, will simply return no record for a Science Group candidate, even though your result has been announced. Double-check the group name on your admit card before searching.

sections.h2: Reading your result: passed all papers, some papers, or not yet
paras: The headline pass percentage counts only candidates who passed all papers. That is why the board also published a breakdown by how many papers each candidate passed. A student who passed six papers, for example, is listed in that category — not in the 'passed all papers' total, and not simply as a failure. Understanding that breakdown is essential, because it tells you exactly how much work remains: only the papers you did not pass need to be cleared in the next examination, under the board's rules.

The reported breakdown, shared by the Controller of Examinations, is: 21,999 candidates passed six papers only, 11,006 passed five papers only, 7,431 passed four papers only, 4,409 passed three papers only, 3,101 passed two papers only, and 2,439 passed one paper only. Candidates who passed only some papers will need to clear the remaining papers in the next examination as per board rules. Do not treat a partial pass as a complete pass, and do not treat it as starting again from zero either — your passed papers stand, and your effort should focus on the remaining ones.

If your result shows a paper as not passed, check the marks in that paper carefully. Under the new grading system described below, a paper below 40 per cent is not counted as passed. If you believe there is an error in your name, roll number or marks, report it to your school and the board promptly, and keep a saved copy of your online result. For general guidance on how an online result differs from a gazette record, see our guide on the [difference between a gazette and an online result](/blog/board-result-gazette-vs-online-result-difference.html).

sections.h2: Key statistics: 69.56% passed all papers
paras: According to the board's press release of 28 October 2026, a total of 180,054 students registered for the Class 9 Science Group First Annual Examinations 2026, of whom 177,923 appeared and 2,131 remained absent. Of those who appeared, 123,757 candidates passed all subjects, giving the overall pass percentage of 69.56 per cent. The board reported that 53,849 candidates failed, as reported in the announcement coverage. These are the figures that were consistently reported across the announcement reports, and this post uses no other totals for this result.

The 69.56 per cent figure is lower than the previous year's Class IX Science Group pass rate. HUM English reported that in 2025, 137,350 of the 175,511 candidates who appeared passed all their papers, a pass rate of 78.26 per cent. The drop does not change any individual student's result, but it does put this year's result in context: a larger share of candidates this year will be clearing remaining papers in the next examination, and schools and students should plan revision for those papers now rather than waiting for a later announcement.

No position-holder list for this result was reported in the announcement coverage used for this post, so none is named here. If BSEK publishes a position list separately, it will be on the board's own website, and this post does not guess at any names or marks.

sections.h2: The new grading rule: passing marks raised to 40%
paras: This is the first year of a new grading system for Class 9, applied from the First Annual Examinations 2026 following a decision of the Inter Boards Coordination Commission (IBCC) and the Sindh government's Universities and Boards Department. Under the new scheme, BSEK has raised the passing marks from 33 per cent to 40 per cent for Class 9 from 2026 (and for Class 10 from 2027). In practical terms, a paper with less than 40 per cent marks is not counted as passed, even if the candidate's overall total looks comfortable.

That change explains why some students who expected to pass on the old 33 per cent threshold may find a paper marked as not passed this year. It is not a marking error: it is the new threshold. The same 40 per cent rule was applied in Karachi's intermediate results this year, where a paper below 40 per cent is declared 'Ungraded'. Our guide to the [new grading system and the 40 per cent rule](/blog/biek-new-grading-system-ungraded-40-percent.html) explains how that rule works at intermediate level; for Class 9, the key point is the same — every paper must individually reach 40 per cent to count as passed.

For revision, that means subject-by-subject preparation, not just total-marks preparation. A student who passed five papers and missed one by a small margin should focus revision on that one paper's syllabus, past papers and weak topics, rather than re-studying everything. The [books catalogue](/books.html) and [solved notes library](/solved.html) can help with that focused revision once you know which papers remain.

sections.h2: What to do next: reappearing, scrutiny and Class 10
paras: First, verify your details. Compare your name, roll number and subject-wise result against your admit card, and report any mismatch to your school and the board promptly — corrections become harder once the official record is finalised. Keep a saved copy of your online result, but remember it is provisional until the board's official record is issued through your school.

If you passed all papers, your next step is Class 10. Start with the subjects you found hardest in Class 9, because Class 10 builds directly on them, and keep your Class 9 notes for revision. If you passed some papers only, make a short list of the remaining papers and start preparing for them now, under the board's next-examination rules — do not wait for a reminder. If you believe a paper was not marked correctly, BSEK's scrutiny and rechecking route is separate from simply checking the result. Apply only through BSEK's official scrutiny notice for this examination, and confirm the fee and deadline in that notice before applying — this post does not state a fee or deadline because none was verified for this announcement. Our guide to [scrutiny and rechecking in Sindh](/blog/board-result-scrutiny-rechecking-sindh-how-to-apply.html) explains how the process works in general, but the board's own notice for SSC Part-I 2026 is the authority for your application.

Finally, do not rely on any SMS code, gazette page count or supplementary date for this result unless BSEK itself publishes it. No SMS code was verified in the announcement reports for this result, so this post does not give one. The confirmed route is the official website, www.bsek.edu.pk, from 5:30 PM on 28 October 2026. Our [after-result guide for BSEK Class 9 students](/blog/bsek-karachi-9th-class-result-2026-after-result-guide.html) covers the next steps in more detail once you have your result in hand.

title: Active Recall: Testing Yourself with the Book Closed
desc: Close the book and test yourself before checking: a simple active recall routine that turns passive re-reading into real memory for school exams.
intro: Most pupils revise by reading a chapter again and again, and most pupils are surprised when the exam paper feels unfamiliar. The reason is simple: reading feels easy, so it feels like learning, but it only trains your eyes to recognise words that are already in front of you. Active recall works the opposite way. You close the book, ask yourself a question, and try to produce the answer from memory before you look. That effort of pulling an answer out of your head is what strengthens the memory itself, so the answer is there again when the exam asks for it. This article explains a closed-book routine you can use for any subject, starting tonight, with nothing more than your notebook and a pen.

sections.h2: Why Re-reading Feels Easy and Fails
paras: Re-reading creates a comfortable illusion. When the answer is sitting on the page, your brain recognises it and mistakes that recognition for knowledge, so you turn the page feeling confident. In the exam hall, though, there is no page to recognise: the question asks you to produce the answer, not to recognise it. That is a completely different mental job, and it is one that re-reading never practises. Pupils who only re-read often say the paper felt harder than their revision did, and this gap between recognition and recall is exactly why.

Active recall closes that gap by making revision match the exam. Every time you try to answer with the book closed, you practise the same skill the exam will demand: retrieving information without help. The attempt does not have to be perfect to be useful. Even a half-remembered answer that you then correct teaches your brain more than a smooth re-reading of the same page, because the struggle itself marks the information as important. Short, effortful attempts beat long, comfortable reading every time, and they take less time too.

sections.h2: The Closed-Book Routine, Step by Step
paras: Start with a small chunk, never a whole chapter at once. Read one section or one set of notes carefully, then close the book and write down everything you can remember about it, in your own words, without peeking. Use rough paper or the back of your notebook so the attempt feels low-pressure; this is practice, not a test, and messy recall is perfectly fine. Give yourself a few minutes of genuine effort before you open the book again, because the benefit comes from the trying, not from getting everything right first time.

Now open the book and check your recall against the original, marking what you missed or got wrong in a different colour. Do not just read the corrections: say them aloud or write them again from memory, so the corrected version gets its own retrieval attempt. Then move to the next small chunk and repeat the cycle. A single study session built this way covers less ground than a re-reading session, but what it covers actually stays with you, which is why it saves time over the whole week. You can find more study methods on the [blog](/blog/) and in the [book collection](/books.html).

diagram.caption: Repeat this cycle for each small chunk of a chapter.

sections.h2: What to Do When You Cannot Recall Anything
paras: A blank mind during recall is not a failure; it is useful information. It tells you exactly which part of the chapter has not been learned yet, and that is far more valuable than a vague feeling that you sort of know it. When you draw a blank, do not sit staring at the page for ten minutes. Open the book, re-read just that small part, close it again, and try once more. Two or three short attempts with checking in between will fix a fact far better than one long stare at the open page.

If the same point keeps slipping away, change how you store it instead of repeating the same failed attempt. Turn it into a question you can ask yourself, connect it to something you already know, or break it into smaller pieces. Pupils often find that the points they struggled most to recall are the ones they remember best in the exam, because the effort spent on them made the memory stronger. Keep a short list of your stubborn points and return to them first in your next session, rather than starting again from the beginning of the chapter.

sections.h2: Using Closed-Book Recall in Every Subject
paras: Active recall adapts to any subject because every subject has something to retrieve. In Islamiat or history, recall the main points of a lesson and the order in which events or ideas follow each other. In science, close the book and write the steps of a process, the parts of a diagram, or the meaning of a term from memory. In mathematics, cover the worked example and try to solve the problem yourself before looking at the solution, because reading a solution feels like understanding it even when you could not produce it alone.

For language subjects, recall works beautifully with vocabulary and grammar. Cover the meanings and try to write them, or read a sentence in one language and reproduce it in the other. The method also works in pairs: one pupil asks questions from the notes while the other answers with the book closed, then they swap roles. Pair recall adds a gentle pressure that feels like exam pressure, which makes it excellent preparation. Browse the [solved notes](/solved.html) for material to practise with, and start with short sessions of twenty minutes before building up.
bullets: Islamiat and history: recall lesson points and their order from memory.
Science: recall process steps, diagram parts, and term meanings with the book closed.
Mathematics: cover the worked example and solve the problem yourself first.
Languages: cover meanings and reproduce vocabulary or sentences from memory.
Pair work: take turns asking and answering questions with the book closed.

sections.h2: Building Recall Into Your Daily Revision
paras: Recall works best as a daily habit, not as a last-minute technique. Begin each study session by recalling yesterday's topic before opening today's chapter, because that short warm-up both revises old work and tells you what needs another look. End each session the same way: close everything and spend five minutes writing down the main points of what you just studied. Those two bookends turn every session into a recall session without adding much time, and they stop the common problem of learning a chapter and then never returning to it.

Keep the sessions short and regular rather than long and rare. Twenty to thirty minutes of closed-book recall, done most days, will beat a three-hour re-reading marathon before the exam, because memory grows through repeated retrieval spread over days. Track your progress simply: note which topics you recalled well and which needed checking, and let that list decide tomorrow's session. Over a few weeks, the list of weak topics shrinks, and that visible progress is one of the most motivating sights in revision. More practical guidance is on the [home page](/) and the [blog](/blog/).

points: Close the book and try to produce answers from memory before checking.
Work in small chunks: read one section, recall it, check it, then move on.
A blank recall is useful information, not failure: re-read the small part and try again.
Use recall in every subject, from science processes to language vocabulary.
Start each session by recalling yesterday's topic and end by recalling today's.

faqs.q: What is active recall in simple words?
faqs.a: Active recall means trying to remember an answer before looking at it. You close the book, ask yourself a question, and produce the answer from memory. The effort of retrieving the answer is what makes the memory stronger.

faqs.q: How is active recall different from re-reading?
faqs.a: Re-reading trains recognition, because the answer is already in front of you. Active recall trains retrieval, which is what an exam actually requires. That is why re-reading can feel confident yet fail in the exam hall.

faqs.q: What should I do if I cannot recall anything at all?
faqs.a: Treat the blank as useful information. Re-read just that small part, close the book, and try again. Two or three short attempts with checking in between will fix a fact better than staring at the open page.

faqs.q: How long should a recall session last?
faqs.a: Twenty to thirty minutes of focused recall is enough for one session, done most days. Short, regular sessions beat long, rare ones, because memory grows through repeated retrieval spread over days.

faqs.q: Can I use active recall with a study partner?
faqs.a: Yes, pair recall works very well. One pupil asks questions from the notes while the other answers with the book closed, then they swap roles. The gentle pressure of answering aloud feels like exam pressure and is excellent preparation.

title: Spaced Repetition for School Revision Without Apps
desc: No app needed: a paper-based spaced revision plan that revisits each chapter on day 1, day 3, and day 7 so knowledge stays fresh until exam day.
kw: spaced repetition school revision without apps
intro: Every pupil knows the frustration of learning a chapter well and then forgetting it a week later. That forgetting is not a personal weakness; it is how memory naturally works. New information fades quickly unless it is revisited, but each revisit slows the fading a little more. Spaced repetition is simply a plan for revisiting material at growing intervals, so you return to a chapter just as it is about to fade, and each return makes it stick longer. You do not need any app to do this. A notebook, a calendar, and a simple day 1, day 3, day 7 schedule will give you the same benefit, and this article shows exactly how to run it.

sections.h2: Why Memory Fades and How Spacing Helps
paras: When you first learn something, the memory is fresh but fragile. Without a revisit, much of it fades within a day or two, which is why a chapter studied on Monday can feel almost new again by the following Monday. Cramming fights this by repeating the material many times in one sitting, but that only creates a short-term memory that fades just as fast once the session ends. The brain treats information repeated in one burst as something needed only right now, so it does not bother storing it deeply.

Spacing works differently. When you revisit a chapter after a gap, your brain has to work a little to retrieve it, and that small effort signals that the information is still needed. Each spaced revisit therefore strengthens the memory more than a repeat inside the same session would. After a few spaced revisits, the memory becomes durable enough to survive until the exam. The schedule matters less than the principle: revisit after a gap, not immediately, and let the gaps grow as the memory gets stronger.

sections.h2: The Paper-Based Day 1, Day 3, Day 7 Plan
paras: The simplest spaced plan uses three revisits. Day 1 is the day you first learn the chapter: study it properly, make short notes, and finish with a closed-book recall of the main points. Day 3 is your first revisit: two days later, recall the chapter from your notes or from memory, spending about half the time of the original study. Day 7 is the second revisit: recall it again, more briefly, and check anything that still feels shaky. If a topic still feels weak on day 7, add one more revisit on day 14, but most school chapters will be solid after the day 7 pass.

Run this plan with a simple table in the back of your notebook. Write the chapter name, the date you learned it, and the three revisit dates, then tick each revisit off as you complete it. At the start of each study session, look at today's column and revise whatever is due, before starting anything new. This takes only a few minutes of planning each week, yet it replaces the usual pattern of learning, forgetting, and relearning from scratch. The [blog](/blog/) has more revision plans, and the [solved notes](/solved.html) are useful material for revisit sessions.

diagram.alt: The Day 1, Day 3, Day 7 Spaced Plan
diagram.caption: Three short revisits turn a fresh lesson into lasting knowledge.

sections.h2: Making Flashcards from Paper and Card
paras: Paper flashcards are the easiest tool for spaced revision, and you can make them from cut-up card or old notebooks. Write a question or a keyword on the front and the answer on the back, keeping each card to one fact: one definition, one process step, one vocabulary meaning. A card that tries to carry a whole paragraph is too big to recall quickly, so split large topics into several small cards. Number your cards or keep them in small labelled bundles by chapter, so a bundle can be picked up and reviewed in five minutes.

Use the cards inside your spaced schedule, not as a separate chore. On a revisit day, shuffle the chapter's bundle and go through it with the answer side hidden, sorting cards into two piles: known and still learning. The known pile can wait until the next revisit, while the still-learning pile gets another pass the same day or the next day. This sorting turns a dull pile of cards into a visible measure of progress, and watching the still-learning pile shrink is genuinely satisfying. Keep the cards safe in an envelope or a rubber band, because a lost bundle means rebuilding the work.

sections.h2: Fitting Spacing Around Homework and Class
paras: Pupils often worry that spaced revision means extra study time, but it mostly replaces time that would otherwise be wasted. The day 3 and day 7 revisits are short, often ten to fifteen minutes, and they replace the long relearning session you would need if the chapter had been forgotten completely. The trick is to treat revisits as the first job of a study session, before homework or new topics, because a revisit left until the end of the day is the one most likely to be skipped.

Build the plan around your real week. If you learn new chapters on school days, your revisit days will naturally fall on a mix of school days and weekends, which is fine: a weekend revisit can be a little longer and can cover two chapters at once. When a test week arrives, your spaced table becomes a ready-made revision list, showing exactly which chapters are due and which are already strong. Pupils who keep the table honestly find test weeks far less frightening, because they have been revising all along in small pieces rather than facing a mountain of forgotten work. See the [book collection](/books.html) for chapters to plan around.
bullets: Do revisits first in a study session, before homework or new topics.
Keep day 3 and day 7 revisits short: ten to fifteen minutes each.
Use weekends for slightly longer revisits covering two chapters.
Let your spaced table become your test-week revision list.

sections.h2: Common Spacing Mistakes to Avoid
paras: The most common mistake is making the gaps too short. Revisiting a chapter an hour later, or even the same evening, feels productive but gives almost no spacing benefit, because the memory has not faded enough for retrieval to require effort. Give the gap at least a day or two before the first revisit. The opposite mistake is making the gaps too long: waiting a month before returning to a chapter usually means relearning it from scratch, which wastes the benefit of the first study session entirely.

Another mistake is revisiting by re-reading instead of recalling. A spaced revisit only works if you try to retrieve the material first, with the notes closed, and use the notes to check afterwards. Re-reading on day 3 and day 7 feels comfortable but adds little strength. Finally, do not abandon the plan after one missed day. A missed revisit is not a failed plan: simply do it the next day and carry on. Spaced revision rewards consistency over weeks, not perfection on any single day, so a plan followed most of the time will still transform your memory. More tips are on the [home page](/) and the [blog](/blog/).

points: Memory fades fast unless revisited; each spaced revisit makes it last longer.
Use the day 1, day 3, day 7 pattern: learn, revisit after two days, revisit after a week.
Track revisits in a simple table at the back of your notebook.
Make one-fact paper flashcards and sort them into known and still-learning piles.
Revisit by recalling with notes closed, not by re-reading, and never quit over one missed day.

faqs.q: Do I need an app for spaced repetition?
faqs.a: No. A notebook table with chapter names and revisit dates works just as well for school revision. The benefit comes from revisiting after gaps, not from any software.

faqs.q: Why day 1, day 3, and day 7?
faqs.a: These gaps are long enough that retrieval takes real effort, which strengthens memory, but short enough that the chapter is not forgotten completely. Most school chapters become solid after the day 7 revisit.

faqs.q: How long should a revisit take?
faqs.a: A day 3 revisit takes about half the original study time, and a day 7 revisit is shorter still, often ten to fifteen minutes. Short revisits replace the long relearning session you would need if the chapter were forgotten.

faqs.q: What if I miss a revisit day?
faqs.a: Simply do the revisit the next day and carry on. Spaced revision rewards consistency over weeks, not perfection on any single day, so one missed day does not spoil the plan.

faqs.q: Should I re-read the chapter on revisit days?
faqs.a: No, try to recall it first with your notes closed, then use the notes to check. Retrieval is what strengthens memory; re-reading on revisit days adds very little.

title: Class 6 Whole Numbers: Place Value Made Simple
desc: Learn place value in Class 6 maths: read, write and compare large numbers with charts, expanded form and simple worked examples.
intro: Every digit in a number has two values: its own face value and its place value, which depends on where it stands. In the number 45,678, the digit 4 is not just 4, because it stands in the ten-thousands place, so its value is 40,000. Pupils who understand this idea stop guessing at large numbers and start reading them with confidence. Place value is the key to adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing large numbers correctly, because every written method lines digits up by their places. This guide explains place value with charts, expanded form, comparing and ordering, so that numbers up to lakhs feel as friendly as numbers up to hundreds. You can find more Class 6 help in the [book collection](/books.html) and the [solved notes](/solved.html).

sections.h2: What Place Value Really Means
paras: Place value means that the same digit is worth a different amount depending on its position in a number. In 45,678, the digits from the right are ones, tens, hundreds, thousands and ten-thousands, so 8 means 8 ones, 7 means 7 tens or 70, 6 means 6 hundreds or 600, 5 means 5 thousands or 5,000, and 4 means 4 ten-thousands or 40,000. Adding these values together, 40,000 + 5,000 + 600 + 70 + 8, gives back 45,678, which proves the breakdown is correct. This is why a zero matters so much: in 405, the zero in the tens place holds the place, so the 4 means 400, not 45. Without place value, we could not write large numbers at all.

A place-value chart is the best tool for seeing this clearly, because it puts each digit in its own labelled column. Write the number into the chart from the right, one digit per column, starting with ones, and read across to name the value of each digit. Try it with 304,050: the chart shows 3 in the hundred-thousands place, 0 in ten-thousands, 4 in thousands, 0 in hundreds, 5 in tens and 0 in ones, so the value of 3 is 300,000 and the value of 4 is 4,000. Practise with your own numbers every day, such as house numbers, page numbers and prices, and soon you will read the value of any digit at a glance. More maths guides are on the [blog](/blog/).

sections.h2: Reading and Writing Large Numbers
paras: Large numbers are read in groups of three digits, counted from the right, and commas mark these groups to make reading easier. The number 304,050 is read as three hundred four thousand and fifty, because the group 304 stands for thousands and the group 050 stands for the rest. Read the thousands group first, say the word thousand, then read the last three digits as an ordinary three-digit number. The number 1,250,000 is read as one million two hundred fifty thousand, following the same grouping rule. Saying numbers aloud in this grouped way stops the common mistake of reading 304,050 as thirty thousand or three million.

Writing numbers from words needs the same grouping skill in reverse, and a chart helps again. To write fifty-six thousand three hundred twenty, first put 56 in the thousands group and 320 in the ones group, giving 56,320. Watch out for missing places: seventy thousand and four is written as 70,004, because the hundreds and tens places both need a zero to hold them. A useful check is to count the digits: thousands numbers have four to six digits, and hundred-thousands numbers have six digits. If your written number has the wrong number of digits, a place has been missed. Practise by writing the numbers you hear in class, then checking them with a chart.
bullets: Group digits in threes from the right before reading a large number.
Read the thousands group first, say thousand, then read the last three digits.
Use a zero to hold any empty place when writing numbers from words.
Count the digits as a final check: four digits means thousands, five or six means ten-thousands and above.

sections.h2: Expanded Form: Breaking Numbers Apart
paras: Expanded form writes a number as the sum of the place values of its digits, and it is the clearest proof that you understand place value. The expanded form of 45,678 is 40,000 + 5,000 + 600 + 70 + 8, and adding those parts gives back the original number. Expanded form also explains written addition and subtraction: when we add 45,678 and 12,345, we really add ones with ones, tens with tens, hundreds with hundreds, and so on. Try the expanded form of 70,409, which is 70,000 + 0 + 400 + 0 + 9, or simply 70,000 + 400 + 9, since zero places add nothing. Leaving the zero places out is fine, as long as you know they were there.

Expanded form helps with mental maths too, because breaking a number apart makes it easier to work with. To add 300 + 45,678, think of 45,678 as 45,000 + 678, add 300 to the hundreds part to get 45,000 + 978, and the answer is 45,978. To subtract 5,000 from 45,678, take it from the thousands part: 5,000 minus 5,000 leaves 40,678. These tricks only work when you can see the place values inside a number, which is why teachers ask for expanded form so often. Make it a habit to expand any new large number before you calculate with it, and written methods will feel much more natural. See the [home page](/) for more study resources.

sections.h2: Comparing and Ordering Numbers
paras: To compare two numbers, first count the digits: the number with more digits is always larger, because it reaches a higher place. So 10,234 is larger than 9,876, even though 9,876 starts with a bigger digit, because 10,234 has five digits and reaches ten-thousands while 9,876 has only four. When both numbers have the same number of digits, compare them place by place from the left until the digits differ, and the number with the larger digit at that first different place is larger. Compare 45,678 and 45,768: the ten-thousands are both 4 and the thousands are both 5, but the hundreds differ, 6 against 7, so 45,768 is larger. The first place where digits differ decides the whole comparison.

Ordering means arranging numbers from smallest to largest or largest to smallest, and the same two rules do all the work. Order 9,876, 10,234 and 9,999 from smallest to largest: first count digits, so 10,234 with five digits must be the largest, then compare the two four-digit numbers, where 9,876 is smaller than 9,999 because at the hundreds place 8 is less than 9, giving 9,876, 9,999, 10,234. The symbols help record this: 9,876 < 9,999 < 10,234, where the symbol opens towards the larger number. Always check your order by reading it back: each step from left to right should genuinely increase, or your ordering has a mistake hiding in it.

diagram.caption: The steps for deciding which of two numbers is larger.

sections.h2: Rounding to the Nearest Thousand
paras: Rounding gives a nearby round number that is easier to use for estimates, and place value tells us which digit decides the rounding. To round 45,678 to the nearest thousand, look at the hundreds digit, which is 6, and since 6 is 5 or more, round the thousands digit up: 45,678 rounds to 46,000. To round 45,321 to the nearest thousand, the hundreds digit is 3, which is less than 5, so round down and keep the thousands digit as it is: 45,321 rounds to 45,000. The simple rule is to look at the digit just right of the place you are rounding to: 5 or more rounds up, 4 or less rounds down, and every digit to the right becomes zero.

Rounding is useful for checking answers and for quick estimates in daily life, such as estimating the total cost of shopping. If a school collects 45,678 rupees and 12,345 rupees in two terms, rounding both to the nearest thousand gives 46,000 and 12,000, whose sum is 58,000, close to the exact total of 58,023. If your exact answer is far from your rounded estimate, you probably made a place-value slip, so go back and check. Never round in the middle of a calculation that needs an exact answer, though: round only for estimates and checks, and keep exact digits for the real working. That habit keeps both your estimates and your exact answers trustworthy.

points: A digit's value depends on its place: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands and ten-thousands from the right.
Read large numbers in groups of three digits from the right, using commas as guides.
Expanded form writes a number as the sum of its digits' place values, for example 45,678 = 40,000 + 5,000 + 600 + 70 + 8.
Compare by counting digits first, then comparing place by place from the left.
Round to the nearest thousand by looking at the hundreds digit: 5 or more rounds up, 4 or less rounds down.

faqs.q: What is the place value of 5 in 45,678?
faqs.a: The 5 stands in the thousands place, so its place value is 5,000. Its face value is 5, but its place value is 5 multiplied by 1,000.

faqs.q: How do I read 304,050?
faqs.a: Group it as 304 and 050 from the right, then read it as three hundred four thousand and fifty. The group 304 gives the thousands part and 050 gives the rest.

faqs.q: Why do we write zero in 70,004?
faqs.a: The zeros hold the hundreds and tens places, which are empty. Without them, 70,004 would collapse into 7,4, which is a different number entirely.

faqs.q: Which is larger, 9,876 or 10,234?
faqs.a: 10,234 is larger, because it has five digits and reaches the ten-thousands place, while 9,876 has only four digits. More digits always means a larger whole number.

faqs.q: How do I round 45,678 to the nearest thousand?
faqs.a: Look at the hundreds digit, which is 6. Since 6 is 5 or more, round the thousands digit up, giving 46,000.

title: Class 6 Factors and Multiples: HCF and LCM Without Fear
desc: Factors, multiples, HCF and LCM explained simply for Class 6, with prime factors and short worked examples you can follow step by step.
intro: Factors and multiples sound alike, but they point in opposite directions, and mixing them up is the most common Class 6 maths mistake. Factors divide into a number exactly, while multiples are what you get when you multiply a number by 1, 2, 3 and so on. From these two ideas come HCF, the highest common factor, and LCM, the lowest common multiple, which solve real problems like sharing things equally and finding when two repeating events happen together. This guide builds the ideas slowly, with short worked examples for the numbers 12 and 18, so that HCF and LCM stop feeling like tricks and start feeling like tools. Find more Class 6 guides in the [book collection](/books.html) and on the [blog](/blog/).

sections.h2: Factors: Numbers That Divide Exactly
paras: A factor of a number is a whole number that divides it exactly, leaving no remainder. The factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12, because each of these divides 12 exactly: 12 divided by 3 is 4, 12 divided by 4 is 3, and so on. A quick way to find all factors is to test numbers in pairs: 1 times 12 is 12, 2 times 6 is 12, and 3 times 4 is 12, and once the pairs start repeating, you have found them all. Every number has 1 and itself as factors, and every number except 1 has at least those two. A number with exactly two factors is called a prime number, like 7, whose only factors are 1 and 7, while a number with more than two factors, like 12, is composite.

Factors are useful whenever things must be shared equally, because the factors of a number are exactly the group sizes that share it with nothing left over. Twelve pencils can be shared equally among 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 or 12 pupils, but not among 5 pupils, because 5 is not a factor of 12 and 12 divided by 5 leaves a remainder of 2. When you list factors, always work in pairs and write both members of each pair, or you will miss one. A neat trick for checking your list is to count the pairs: if the number is not a perfect square, its factors come in an even count of pairs, and a missing partner means the list is incomplete. Practise with 18, 20 and 30 until listing factors feels automatic.

sections.h2: Multiples: The Times Table Going On Forever
paras: A multiple of a number is the result of multiplying that number by a whole number, so the multiples of 6 are 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36 and so on, without end. Unlike factors, which are limited, multiples never stop, which is why questions always ask for the first few multiples or for multiples within a range. The first five multiples of 8 are 8, 16, 24, 32 and 40, found by multiplying 8 by 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5. A number is always a multiple of itself and of 1, and every multiple of a number is at least as large as the number itself. If you know your times tables, you already know multiples: the 6 times table is simply the multiples of 6.

Multiples appear in daily life whenever something repeats at regular steps, such as bus times, packet sizes and calendar patterns. If one shop sells pens in packs of 6 and another in packs of 8, the numbers of pens you could buy equally from either shop are the common multiples of 6 and 8, which are 24, 48, 72 and so on. Spotting multiples quickly comes from times-table fluency, so a few minutes of times-table practice each day pays off directly here. When a question asks for multiples up to a limit, write them in order and stop at the limit, rather than writing an endless list. That discipline keeps your work tidy and your answers complete. More study help is in the [solved notes](/solved.html).

sections.h2: Prime Factors: Breaking Numbers to Their Bones
paras: Every composite number can be broken down into prime factors, which are prime numbers that multiply to give the original number. The prime factors of 12 are 2, 2 and 3, because 2 times 2 times 3 is 12, written as 2 squared times 3. To find them, divide by the smallest prime that divides exactly, and keep dividing the result until only primes remain: 12 divided by 2 is 6, 6 divided by 2 is 3, and 3 is prime, so the work stops. The prime factors of 18 are 2, 3 and 3, because 18 divided by 2 is 9, and 9 divided by 3 is 3. Writing prime factors as a product, 12 = 2 x 2 x 3 and 18 = 2 x 3 x 3, is called prime factorisation.

Prime factorisation is worth learning because it makes HCF and LCM almost mechanical, as the next sections show. It also settles questions like whether a number is prime: try dividing it by primes in order, and if no prime up to its square root divides it, it is prime. For Class 6, the practical skill is a factor tree: write the number, split it into any factor pair, then keep splitting every composite branch until only primes are left at the ends. The primes at the ends are your prime factors, whatever pair you started with, which is a good check: if two pupils start with different pairs, they must still finish with the same prime factors. Try factor trees for 20, 30 and 36 and compare your endings with a friend.

sections.h2: HCF: The Biggest Number That Divides Both
paras: The highest common factor of two numbers is the largest number that divides both of them exactly. To find the HCF of 12 and 18, list their factors: the factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12, and the factors of 18 are 1, 2, 3, 6, 9 and 18. The common factors are 1, 2, 3 and 6, and the highest of these is 6, so the HCF of 12 and 18 is 6. Using prime factors gives the same answer faster: 12 = 2 x 2 x 3 and 18 = 2 x 3 x 3, and the primes common to both, taking the smallest power of each, are 2 and 3, whose product is 6. Both methods agree, which is a useful way to check your work.

HCF solves sharing problems where the groups must be as large as possible. Suppose a teacher has 12 red pens and 18 blue pens and wants identical packets with no pens left over: the largest possible packet size is the HCF, 6, so she can make packets of 6 pens, using 2 red packets and 3 blue packets in each mixed set, or more simply, the greatest equal group size is 6. Another example: the HCF of 15 and 20 is 5, because the factors of 15 are 1, 3, 5 and 15, the factors of 20 are 1, 2, 4, 5, 10 and 20, and the highest common factor is 5. Always finish by checking that your HCF divides both original numbers exactly, or it is not a common factor at all. See the [home page](/) for more guides.

diagram.alt: Finding HCF and LCM by Prime Factors
diagram.caption: One prime factorisation gives both HCF and LCM.

sections.h2: LCM: The Smallest Number Both Divide Into
paras: The lowest common multiple of two numbers is the smallest number that is a multiple of both. To find the LCM of 12 and 18 by listing, write the multiples of 12, which are 12, 24, 36, 48, and the multiples of 18, which are 18, 36, 54, and the first number appearing in both lists is 36, so the LCM is 36. By prime factors, take the highest power of every prime that appears: 12 = 2 x 2 x 3 and 18 = 2 x 3 x 3, so the LCM is 2 x 2 x 3 x 3 = 36. Both methods agree again, and the prime-factor method is faster when the numbers are large. As a check, note that the LCM is never smaller than either number, and the HCF is never larger than either number.

LCM answers questions about things happening together again. If one bell rings every 12 minutes and another every 18 minutes, and they ring together now, they will ring together again after the LCM of 12 and 18 minutes, which is 36 minutes. Similarly, the LCM of 15 and 20 is 60, because 15 = 3 x 5 and 20 = 2 x 2 x 5, so the LCM is 2 x 2 x 3 x 5 = 60, and indeed 60 is the first number in both times tables. A quick check is that HCF times LCM equals the product of the two numbers: for 12 and 18, 6 times 36 is 216, and 12 times 18 is also 216. If your HCF and LCM fail this check, one of them is wrong, so redo the factorisation.

points: Factors divide a number exactly; the factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12.
Multiples go on forever: the multiples of 6 are 6, 12, 18, 24, 30 and so on.
Prime factorisation breaks a number into primes: 12 = 2 x 2 x 3 and 18 = 2 x 3 x 3.
The HCF of 12 and 18 is 6, the largest number dividing both exactly.
The LCM of 12 and 18 is 36, the smallest number that is a multiple of both.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a factor and a multiple?
faqs.a: A factor divides into a number exactly, while a multiple is made by multiplying the number. Factors of 12 are limited, but multiples of 12 go on forever: 12, 24, 36, 48 and so on.

faqs.q: How do I find the HCF of 12 and 18?
faqs.a: List the factors of 12 (1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12) and of 18 (1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18). The common factors are 1, 2, 3 and 6, and the highest is 6, so the HCF is 6.

faqs.q: How do I find the LCM of 12 and 18?
faqs.a: List multiples of 12 (12, 24, 36) and of 18 (18, 36). The first number in both lists is 36, so the LCM is 36. By prime factors it is 2 x 2 x 3 x 3 = 36.

faqs.q: What is prime factorisation?
faqs.a: It is breaking a number into prime numbers that multiply to give it. For example, 12 = 2 x 2 x 3, because 2, 2 and 3 are all prime and their product is 12.

faqs.q: How can I check my HCF and LCM answers?
faqs.a: Multiply them: HCF times LCM should equal the product of the two numbers. For 12 and 18, 6 times 36 is 216, and 12 times 18 is also 216, so both answers check out.

title: Class 6 Fractions and Decimals: From Halves to Hundredths
desc: Class 6 fractions and decimals made easy: compare fractions, convert to decimals, and use halves, quarters and hundredths in daily life.
intro: Fractions and decimals are two ways of writing the same idea: a part of a whole. One half can be written as the fraction 1/2 or as the decimal 0.5, and three quarters can be written as 3/4 or 0.75. Pupils often treat them as two separate topics, but once you see how they convert into each other, both become much easier. This guide starts with simple fractions, shows how to compare them, converts them into decimals, and finishes with everyday examples like money and measuring, where decimals appear all the time. More Class 6 maths help is in the [book collection](/books.html) and the [solved notes](/solved.html).

sections.h2: What a Fraction Means
paras: A fraction has a numerator on top and a denominator below, and the denominator tells you how many equal parts the whole is split into, while the numerator tells you how many of those parts you have. In 3/4, the whole is split into 4 equal parts and you have 3 of them, so 3/4 is three quarters of the whole. In 1/2, the whole is split into 2 parts and you have 1, which is one half. Equal parts matter: if the parts are not equal, the fraction does not describe them properly, which is why fraction diagrams always show pieces of the same size. A fraction like 5/5 means the whole thing, because you have all 5 of the 5 parts.

Fractions also appear as parts of a group, not just parts of a shape. If a class has 20 pupils and 12 of them walk to school, the fraction that walks is 12/20, which simplifies to 3/5 by dividing numerator and denominator by 4. Simplifying means dividing both parts by their common factor, and a fraction is in simplest form when numerator and denominator share no common factor except 1. So 12/20 simplifies to 3/5, and 6/8 simplifies to 3/4 by dividing by 2. Always simplify your final answer unless the question asks otherwise, because simplest form is the standard way to present a fraction. Practise simplifying 10/15, which becomes 2/3, and 9/12, which becomes 3/4.

sections.h2: Comparing Fractions the Easy Way
paras: When fractions share the same denominator, comparing them is easy: the one with the larger numerator is larger, so 3/8 is larger than 2/8 because 3 parts out of 8 beat 2 parts out of 8. When the denominators differ, cross-multiplication gives a reliable comparison without finding a common denominator. To compare 2/3 and 3/5, multiply the numerator of each by the denominator of the other: 2 times 5 is 10, and 3 times 3 is 9, and since 10 is larger than 9, 2/3 is larger than 3/5. Write the products above the fractions they belong to, so you never mix up which product goes with which fraction, and the larger product marks the larger fraction.

Another way to compare is to convert both fractions to a common denominator, which works well when the denominators are small. To compare 1/2 and 3/4, convert 1/2 to 2/4, and then 3/4 is clearly larger than 2/4. For 2/3 and 3/4, the common denominator 12 gives 8/12 and 9/12, so 3/4 is larger. A quick sense check helps too: any fraction larger than 1/2 has a numerator more than half its denominator, so 5/8 is larger than 1/2 while 3/8 is smaller. Use whichever method you find clearest, but always show your working, because a bare answer to a comparison question earns little credit. Find more guides on the [blog](/blog/).

sections.h2: Turning Fractions Into Decimals
paras: A fraction means division: 3/4 means 3 divided by 4, so dividing gives the decimal form. Three divided by 4 is 0.75, so 3/4 = 0.75, and one divided by 2 is 0.5, so 1/2 = 0.5. Fractions with denominator 10 or 100 convert by place value alone: 7/10 = 0.7, because the 7 sits in the tenths place, and 45/100 = 0.45, because 4 is in tenths and 5 is in hundredths. For other denominators, first convert to tenths or hundredths if you can: 3/5 becomes 6/10 by multiplying numerator and denominator by 2, so 3/5 = 0.6. The fractions worth memorising are 1/2 = 0.5, 1/4 = 0.25, 3/4 = 0.75, 1/5 = 0.2 and 1/10 = 0.1, because they appear constantly.

Decimals can also be turned back into fractions, which is useful for simplifying and comparing. The decimal 0.45 means 45 hundredths, so it equals 45/100, which simplifies to 9/20 by dividing by 5. The decimal 0.6 means 6 tenths, so it equals 6/10, which simplifies to 3/5. Read the decimal aloud to find its fraction: 0.25 is twenty-five hundredths, giving 25/100, which simplifies to 1/4. This two-way skill means you can always switch to whichever form makes a question easier: use decimals for money and measuring, and fractions for exact parts and sharing. Try converting 0.8, which is 8/10 or 4/5, and 0.35, which is 35/100 or 7/20.

diagram.caption: The same part of a whole, written two ways.

sections.h2: Comparing Decimals Without Confusion
paras: Comparing decimals is easy once you line up the decimal points and compare place by place, just like whole numbers. To compare 0.45 and 0.5, first write 0.5 as 0.50 so both numbers have two decimal places, then compare the hundredths: 45 hundredths is less than 50 hundredths, so 0.45 is smaller than 0.5. The common mistake is to think 0.45 is larger because 45 is a bigger number than 5, but the place values decide, not the digits alone. Comparing 0.6 and 0.65 works the same way: write 0.6 as 0.60, and 60 hundredths is less than 65 hundredths, so 0.6 is smaller than 0.65. Padding with zeros never changes a decimal's value, so use it freely.

Ordering decimals follows the same method: pad them to the same number of decimal places, then order them like whole numbers. Order 0.5, 0.45 and 0.75: padded, they are 0.50, 0.45 and 0.75, so from smallest to largest they are 0.45, 0.5, 0.75. In money, this skill is used daily: Rs 12.50 is more than Rs 12.05, because at the tenths place both have 5, but at the hundredths place 0 is less than 5, so Rs 12.05 is the smaller amount. Always write decimals with their points lined up in a column when you compare them on paper, because a misaligned point is the usual cause of a wrong comparison. The [home page](/) has more study material.

sections.h2: Fractions and Decimals in Daily Life
paras: Fractions and decimals are everywhere once you start looking, especially in shopping, cooking and measuring. A shopkeeper who sells half a litre of milk sells 0.5 litres, and a bottle marked 0.25 litres holds one quarter of a litre. A discount of one quarter off a Rs 400 shirt saves Rs 100, because 1/4 of 400 is 100, leaving Rs 300 to pay. In cooking, half a cup is 0.5 cups, and three quarters of a cup is 0.75 cups, so recipes written either way describe the same amounts. Cricket fans meet decimals in run rates, and petrol is sold by the litre with two decimal places, so reading decimals correctly saves real money.

Marks and test scores use both forms too, and converting between them helps you understand your results. Scoring 15 out of 20 is the fraction 15/20, which simplifies to 3/4, which as a decimal is 0.75, which as a percentage is 75 percent. A pupil who scored 0.8 on a quiz scored 4/5, or 80 percent, which is a strong result. When you see a decimal in daily life, try naming its fraction: 0.5 litres is half a litre, 2.5 kilograms is two and a half kilograms, and Rs 7.25 is seven rupees and twenty-five paisa. This habit turns every price tag and measuring jug into fraction practice, and soon converting between the two forms will feel automatic rather than like a school exercise.

points: A fraction shows equal parts: in 3/4, the whole is split into 4 parts and you have 3.
Compare fractions with the same denominator by numerator, or use cross-multiplication: 2/3 beats 3/5 because 10 beats 9.
Convert fractions to decimals by dividing: 3/4 = 0.75, 3/5 = 0.6, 7/10 = 0.7.
