Compare decimals by lining up decimal points and padding with zeros: 0.45 is smaller than 0.50.
Simplify fractions by dividing numerator and denominator by their common factor: 12/20 = 3/5.

faqs.q: How do I convert 3/4 into a decimal?
faqs.a: Divide the numerator by the denominator: 3 divided by 4 is 0.75, so 3/4 = 0.75. You can also write 3/4 as 75/100, which is 0.75 by place value.

faqs.q: Which is larger, 2/3 or 3/5?
faqs.a: Cross-multiply: 2 times 5 is 10, and 3 times 3 is 9. Since 10 is larger than 9, 2/3 is larger than 3/5.

faqs.q: Is 0.45 larger than 0.5?
faqs.a: No. Write 0.5 as 0.50, then compare: 45 hundredths is less than 50 hundredths, so 0.45 is smaller than 0.5.

faqs.q: How do I simplify 12/20?
faqs.a: Divide numerator and denominator by their common factor 4: 12 divided by 4 is 3, and 20 divided by 4 is 5, so 12/20 simplifies to 3/5.

faqs.q: What is 0.25 as a fraction?
faqs.a: 0.25 means 25 hundredths, so it is 25/100, which simplifies to 1/4 by dividing numerator and denominator by 25.

title: Class 6 Percentages: A First Introduction With Shop Examples
desc: A first introduction to percentages for Class 6: per hundred made simple, with shop discounts, marks and easy worked examples.
intro: Percent means per hundred, and the symbol % is simply a short way of writing out of 100. When a shop says 25% off, it means 25 rupees off for every 100 rupees of price, and when a pupil scores 75%, it means 75 marks out of every 100. Percentages turn fractions and decimals into a single common scale, which is why shops, banks, exams and news reports all use them. This guide explains percentages from the beginning, with shop discounts and school marks as the main examples, so that the idea feels useful rather than abstract. More Class 6 maths guides are in the [book collection](/books.html) and the [solved notes](/solved.html).

sections.h2: Percent Means Per Hundred
paras: The word percent comes from per centum, meaning per hundred, so 25% is simply another way of writing the fraction 25/100 and the decimal 0.25. This is why percentages are so easy to compare: every percentage is measured on the same scale of 100, so 60% is always larger than 45%, whatever the original totals were. Converting a fraction to a percentage means making its denominator 100: 1/2 becomes 50/100, which is 50%, and 3/4 becomes 75/100, which is 75%. Converting a decimal is even quicker: move the decimal point two places to the right and add the % sign, so 0.6 becomes 60% and 0.05 becomes 5%.

Percentages above 100 are possible too, and they simply mean more than the whole: 150% of Rs 200 is Rs 300, because 100% is Rs 200 and another 50% is Rs 100. Percentages below 1% are rare in Class 6 work, but the idea is the same: 1% means 1 out of every 100. A useful picture is a 10 by 10 grid of 100 small squares: shading 25 squares shows 25%, shading half the grid shows 50%, and shading the whole grid shows 100%. Drawing this grid for a few percentages makes the per-hundred idea concrete, and it also shows why 25% is the same as one quarter and 50% is the same as one half. Keep this grid picture in mind whenever a percentage question feels confusing.

sections.h2: Finding a Percentage of a Number
paras: To find a percentage of a number, turn the percentage into a fraction over 100 and multiply. To find 25% of 200, write 25/100 times 200, which is 25 times 200 divided by 100, giving 5,000 divided by 100, which is 50. A shorter method is to find 1% first and then multiply: 1% of 200 is 2, so 25% is 25 times 2, which is 50. Both methods agree, and the 1% method is especially handy for percentages like 30% or 45%, where the fraction method involves larger numbers. Try 20% of 500: 1% of 500 is 5, so 20% is 20 times 5, which is 100.

Some percentages have quick mental shortcuts worth memorising, because they appear constantly in shops and exams. Ten percent means divide by 10, so 10% of 800 is 80. Fifty percent means halve the number, so 50% of 800 is 400. Twenty-five percent means divide by 4, so 25% of 800 is 200. Seventy-five percent means three quarters, so 75% of 800 is 600. Combining shortcuts handles other percentages: 30% of 800 is three times 10%, which is 3 times 80, giving 240. Practise these shortcuts until they are instant, because they make discount and marks questions much faster, and they also give you a quick check on longer written methods. More guides are on the [blog](/blog/).

sections.h2: Shop Discounts: Percentages That Save Money
paras: A discount is a percentage taken off the marked price, and the steps are always the same: find the discount amount, then subtract it from the price. A shirt marked Rs 800 with 10% off has a discount of 10% of 800, which is 80, so the sale price is 800 minus 80, which is Rs 720. A school bag marked Rs 1,200 with 25% off has a discount of 25% of 1,200, which is 300, so the sale price is 1,200 minus 300, which is Rs 900. Always check that the sale price is less than the marked price and that the discount is a sensible fraction of it: a 10% discount on Rs 800 cannot be Rs 400, because that would be half the price, not a tenth.

Some shops show two discounts in words, such as 20% off plus an extra 10% off, and pupils often add them to get 30% off, which is wrong. The second discount applies to the already-reduced price, not the original price, so a Rs 1,000 item at 20% off costs Rs 800, and a further 10% off Rs 800 saves Rs 80, giving a final price of Rs 720, which is a total saving of Rs 280, or 28%, not 30%. This is a good example of why percentages need care: they always act on a particular amount, and changing the amount changes the result. When a question says percent off, first ask: percent of what? Answering that question correctly is half the problem solved.

diagram.caption: The same three steps solve every discount question.

sections.h2: Percentages From Marks and Tests
paras: Exam percentages are found by dividing the marks obtained by the total marks and multiplying by 100. A pupil who scores 45 out of 60 has a percentage of 45 divided by 60 times 100, which is 0.75 times 100, giving 75%. A pupil who scores 36 out of 50 has 36 divided by 50 times 100, which is 0.72 times 100, giving 72%. The method never changes, whatever the total: divide by the total, multiply by 100, and add the % sign. Simplifying the fraction first often makes the division easier: 45/60 simplifies to 3/4, and 3/4 of 100 is 75, which matches the first answer.

Percentages let you compare results from tests with different totals, which raw marks cannot do fairly. Scoring 36 out of 50 beats scoring 45 out of 60 in percentage terms? No: 36 out of 50 is 72%, while 45 out of 60 is 75%, so the 45 out of 60 result is actually better, even though 45 is only 9 marks more than 36. This is the real power of percentages: they put different totals on the same 100-point scale. When you work out your own test percentages, always write the fraction first, then the division, then the multiplication by 100, so that a small arithmetic slip is easy to spot. A percentage above 100 in a test would mean scoring more than the total, which is impossible, so such an answer signals an error.

sections.h2: Common Percentage Mistakes to Avoid
paras: The most common percentage mistake is forgetting what the percentage is a percentage of, especially when a price changes twice. If a Rs 400 item rises by 25%, the increase is 25% of 400, which is 100, giving a new price of Rs 500. If it then falls by 25%, the decrease is 25% of 500, which is 125, giving Rs 375, not the original Rs 400, because the second percentage acted on a larger amount. Equal percentage rises and falls do not cancel out, and remembering this saves many marks. Another common slip is writing 0.5 as 5% instead of 50%: moving the decimal point two places, not one, is the rule for converting decimals to percentages.

A second mistake is confusing percentage points with percentages, though Class 6 pupils mainly need to avoid mixing up the percentage and the amount it produces. In the discount example, 10% is the rate and Rs 80 is the amount: the question may ask for either, so read it twice. If it asks how much you save, the answer is Rs 80; if it asks the sale price, the answer is Rs 720. Labelling your working helps: write discount = Rs 80 and sale price = Rs 720 as separate lines, so you can pick the one the question asked for. Finally, always finish with a sense check: a 10% discount should be a small part of the price, a 50% discount should be half, and a percentage of a number should never exceed the number itself unless the percentage exceeds 100%. The [home page](/) has more study help.

points: Percent means per hundred: 25% = 25/100 = 0.25.
Find a percentage by multiplying by the fraction over 100, or by finding 1% first.
A discount is found first, then subtracted: 10% off Rs 800 gives a sale price of Rs 720.
Test percentage = marks obtained divided by total marks, multiplied by 100: 45 out of 60 is 75%.
Percentages always act on a particular amount: a rise and fall by the same percentage do not cancel out.

faqs.q: What does 25% mean?
faqs.a: It means 25 out of every 100. As a fraction it is 25/100, which simplifies to 1/4, and as a decimal it is 0.25.

faqs.q: How do I find 25% of 200?
faqs.a: Multiply 25/100 by 200, which is 5,000 divided by 100, giving 50. Or find 1% of 200, which is 2, and multiply by 25 to get 50.

faqs.q: A shirt costs Rs 800 with 10% off. What is the sale price?
faqs.a: The discount is 10% of 800, which is 80. Subtract it from the price: 800 minus 80 is 720, so the sale price is Rs 720.

faqs.q: How do I turn 45 out of 60 into a percentage?
faqs.a: Divide 45 by 60 to get 0.75, then multiply by 100 to get 75%. So 45 out of 60 is 75%.

faqs.q: Why is 20% off then 10% off not 30% off?
faqs.a: The second discount applies to the reduced price, not the original. On Rs 1,000, 20% off gives Rs 800, and 10% off Rs 800 gives Rs 720, a total saving of 28%, not 30%.

title: Class 6 Geometry: Lines, Angles and Triangles
desc: Class 6 geometry made simple: lines, types of angles, triangle names, and how to draw and measure angles with a protractor.
intro: Geometry is the maths of shapes, and it starts with two simple ideas: lines and angles. Lines can run side by side forever without meeting, cross each other, or meet at a square corner, and the angle between two lines tells you how much one has turned from the other. Triangles, the simplest closed shape, are built entirely from three lines and three angles, and their names come straight from those angles and sides. This guide explains lines, angle types, triangle names, and how to use a protractor, with examples you can draw yourself. More Class 6 help is in the [book collection](/books.html) and the [solved notes](/solved.html).

sections.h2: Lines: Parallel, Intersecting and Perpendicular
paras: A line goes on forever in both directions, while a line segment has two endpoints and a ray has one endpoint and goes on in one direction. The edges of your notebook page are line segments, a sunbeam is like a ray, and a road stretching to the horizon is like a line. Parallel lines are lines in the same plane that never meet, however far they are extended, like the two long edges of a ruler or railway tracks. Intersecting lines are lines that cross at a point, like the diagonals of a square, and perpendicular lines are intersecting lines that meet at a right angle of 90 degrees, like the corner of a page where its edges meet.

Spotting these lines in daily life makes the definitions stick. The lines of a ruled notebook page are parallel, the hands of a clock at 3 o'clock are perpendicular, and the letter X is made of two intersecting lines. In a rectangle, opposite sides are parallel and neighbouring sides are perpendicular, which is why rectangles look so neat. When you draw parallel lines, use a ruler and keep the distance between them the same all along; when you draw perpendicular lines, check the corner with the square corner of a book or a set square. Naming the lines you see around you, in doors, windows and floor tiles, turns the whole classroom into a geometry lesson. Find more guides on the [blog](/blog/).

sections.h2: Types of Angles by Size
paras: An angle is formed when two rays meet at a point called the vertex, and its size is measured in degrees. An acute angle is smaller than 90 degrees, like the angle of a partly opened book or the hands of a clock at 2 o'clock, which show about 60 degrees. A right angle is exactly 90 degrees, like the corner of a page, and it is usually marked with a small square at the vertex. An obtuse angle is larger than 90 degrees but smaller than 180 degrees, like the hands of a clock at 4 o'clock, which show about 120 degrees. A straight angle is exactly 180 degrees, a flat line, like the hands of a clock at 6 o'clock.

A reflex angle is larger than 180 degrees but smaller than 360 degrees, and a full turn is 360 degrees, which brings a ray back to where it started. Pupils often confuse obtuse and reflex angles, so remember the boundary: anything under 180 degrees that is not acute or right is obtuse, while anything over 180 degrees is reflex. Estimating angles before measuring them is a good habit: look at the angle and guess whether it is acute, right or obtuse, then measure to check. If your guess and your measurement disagree wildly, you have probably read the wrong scale on the protractor, which is the most common measuring mistake. Practise estimating the angles of clock hands, open doors and roof slopes until your guesses are close.

sections.h2: Measuring and Drawing With a Protractor
paras: A protractor measures angles up to 180 degrees, and using it correctly needs three careful steps. First, place the centre mark of the protractor exactly on the vertex of the angle, so the protractor cannot slide. Second, line up the base line of the protractor with one arm of the angle, so that arm reads zero. Third, read the scale where the other arm crosses the protractor, choosing the scale that starts at zero on the arm you lined up: if the first arm is on the right, read the inner scale, and if it is on the left, read the outer scale. Reading the wrong scale gives the supplement of the angle, for example 120 degrees instead of 60 degrees, so your earlier estimate is your best protection.

Drawing an angle is the reverse process, and it also needs care. To draw a 60-degree angle, draw one arm with a ruler, place the protractor's centre on the endpoint and its base line on the arm, mark a small dot at 60 degrees on the correct scale, remove the protractor, and join the endpoint to the dot with a ruler. Check your drawing by measuring it back: the measured angle should match the angle you intended. Use a sharp pencil, because a thick pencil line can hide a few degrees of error, and draw arms long enough to read clearly. Pupils who rush protractor work usually lose marks on the scale choice, not on the drawing itself, so slow down at the reading step. The [home page](/) has more study resources.

diagram.alt: Measuring an Angle With a Protractor
diagram.caption: Four steps to a correct protractor reading.

sections.h2: Triangles by Their Angles and Sides
paras: Triangles are named by their angles and by their sides, and both naming systems are used together. By angles, a triangle with one right angle is right-angled, a triangle with one obtuse angle is obtuse-angled, and a triangle with all three angles acute is acute-angled. By sides, a triangle with all three sides equal is equilateral, a triangle with two sides equal is isosceles, and a triangle with no sides equal is scalene. An equilateral triangle is also acute-angled, because each of its angles is 60 degrees, and an isosceles triangle has two equal angles opposite its two equal sides. Learning both systems means you can describe any triangle fully, such as a right-angled isosceles triangle.

The angles of any triangle add up to 180 degrees, which is one of the most useful facts in geometry. If a triangle has angles of 60 degrees and 70 degrees, the third angle must be 180 minus 60 minus 70, which is 50 degrees, because 60 plus 70 is 130 and 180 minus 130 is 50. This rule lets you find a missing angle whenever you know the other two, and it also checks your protractor work: if your three measured angles add to much more or less than 180 degrees, at least one measurement is wrong. Try tearing the three corners off a paper triangle and placing them together: they form a straight line of 180 degrees, which is a convincing proof you can do at your desk. Triangles also appear in bridges and roofs because they are rigid shapes that do not wobble.

sections.h2: Drawing Triangles and Checking Your Work
paras: Drawing a triangle from given sides needs a ruler and a pair of compasses, and the method is satisfying once you practise it. To draw a triangle with sides 5 cm, 6 cm and 7 cm, first draw the 7 cm base with a ruler, then open the compasses to 5 cm, place the point on one end of the base and draw an arc, then open them to 6 cm, place the point on the other end and draw a second arc. The point where the arcs cross is the third vertex: join it to both ends of the base, and the triangle is complete. If the arcs do not cross, the three lengths cannot form a triangle, which happens when the longest side is longer than the other two sides added together.

Always check a drawn triangle by measuring its sides and angles back against the question. The sides should match the given lengths within a millimetre or two, and the angles should add to 180 degrees. Label the vertices with capital letters, usually A, B and C, and label the sides with their lengths, so that anyone reading your drawing can check it without asking. Neat construction lines, the light arcs left by the compasses, show your method and earn marks, so do not rub them out. Geometry rewards patience: a slow, careful drawing beats a quick, rough one every time, and the checking step is what turns a good drawing into a reliable one. See the [solved notes](/solved.html) for more practice.

points: Parallel lines never meet; perpendicular lines meet at a right angle of 90 degrees.
Acute angles are under 90 degrees, right angles are exactly 90, obtuse angles are between 90 and 180, and straight angles are 180.
Measure with a protractor by centring it on the vertex, lining up the base line, and reading the scale that starts at zero.
The three angles of any triangle add up to 180 degrees: 60 plus 70 leaves a third angle of 50 degrees.
Triangles are named by angles (acute, right, obtuse) and by sides (equilateral, isosceles, scalene).

faqs.q: What is the difference between parallel and perpendicular lines?
faqs.a: Parallel lines never meet, however far they are extended, like railway tracks. Perpendicular lines meet at a right angle of 90 degrees, like the corner of a page.

faqs.q: Is a 120-degree angle acute or obtuse?
faqs.a: It is obtuse, because obtuse angles are larger than 90 degrees and smaller than 180 degrees. Acute angles are smaller than 90 degrees.

faqs.q: Why do I sometimes read 120 degrees instead of 60 degrees on a protractor?
faqs.a: You read the wrong scale. Use the scale that starts at zero on the arm you lined up with the base line, and check your reading against your estimate of acute or obtuse.

faqs.q: A triangle has angles of 60 and 70 degrees. What is the third angle?
faqs.a: The angles of a triangle add to 180 degrees, so the third angle is 180 minus 60 minus 70, which is 50 degrees.

faqs.q: What is an isosceles triangle?
faqs.a: It is a triangle with two equal sides. The two angles opposite those equal sides are also equal.

title: Class 6 Ratio and Proportion in Simple Words
desc: Ratio and proportion in simple words for Class 6: recipes, class strength and the unitary method, with easy worked examples.
intro: A ratio compares two quantities of the same kind, and it tells you how many times one fits into the other. If a class has 24 boys and 16 girls, the ratio of boys to girls is 24 to 16, which simplifies to 3 to 2. Ratios appear in recipes, in maps, in mixing paint, and in sharing money fairly, and they are the doorway to proportion, which says that two ratios are equal. This guide explains ratios with recipes and class strength, shows how to simplify them, and teaches the unitary method, which solves a huge family of daily-life problems. More Class 6 maths is in the [book collection](/books.html) and the [solved notes](/solved.html).

sections.h2: What a Ratio Is
paras: A ratio is written with a colon, like 3:2, and it compares two quantities measured in the same unit. The order matters: the ratio of boys to girls in a class of 24 boys and 16 girls is 24:16, but the ratio of girls to boys is 16:24, which is a different comparison. Ratios have no units, because the units cancel when you compare like with like, and a ratio only makes sense when both quantities are in the same unit: comparing 2 metres with 50 centimetres needs a conversion first, giving 200 centimetres to 50 centimetres, or 4:1. Always check the units and the order before you write a ratio, because both mistakes are common and both change the answer.

A ratio is not a fraction of a whole, though the two ideas are related, and keeping them apart avoids confusion. In a class with 24 boys and 16 girls, the ratio of boys to girls is 24:16, but the fraction of the class that is boys is 24 out of 40, or 3/5, because the whole class is 40 pupils. The ratio compares one part with another part, while the fraction compares one part with the whole. Both are useful: the ratio tells you the mixture, and the fraction tells you the share. When a question asks for a ratio, give it with a colon and simplified; when it asks for a fraction, give it out of the total. Reading the question's exact words is the key to choosing correctly.

sections.h2: Simplifying Ratios
paras: A ratio is simplified by dividing both parts by their highest common factor, just like simplifying a fraction. The ratio 24:16 simplifies by dividing both parts by 8, giving 3:2, because 24 divided by 8 is 3 and 16 divided by 8 is 2. The ratio 15:25 simplifies by dividing by 5, giving 3:5, and the ratio 12:18 simplifies by dividing by 6, giving 2:3. A simplified ratio is the standard answer, and it also makes the comparison easier to understand: 3:2 is clearer than 24:16, because it says that for every 3 boys there are 2 girls. If the two parts share no common factor except 1, the ratio is already in simplest form.

Simplifying also works when a ratio has more than two parts, which happens in recipes and mixtures. A mixture of 12 spoons of flour, 6 spoons of sugar and 3 spoons of cocoa simplifies by dividing all three parts by 3, giving 4:2:1. Decimal ratios should be converted to whole numbers first: the ratio 1.5:2.5 becomes 15:25 by multiplying both parts by 10, and then simplifies to 3:5 by dividing by 5. Always divide by the highest common factor in one step when you can, but dividing step by step also works if you keep going until no common factor remains. Check your simplified ratio by confirming that both parts divided by the same number give your answer, and that no further common factor exists.

sections.h2: Ratios in Recipes and Mixtures
paras: Recipes are ratios in disguise, because they fix the proportions of ingredients whatever the batch size. A recipe that uses 2 cups of flour to 1 cup of sugar has the ratio 2:1, so doubling the recipe needs 4 cups of flour and 2 cups of sugar, keeping the same ratio, and halving it needs 1 cup of flour and half a cup of sugar. If a recipe for 4 people uses 3 cups of rice, then the same recipe for 8 people needs 6 cups, because the number of people has doubled and so must the rice. Scaling a recipe means multiplying every ingredient by the same number, which keeps the taste the same; changing only one ingredient changes the ratio and changes the dish.

Mixtures follow the same rule, from paint to squash to cement. A paint mixture in the ratio 3:1 of white to red paint means that for every 3 parts of white paint there is 1 part of red, so a batch of 12 litres contains 9 litres of white and 3 litres of red, because the mixture has 4 parts in total and each part is 3 litres. Finding the value of one part, by dividing the total by the number of parts, is the key step in mixture questions. A squash mixture in the ratio 1:4 of squash to water means 1 part squash and 4 parts water, so a 500 ml jug holds 100 ml of squash and 400 ml of water. Practise with your own kitchen: the ratio of rice to water in cooking is a ratio you already use every day. More guides are on the [blog](/blog/).

sections.h2: Proportion: When Two Ratios Are Equal
paras: Two ratios are in proportion when they are equal, even though their numbers look different. The ratios 2:3 and 4:6 are in proportion, because 4:6 simplifies to 2:3, and the ratios 3:5 and 6:10 are in proportion for the same reason. Proportion is written as 2:3 :: 4:6, and it can be checked by cross-multiplication: 2 times 6 is 12, and 3 times 4 is 12, and since both products are equal, the ratios are in proportion. If the cross products differ, the ratios are not in proportion: 2:3 and 3:5 give 2 times 5 is 10 and 3 times 3 is 9, which differ, so they are not in proportion. Cross-multiplication is the quickest proportion check, and it also finds missing values.

To find a missing value in a proportion, cross-multiply and solve the small equation that results. If 3 pencils cost Rs 30, how much do 7 pencils cost? The ratio of pencils to cost must stay in proportion, so 3:30 :: 7:x, cross-multiplying gives 3 times x is 210, so x is 210 divided by 3, which is 70, and 7 pencils cost Rs 70. This method works whenever two quantities grow together at a steady rate, which is called direct proportion: more pencils cost more money, more workers take more food, and more hours of work earn more pay. If the quantities move in opposite directions, such as more workers finishing a job faster, the proportion is inverse, and Class 6 questions usually stick to direct proportion, so check which kind you have before calculating.

diagram.caption: The ideas behind every ratio question.

sections.h2: The Unitary Method: Find One, Then Find Many
paras: The unitary method solves rate problems in two steps: first find the value of one unit, then multiply to find the value of many. If 5 pencils cost Rs 50, one pencil costs 50 divided by 5, which is Rs 10, and 8 pencils cost 8 times 10, which is Rs 80. If a car travels 180 km in 3 hours, it travels 180 divided by 3, which is 60 km in one hour, and in 5 hours it travels 5 times 60, which is 300 km. The method is called unitary because it goes through the unit, the value of one, and it works for any steady rate: price per item, speed per hour, or food per person. Always label the one-unit value clearly, because it is the bridge to every other answer.

The unitary method also handles division problems, where you need the value of one share. If 6 friends share Rs 720 equally, one friend gets 720 divided by 6, which is Rs 120. If 4 kg of rice costs Rs 480, one kilogram costs 480 divided by 4, which is Rs 120, and 7 kg costs 7 times 120, which is Rs 840. A common mistake is multiplying when you should divide in the first step: to find the value of one, you divide the total by the number of units, and only then do you multiply. Write both steps out, even when the numbers look easy, because the written steps earn method marks and make errors easy to find. The [home page](/) has more maths guides.

points: A ratio compares two quantities in the same unit, written with a colon, and order matters: 24:16 is not 16:24.
Simplify ratios by dividing both parts by their highest common factor: 24:16 becomes 3:2.
Scale a recipe by multiplying every ingredient by the same number, keeping the ratio unchanged.
Two ratios are in proportion when their cross products are equal: 2:3 :: 4:6 because 12 = 12.
The unitary method finds the value of one unit first, then multiplies: 5 pencils at Rs 50 means 8 pencils cost Rs 80.

faqs.q: What is the ratio of 24 boys to 16 girls?
faqs.a: It is 24:16, which simplifies by dividing both parts by 8 to give 3:2. The order matters: boys to girls is 3:2, while girls to boys is 2:3.

faqs.q: How do I simplify 15:25?
faqs.a: Divide both parts by their highest common factor, which is 5: 15 divided by 5 is 3, and 25 divided by 5 is 5, so the simplified ratio is 3:5.

faqs.q: How do I check if 2:3 and 4:6 are in proportion?
faqs.a: Cross-multiply: 2 times 6 is 12, and 3 times 4 is 12. Since both products are equal, the ratios are in proportion.

faqs.q: If 5 pencils cost Rs 50, how much do 8 pencils cost?
faqs.a: Use the unitary method: one pencil costs 50 divided by 5, which is Rs 10, so 8 pencils cost 8 times 10, which is Rs 80.

faqs.q: A paint mixture is 3:1 white to red. How much of each in 12 litres?
faqs.a: The mixture has 4 parts in total, so each part is 12 divided by 4, which is 3 litres. That gives 9 litres of white paint and 3 litres of red paint.

title: Class 6 Integers on the Number Line
desc: Positive and negative integers on the number line for Class 6: ordering, opposites, and adding with jumps, with simple examples.
intro: Integers are the whole numbers plus their negatives: ..., -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, ... Positive numbers sit to the right of zero on the number line, negative numbers sit to the left, and zero sits in the middle, neither positive nor negative. Negative numbers describe real things: temperatures below zero, floors below ground level, money owed, and depths below sea level. This guide shows how to place integers on the number line, order them, find their opposites, and add and subtract them with jumps, so that negative numbers stop feeling strange and start feeling useful. More Class 6 maths is in the [book collection](/books.html) and the [solved notes](/solved.html).

sections.h2: The Number Line and Where Integers Live
paras: A number line is a straight line marked with numbers at equal gaps, with zero in the middle, positive numbers marching to the right and negative numbers marching to the left. Moving right increases a number by one at each step, and moving left decreases it by one, so the number line is really a picture of counting in both directions. The integer -3 sits three steps left of zero, and the integer 4 sits four steps right of zero, and the distance of a number from zero is called its absolute value: the absolute value of -3 is 3, and the absolute value of 4 is 4. Drawing a number line is the first step for almost every integers question, because seeing the positions makes ordering and adding far easier than trying to do them in your head.

Equal gaps are essential on a number line, because the gaps are what make the picture honest: if the gap between 0 and 1 is wider than the gap between 1 and 2, the line lies about the numbers. Always mark zero first, then mark equal steps on both sides, and label at least the numbers you need for the question. A number line also shows why negative numbers behave as they do: -1 is greater than -5, even though 5 is greater than 1, because -1 sits closer to zero on the right side of the negative region. Pupils who draw the line rarely make this mistake, while pupils who guess from the digits alone often do. Keep a ruler handy and draw the line for every integers question until the picture lives in your head. More guides are on the [blog](/blog/).

sections.h2: Ordering Integers and Finding Opposites
paras: On the number line, a number is larger when it sits further to the right, whatever its sign. So -5 is smaller than -2, because -5 sits further left, and -2 is smaller than 0, and 0 is smaller than 3, giving the order -5 < -2 < 0 < 3. A useful rule for negatives is that the larger the digits, the smaller the number: -8 is smaller than -3, because 8 is further from zero on the left. To order a mixed set like 4, -1, 0, -6 and 2, first separate the negatives and positives, order the negatives by closeness to zero in reverse, giving -6 then -1, then put zero, then the positives in order, giving -6, -1, 0, 2, 4. Checking your order by reading it left to right on a drawn number line catches most errors.

The opposite of a number is the number the same distance from zero on the other side, so the opposite of 5 is -5, the opposite of -3 is 3, and the opposite of 0 is 0. Opposites add to zero, which is why they are also called additive inverses: 5 plus -5 is 0, and -3 plus 3 is 0. Opposites appear in daily life as pairs that cancel: a lift that goes up 3 floors and then down 3 floors returns to its start, and a temperature that rises 4 degrees and then falls 4 degrees returns to its start. When a question asks for the opposite of an integer, simply change its sign, and leave zero unchanged. The symbol for the opposite of a number is a minus sign in front of it, so the opposite of -7 is written as -(-7), which equals 7.

sections.h2: Adding Integers With Jumps
paras: Adding an integer means jumping on the number line: a positive addend means jump right, and a negative addend means jump left. To work out -3 + 5, start at -3 and jump 5 steps right: -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, landing on 2, so -3 + 5 = 2. To work out 4 + (-7), start at 4 and jump 7 steps left: 3, 2, 1, 0, -1, -2, -3, landing on -3, so 4 + (-7) = -3. The jump method never fails, and it explains the shortcut rules: when the signs are the same, add the absolute values and keep the sign, so (-2) + (-3) = -5, and when the signs differ, subtract the smaller absolute value from the larger and keep the sign of the larger, so -3 + 5 = 2 because 5 minus 3 is 2 and 5 is positive.

Adding integers is also how temperature and money problems work, which makes the jumps easy to picture. If the morning temperature is -2 degrees and it rises by 6 degrees, the new temperature is -2 + 6 = 4 degrees, found by jumping 6 steps right from -2. If a shopkeeper has Rs 100 and owes Rs 150, his balance is 100 + (-150) = -50, meaning he is Rs 50 short, found by jumping 150 steps left from 100, or more simply by the different-signs rule: 150 minus 100 is 50, and the larger absolute value belongs to the negative side. Practise jumps with small numbers first, saying each landing point aloud, and the shortcut rules will soon feel obvious rather than memorised. The [home page](/) has more study material.

diagram.caption: Start on the number line and jump in the direction of the sign.

sections.h2: Subtracting Integers
paras: Subtracting an integer means jumping in the opposite direction to adding it: subtracting a positive number means jumping left, and subtracting a negative number means jumping right. To work out 3 - 5, start at 3 and jump 5 steps left, landing on -2, so 3 - 5 = -2. To work out -1 - 4, start at -1 and jump 4 steps left, landing on -5, so -1 - 4 = -5. The trickiest case is subtracting a negative: 5 - (-2) means jumping 2 steps right from 5, landing on 7, so 5 - (-2) = 7. This matches the rule that subtracting a negative is the same as adding its opposite: 5 - (-2) = 5 + 2 = 7, because taking away a debt is like gaining money.

A reliable shortcut turns every subtraction into an addition: keep the first number, change the minus to a plus, and change the sign of the second number, then use the addition rules. So 3 - 5 becomes 3 + (-5), which is -2, and -1 - 4 becomes -1 + (-4), which is -5, and 5 - (-2) becomes 5 + 2, which is 7. Write this conversion out for every subtraction until it is automatic, because skipping it is how sign errors creep in. Check each answer by adding back: if 5 - (-2) = 7, then 7 + (-2) should equal 5, and indeed it does, because 7 minus 2 is 5. This inverse check, adding the subtracted number back to the answer to recover the first number, works for every subtraction question. See the [solved notes](/solved.html) for more practice.

sections.h2: Integers in Daily Life
paras: Integers describe any situation with two opposite directions, and recognising them is the first step to solving such problems. Temperatures use integers naturally: -4 degrees is 4 degrees below zero, and a rise from -4 degrees by 10 degrees gives -4 + 10 = 6 degrees. Buildings use integers too: ground floor is 0, floors above are positive, and basement floors are negative, so going from basement 2 up 5 floors reaches floor 3, because -2 + 5 = 3. Bank balances use integers: a balance of -Rs 500 means Rs 500 owed, and depositing Rs 800 gives -500 + 800 = Rs 300 in credit. Sea level works the same way: a submarine at -200 metres that rises 50 metres reaches -150 metres, because -200 + 50 = -150.

Sports and games also use integers, from golf scores below par to points lost in a quiz. A quiz team that scores 10 points, loses 4 points and then gains 7 points finishes on 10 - 4 + 7 = 13 points, worked left to right: 10 minus 4 is 6, and 6 plus 7 is 13. When a problem mixes gains and losses, write each gain as a positive number and each loss as a negative number, then add them in order on a number line. This turns a confusing story into a plain addition problem, which the jump method solves reliably. The habit of translating words into signed numbers, up as positive and down as negative, in as positive and out as negative, is the real skill of this chapter, and it transfers to every later topic that uses negative numbers.

points: Integers are whole numbers and their negatives: positives sit right of zero, negatives sit left, and zero is neither.
A number further right on the number line is larger: -5 < -2 < 0 < 3.
Add by jumping: positive addends jump right, negative addends jump left, so -3 + 5 = 2.
Subtract by converting to addition: change the sign of the second number, so 5 - (-2) = 5 + 2 = 7.
The opposite of a number is the same distance from zero on the other side: the opposite of -3 is 3.

faqs.q: Is -5 larger or smaller than -2?
faqs.a: Smaller, because -5 sits further left on the number line. For negative numbers, the larger the digits, the smaller the number.

faqs.q: How do I work out -3 + 5?
faqs.a: Start at -3 on the number line and jump 5 steps right: -2, -1, 0, 1, 2. You land on 2, so -3 + 5 = 2.

faqs.q: How do I work out 5 - (-2)?
faqs.a: Subtracting a negative is the same as adding its opposite, so 5 - (-2) = 5 + 2 = 7. On the number line, jump 2 steps right from 5.

faqs.q: What is the opposite of -7?
faqs.a: It is 7, because 7 is the same distance from zero on the opposite side. Opposites add to zero: -7 + 7 = 0.

faqs.q: Is zero positive or negative?
faqs.a: Neither. Zero sits between the positives and the negatives on the number line, and it is its own opposite.

title: Class 6 Averages: Mean, Median and Mode
desc: Mean, median and mode for Class 6: find averages from marks and heights with tables, and learn when to use each average.
intro: An average is a single number that represents a whole set of numbers, and Class 6 teaches three kinds: mean, median and mode. The mean is the total shared equally, the median is the middle value when the numbers are in order, and the mode is the value that appears most often. Each kind is useful in a different situation: the mean describes test scores, the median describes heights when one pupil is much taller than the rest, and the mode describes the most popular shoe size. This guide works through all three with marks and heights, shows how to use tables, and explains which average to choose. More Class 6 maths is in the [book collection](/books.html) and the [solved notes](/solved.html).

sections.h2: The Mean: Sharing the Total Equally
paras: The mean is found by adding all the values and dividing by how many values there are, which is exactly like sharing a total equally. Five test scores of 70, 80, 90, 60 and 100 add to 400, because 70 plus 80 is 150, plus 90 is 240, plus 60 is 300, plus 100 is 400, and dividing 400 by 5 gives a mean of 80. The mean of 80 means that if all five pupils had scored equally, each would have scored 80, even though their real scores ranged from 60 to 100. The mean uses every value in the set, which is its strength and its weakness: one very high or very low value pulls the mean towards itself, so the mean of 10, 10, 10 and 90 is 30, which describes nobody in the group well.

Tables make mean calculations tidy, especially when values repeat. Suppose five pupils have heights of 120 cm, 130 cm, 140 cm, 150 cm and 160 cm: the total is 120 plus 130 plus 140 plus 150 plus 160, which is 700, and dividing by 5 gives a mean height of 140 cm. With a frequency table, multiply each value by how many times it appears, add those products, and divide by the total count: if the score 70 appears twice and 80 appears three times, the total is 2 times 70 plus 3 times 80, which is 140 plus 240, giving 380, and dividing by 5 pupils gives a mean of 76. Always check that your mean lies between the smallest and largest values: a mean outside that range is certainly wrong. Find more guides on the [blog](/blog/).

sections.h2: The Median: The Middle Value
paras: The median is the middle value when the numbers are arranged in order, smallest to largest, and ordering first is essential. The scores 55, 60, 70, 80 and 95 are already in order, and the middle value, with two values on each side, is 70, so the median is 70. The same set in a different order, 95, 55, 80, 70, 60, has the same median, because ordering it gives the same middle value. When there is an even number of values, there is no single middle value, so the median is the mean of the two middle values: for 60, 70, 80 and 90, the two middle values are 70 and 80, and their mean is 75, so the median is 75. Pupils who forget to order first, or who pick the middle of an unordered list, get the median wrong most of the time.

The median is the best average when an extreme value would distort the mean, which happens often with money and heights. The incomes 1,000, 1,200, 1,300, 1,500 and 20,000 have a mean of 5,000, because the total is 25,000 divided by 5, but the median is 1,300, which describes the typical income far better. Similarly, if one pupil in a class is much taller than the rest, the median height stays typical while the mean is pulled up. The median ignores the actual size of extreme values and cares only about their position in the order, which is why it stays steady when an outlier changes. When a question asks for a typical value and the data contains an outlier, choose the median and say why.

sections.h2: The Mode: The Most Frequent Value
paras: The mode is the value that appears most often in a set, and it is the only average that works for non-numerical data like favourite colours. The scores 60, 70, 70, 80 and 90 have the mode 70, because 70 appears twice while every other score appears once. A set can have two modes: the scores 60, 60, 70, 80 and 80 have two modes, 60 and 80, because both appear twice, and such a set is called bimodal. A set can also have no mode: the scores 60, 70, 80, 90 and 100 all appear once, so no value is most frequent. The mode is quick to find from a tally table, where the tallest tally column marks the mode at a glance, and it never needs division, which makes it the simplest average to calculate.

The mode is the right average when the question is about popularity or the most common choice. A shoe shop deciding which size to stock most of checks the mode of sizes sold, not the mean size, because a mean size of 6.5 might correspond to no shoe anyone wears. A teacher asking which question most pupils got wrong looks at the mode of the wrong answers. The mode's weakness is that it may ignore most of the data: in the set 70, 70, 70, 90, 95 and 100, the mode is 70, but the mean is 82.5, which better reflects the higher scores. Choosing between mean, median and mode means asking what the average is for, and the next section gives a simple guide to that choice. The [home page](/) has more study help.

sections.h2: Which Average Should You Use?
paras: Choosing the right average depends on the data and the question, and examiners often ask you to justify your choice. Use the mean when every value matters and there are no extreme outliers, such as ordinary test scores in a class, because the mean uses all the data. Use the median when an outlier would distort the mean, such as incomes or heights with one extreme value, because the median stays typical. Use the mode when you need the most common value or when the data is not numerical, such as favourite subjects or shoe sizes, because only the mode answers those questions. A strong answer names the average, gives its value, and explains the choice in one sentence, for example: the median is 70, chosen because one very low score would drag the mean down.

Sometimes a question asks for all three averages so that they can be compared, and the comparison itself is informative. For the scores 70, 80, 90, 60 and 100, the mean is 80, the median is 80, and there is no mode, because every score appears once, so the mean and median agree and the data looks balanced. For the scores 60, 70, 70, 80 and 90, the mean is 74, because the total is 370 divided by 5, the median is 70, and the mode is 70, so the mean sits above the median because of the high score of 90. Noticing whether the mean is above or below the median tells you which side the extreme values sit on, which is a useful skill for reading data in later classes.

diagram.caption: Three averages, three different jobs.

sections.h2: Averages From Tables
paras: Frequency tables organise data before averaging, and they are worth using whenever values repeat. A table of marks might show that 2 pupils scored 60, 3 pupils scored 70 and 1 pupil scored 80: the total number of pupils is 2 plus 3 plus 1, which is 6, and the total of the marks is 2 times 60 plus 3 times 70 plus 1 times 80, which is 120 plus 210 plus 80, giving 410, so the mean is 410 divided by 6, which is about 68.3. The mode is read straight from the table as the value with the highest frequency, which is 70, because 3 pupils scored it. The median needs the ordered list, which the table lets you rebuild: 60, 60, 70, 70, 70, 80, whose two middle values are both 70, so the median is 70.

Tally tables are the first step when raw data arrives as a list, because they turn counting into a table. Suppose the heights in centimetres are 130, 140, 130, 150, 140, 130 and 140: tallying gives 130 three times, 140 three times and 150 once, so the mode is shared between 130 and 140, the total is 3 times 130 plus 3 times 140 plus 1 times 150, which is 390 plus 420 plus 150, giving 960, and dividing by 7 pupils gives a mean of about 137.1 cm. Always check that your frequencies add to the number of data values, or your total will be wrong before you even divide. Tables also make checking easy: a classmate can recount your tallies and confirm your frequencies without redoing the whole calculation. See the [solved notes](/solved.html) for more practice.

points: Mean = total divided by count: 70, 80, 90, 60 and 100 give a mean of 80.
Median = middle value in order: 55, 60, 70, 80 and 95 give a median of 70.
Mode = most frequent value: in 60, 70, 70, 80 and 90, the mode is 70.
With an even count, the median is the mean of the two middle values: 60, 70, 80, 90 give 75.
Use the mean for balanced data, the median when outliers distort, and the mode for popularity.

faqs.q: How do I find the mean of 70, 80, 90, 60 and 100?
faqs.a: Add them to get 400, then divide by 5, the number of values, giving a mean of 80.

faqs.q: How do I find the median of 60, 70, 80 and 90?
faqs.a: They are already in order, and with an even count there are two middle values, 70 and 80. Their mean is 75, so the median is 75.

faqs.q: What is the mode of 60, 70, 70, 80 and 90?
faqs.a: It is 70, because 70 appears twice while every other value appears once.

faqs.q: Can a set of numbers have no mode?
faqs.a: Yes. If every value appears the same number of times, such as 60, 70, 80, 90 and 100, there is no most frequent value and therefore no mode.

faqs.q: Why use the median instead of the mean sometimes?
faqs.a: Because one extreme value pulls the mean away from the typical value, while the median stays in the middle. For incomes 1,000, 1,200, 1,300, 1,500 and 20,000, the median 1,300 is far more typical than the mean 5,000.

title: Class 6 Perimeter and Area of Rectangles and Squares
desc: Perimeter and area of rectangles and squares for Class 6: fencing and flooring examples, formulas, and correct units explained.
intro: Perimeter is the distance around a shape, and area is the space inside it, and confusing the two is one of the most common Class 6 errors. A farmer fencing a field needs the perimeter, because fencing runs around the edge, while a farmer planting the field needs the area, because seeds cover the inside. Both are found from the same two measurements of a rectangle, its length and its width, but they use different formulas and different units: perimeter is measured in metres, while area is measured in square metres. This guide explains both formulas with fencing and flooring examples, so you always know which one a question is asking for. More Class 6 maths is in the [book collection](/books.html) and the [solved notes](/solved.html).

sections.h2: Perimeter: The Distance Around
paras: The perimeter of a shape is the total length of its boundary, found by adding the lengths of all its sides. A rectangle has two lengths and two widths, so its perimeter is length plus width plus length plus width, which shortens to 2 times (length + width). For a rectangle 12 m long and 8 m wide, the perimeter is 2 times (12 + 8), which is 2 times 20, giving 40 m. A square has four equal sides, so its perimeter is 4 times the side: a square with side 9 m has a perimeter of 4 times 9, which is 36 m. The brackets matter in the rectangle formula: 2 times (12 + 8) is 40, but 2 times 12 plus 8, without brackets, is 32, which is wrong, so always add length and width first.

Perimeter questions usually hide the sides in a story, and the first job is to find them. If a rectangular garden is 15 m long and its perimeter is 50 m, the width is found by working backwards: half the perimeter is 25 m, because 50 divided by 2 is 25, and half the perimeter equals length plus width, so the width is 25 minus 15, which is 10 m. Check it: 2 times (15 + 10) is 50 m, which matches. Perimeter is always measured in ordinary length units, metres, centimetres or kilometres, never in square units, because it is a length, not a surface. When a question mentions fencing, a border, a frame or walking around a field, it is asking for perimeter, and that word picture is your best clue.

sections.h2: Area: The Space Inside
paras: The area of a rectangle is length times width, which counts how many unit squares fit inside it. A rectangle 12 m long and 8 m wide has an area of 12 times 8, which is 96 square metres, written as 96 m squared, because it holds 96 squares of 1 m by 1 m. A square with side 9 m has an area of 9 times 9, which is 81 square metres, because its length and width are both 9 m. Area units are always square units: square centimetres, square metres or square kilometres, and writing plain metres for an area is a unit error that loses marks. The picture behind the formula is simple: area counts squares, so its unit must be a square.

Area questions also hide in stories, and the clue words are covering, painting, tiling and planting. If a floor is 12 m by 8 m, its area is 96 square metres, and if each floor tile covers 1 square metre, the floor needs 96 tiles. If a wall 10 m long and 3 m high is to be painted, its area is 10 times 3, which is 30 square metres, and paint bought by the square metre can then be worked out. When the sides are in different units, convert first: a rectangle 2 m long and 50 cm wide must become 200 cm by 50 cm, giving 10,000 square centimetres, or 2 m by 0.5 m, giving 1 square metre, and both answers describe the same area. Converting before multiplying is the step pupils most often forget. More guides are on the [blog](/blog/).

sections.h2: Fencing a Field: A Worked Example
paras: A farmer wants to fence a rectangular field 12 m long and 8 m wide, with fencing that costs Rs 50 per metre, and the question asks for the total cost. First find the perimeter, because fencing runs around the edge: the perimeter is 2 times (12 + 8), which is 2 times 20, giving 40 m. Then multiply the perimeter by the cost per metre: 40 times 50 is Rs 2,000, so the fencing costs Rs 2,000. The two steps must stay in order: finding the area here would give 96 square metres, which cannot be multiplied by a per-metre price, and the units would not match. Checking units is a powerful habit: metres times rupees per metre gives rupees, which is the answer the question wants.

Fencing questions sometimes add a gate, which changes the length to be fenced. If the same field has a gate 2 m wide that needs no fencing, the length to fence is 40 minus 2, which is 38 m, and the cost is 38 times 50, which is Rs 1,900. If the field is fenced twice around, with a double row of wire, the length doubles to 80 m and the cost doubles to Rs 4,000. Read the story twice before calculating: does it mention a gate, a double row, or more than one field? Each detail changes the perimeter before the cost step, and catching it early saves redoing the whole question. A sketch of the field with its sides labelled makes these details visible instead of hiding them in words.

diagram.caption: Perimeter first, then multiply by the price per metre.

sections.h2: Flooring a Room: A Worked Example
paras: A room floor 12 m long and 8 m wide is to be covered with square tiles, each 1 m by 1 m, and the question asks how many tiles are needed. First find the area, because tiles cover the inside: the area is 12 times 8, which is 96 square metres. Each tile covers 1 times 1, which is 1 square metre, so the number of tiles is 96 divided by 1, which is 96 tiles. If the tiles were 2 m by 2 m instead, each would cover 4 square metres, and the room would need 96 divided by 4, which is 24 tiles. The method never changes: find the floor area, find one tile's area, and divide the first by the second.

Flooring questions sometimes ask for cost as well, which adds one more multiplication. If each 1-square-metre tile costs Rs 120, then 96 tiles cost 96 times 120, which is Rs 11,520, because 100 times 120 is 12,000 and 4 times 120 is 480, so 12,000 minus 480 is 11,520. Always allow a few spare tiles in real life for cutting and breakage, though exam questions usually ask for the exact count. A common error is dividing the perimeter by the tile size instead of the area, which gives 40 tiles for this room, a meaningless number, because tiles cover a surface, not a boundary. Asking yourself whether the question is about the edge or the inside, before choosing a formula, prevents this error every time. The [home page](/) has more study help.

sections.h2: Squares, Units and Checking Your Answers
paras: Squares are rectangles with all sides equal, so both formulas simplify: perimeter is 4 times the side, and area is side times side. A square garden with side 9 m has a perimeter of 36 m and an area of 81 square metres, and a square with side 15 cm has a perimeter of 60 cm and an area of 225 square centimetres, because 15 times 15 is 225. When a question gives only the area of a square, the side is found by asking which number multiplied by itself gives the area: an area of 81 square metres means a side of 9 m, because 9 times 9 is 81. This reverse skill, finding a square root for small perfect squares, appears often in perimeter and area questions.

Checking answers means checking numbers and units together. A perimeter answer in square metres is wrong, an area answer in plain metres is wrong, and an area smaller than the perimeter is possible but worth a second look, since area and perimeter measure different things. A quick estimate also helps: a 12 m by 8 m rectangle has an area near 100 square metres, because 12 times 8 is close to 10 times 10, so an answer of 960 or 9.6 signals a decimal or multiplication slip. Finally, remember that doubling the side of a square doubles its perimeter but quadruples its area: a 9 m square has area 81 square metres, while an 18 m square has area 324 square metres, which is 4 times 81. This is why area grows faster than perimeter, and why unit checks matter so much. See the [solved notes](/solved.html) for more practice.

points: Perimeter is the distance around a shape: a 12 m by 8 m rectangle has a perimeter of 40 m.
Area is the space inside: the same rectangle has an area of 96 square metres.
Fencing uses perimeter: 40 m at Rs 50 per metre costs Rs 2,000.
Flooring uses area: a 96-square-metre floor needs 96 tiles of 1 square metre each.
Perimeter uses length units (m) and area uses square units (m squared) — never mix them up.

faqs.q: What is the perimeter of a rectangle 12 m by 8 m?
faqs.a: It is 2 times (12 + 8), which is 2 times 20, giving 40 m.

faqs.q: What is the area of a rectangle 12 m by 8 m?
faqs.a: It is 12 times 8, which is 96 square metres.

faqs.q: What is the perimeter and area of a square with side 9 m?
faqs.a: The perimeter is 4 times 9, which is 36 m, and the area is 9 times 9, which is 81 square metres.

faqs.q: How much does fencing cost for a 40 m boundary at Rs 50 per metre?
faqs.a: Multiply 40 by 50, which is Rs 2,000.

faqs.q: How do I know whether a question wants perimeter or area?
faqs.a: Fencing, borders, frames and walking around mean perimeter. Covering, painting, tiling and planting mean area.

title: Class 7 English Tenses: Present and Past in Real Sentences
desc: Learn Class 7 English tenses with real daily-routine sentences: present simple, present continuous, past simple and past continuous, explained clearly with examples.
intro: Tenses tell your reader when something happens, and getting them right makes your English clear at once. In Class 7, four tenses do most of the work in your writing: the present simple, the present continuous, the past simple, and the past continuous. Pupils often know the rules but still mix the tenses up in sentences, writing things like "I am go to school every day" when they mean "I go to school every day". This guide fixes that confusion with daily-routine sentences you can copy, change, and reuse. By the end, you will be able to choose the right tense for habits, actions happening now, finished past actions, and actions that were in progress.

sections.h2: Present Simple: Habits and Daily Routines
paras: We use the present simple for habits, routines, and facts that are generally true. Think of the things you do every day: "I wake up at six o'clock." "My mother cooks breakfast." "We walk to school together." The verb stays in its base form with I, we, you, and they, but with he, she, and it we add -s or -es: "He wakes up at six o'clock." "She watches the news after dinner." This small -s ending is the most common mark lost in Class 7 writing, so check every present simple sentence for it when the subject is he, she, or it.

Signal words help you spot the present simple: every day, always, usually, often, sometimes, and never. For example, "I always brush my teeth before breakfast" and "Ali sometimes plays cricket in the evening" both describe repeated actions, not actions happening right now. Negative sentences use do not or does not: "I do not like cold milk" and "She does not watch television at night." Questions use do or does: "Do you walk to school?" "Does your brother play football?" Practise by writing five sentences about your own morning routine, then read them aloud and check each verb ending.

sections.h2: Present Continuous: Actions Happening Now
paras: We use the present continuous for actions happening at this moment or around now. The form is am, is, or are plus the verb with -ing: "I am writing my homework now." "She is reading a storybook." "They are playing in the garden." Compare this with the present simple: "I write in my diary every night" is a habit, but "I am writing in my diary now" is happening at this moment. That contrast is exactly what examiners test, so learn the pair together rather than learning each tense alone.

Signal words for the present continuous include now, right now, at the moment, today, and Look! or Listen! For example, "Look! The cat is climbing the tree" and "At the moment, we are preparing for the test." A common mistake is dropping the helping verb: "She reading a book" is wrong, while "She is reading a book" is correct. Another mistake is using the continuous for a habit: "I am going to school every day" is wrong, because every day signals a habit and needs the present simple, "I go to school every day." Keep the two uses separate and your sentences will sound natural.

sections.h2: Past Simple: Finished Actions in the Past
paras: We use the past simple for actions that started and finished in the past. Regular verbs add -ed: "We walked to the market yesterday." "She cleaned her room last Sunday." Irregular verbs change their form, and these must be learned by heart: "I went to school early." "He ate his lunch quickly." "They saw a beautiful rainbow." Time words such as yesterday, last night, last week, and two days ago are strong signals for the past simple, and they should always sit with a past verb, never a present one.

Negatives in the past simple use did not plus the base verb, not the past form: "I did not go to the park yesterday" is correct, while "I did not went to the park" is wrong. Questions work the same way: "Did you finish your homework?" not "Did you finished your homework?" This is the single most tested past-tense rule in Class 7, so practise it until it feels automatic. Write ten past simple sentences about yesterday, then turn five of them into negatives and five into questions, checking each time that the main verb is back in its base form after did.

sections.h2: Past Continuous: Actions in Progress in the Past
paras: We use the past continuous for an action that was in progress at a particular time in the past. The form is was or were plus verb-ing: "I was reading when the lights went out." "They were playing cricket at four o'clock." It often appears together with the past simple: the longer action takes the past continuous and the shorter, interrupting action takes the past simple. For example, "While I was walking home, it started to rain" — the walk was in progress and the rain interrupted it. Learning this pair of sentences together makes both tenses easier to remember.

The words while and when are your best guides here. While usually introduces the longer, continuing action: "While she was cooking dinner, her friend called." When usually introduces the shorter action: "She was cooking dinner when her friend called." Both orders are correct, and both mean the same thing, so choose the one that sounds smoother in your paragraph. Avoid the mistake of putting both verbs in the past simple — "While I walked home, it started to rain" loses the sense that the walk was still going on. The past continuous adds that background feeling, which is why story writers use it so often.

diagram.caption: Ask these questions in order to choose the correct tense for your sentence.

sections.h2: A Daily-Routine Drill You Can Reuse
paras: Here is a drill that practises all four tenses with one routine. First, write your morning in the present simple: "I wake up at six. I wash my face. I eat breakfast. I go to school." Second, rewrite the same morning as if it is happening now: "I am waking up. I am washing my face. I am eating breakfast." Third, rewrite it as yesterday: "I woke up at six. I washed my face. I ate breakfast. I went to school." Fourth, add a past continuous background: "While I was eating breakfast, my friend arrived." One routine, four tenses, and every sentence checked against its signal words — that is how tense sense becomes automatic.

Finally, build a self-check habit before you hand in any written work. Read each paragraph once only for verbs, underlining every verb and asking whether its tense matches its time words. If you see yesterday beside a present verb, or every day beside a continuous verb, fix it before the examiner finds it. Keep a small notebook list of irregular past forms — go and went, see and saw, eat and ate, write and wrote — and add one new verb each week. For more English study help, visit the [book collection](/books.html), the [solved notes](/solved.html), and the [blog](/blog/), and start from the [home page](/) whenever you need a fresh guide.

points: Present simple is for habits and routines, with -s or -es for he, she, and it.
Present continuous is am, is, or are plus verb-ing for actions happening now.
Past simple describes finished past actions; use did not plus the base verb for negatives.
Past continuous shows an action in progress in the past, often interrupted by a past simple action.
Practise all four tenses on one daily routine to learn the contrasts quickly.

faqs.q: When do I use the present simple instead of the present continuous?
faqs.a: Use the present simple for habits and routines, such as "I go to school every day", and the present continuous for actions happening now, such as "I am going to school now". Time words like every day and now usually tell you which one fits.

faqs.q: Why is "I did not went" wrong?
faqs.a: After did, the main verb returns to its base form, so the correct sentence is "I did not go". The past meaning is already carried by did, and adding a past verb as well doubles the past marking.

faqs.q: What is the difference between "I read yesterday" and "I was reading at six"?
faqs.a: "I read yesterday" reports a finished past action, while "I was reading at six" describes an action in progress at that past time. Use the past continuous when you want the background feeling of an action still going on.

faqs.q: How do I remember irregular past forms?
faqs.a: Learn them in small groups and use them in your own sentences: go and went, see and saw, eat and ate, write and wrote. A notebook list with one new verb added each week builds the set steadily without cramming.

faqs.q: Which tense goes with "while"?
faqs.a: While usually introduces the longer action in the past continuous, as in "While I was walking home, it started to rain". The shorter, interrupting action takes the past simple.

title: Class 7 Prepositions: In, On and At Explained
desc: Master Class 7 prepositions in, on and at for place and time: clear rules, picture examples and common mistakes, so you never mix them up again.
intro: In, on, and at are tiny words that cause big mistakes, because each one can describe both place and time, and the choice depends on size and precision. Pupils write "in Monday" or "at the table" when they mean something else entirely, and the error stands out to any examiner. The good news is that the rules follow a simple picture: at is a point, on is a surface, and in is a space you can be inside. Once that picture is fixed in your mind, most preposition questions answer themselves. This guide covers place and time separately, with picture examples and the fixed phrases you simply have to learn.

sections.h2: Place: At a Point, On a Surface, In a Space
paras: Picture the three prepositions as a target. At is the exact point: "We met at the gate." "She is waiting at the bus stop." Use at for small, specific places such as an address point, a station, or a corner. On is a surface something rests on: "The book is on the table." "The picture hangs on the wall." Use on whenever one thing touches the surface of another. In is an enclosed space: "The books are in the bag." "We live in Karachi." Use in for rooms, buildings, cities, and countries — any space with boundaries you can be inside.

The size rule helps with towns and addresses. We say "at the school gate" for the point, "on Main Street" for the street as a line, and "in Karachi" for the city as an area. The same building can take different prepositions depending on what you mean: "at school" for the point where you are, but "in the classroom" for the room you sit inside. Test yourself by picturing each sentence: point, surface, or enclosed space? If you can see the picture, the preposition usually follows. Draw the three pictures once in your notebook and the rule will stay with you far longer than a memorised list.

sections.h2: Time: At a Moment, On a Day, In a Period
paras: Time works the same way, with at for a point in time, on for a day, and in for a longer period. At takes clock times and single moments: "The class starts at eight o'clock." "We eat dinner at night." On takes days and dates: "We have a test on Monday." "Her birthday is on 14 August." In takes months, years, seasons, and parts of the day: "School opens in April." "He was born in 2013." "It rains in summer." "We study in the morning." The pattern is point, day, period — and it mirrors the place rule exactly, which makes both rules easier to remember together.

Three fixed time phrases break the pattern and must be learned as they are: at night, at the weekend, and in the morning, afternoon, and evening. Notice that night takes at even though morning takes in — English is not perfectly logical here, and examiners know it, which is why these phrases are tested so often. Also note at noon and at midnight, both points in time. A useful drill is to write your whole weekly timetable with prepositions: "I have English on Monday at nine o'clock in the morning" practises all three in one sentence. Read such sentences aloud until the combinations sound right, because the ear catches preposition errors faster than the eye.

sections.h2: Picture Examples You Can Remember
paras: Let us fix the rules with one picture you can replay in your head. Imagine a cat. The cat sits at the door when it waits at a point. The cat sleeps on the mat when it rests on a surface. The cat hides in the box when it is inside an enclosed space. Now imagine the same cat through a week: it visits the vet on Friday, it naps at noon, and it stays indoors in winter. Six sentences, and every preposition follows the point, surface, and space picture. When a test question confuses you, bring back the cat and ask which picture your sentence matches.

The same picture trick works for trickier sentences. "The keys are in the drawer" is a space, so in is right. "The keys are on the shelf" is a surface, so on is right. "Meet me at the library" is a point, so at is right — but "The books are in the library" is a space, so in is right, even for the same building. The building did not change; your way of picturing it did. That is the real secret of prepositions: they describe how you see the place or time, not the place or time itself. Practise by describing your own room with ten in, on, and at sentences, and check each one against its picture.

sections.h2: Fixed Phrases to Learn by Heart
paras: Some prepositions cannot be worked out from rules and must be learned as fixed phrases. We say in the morning but at night, on foot but by bus, at home but in the house, interested in, good at, afraid of, and arrive at a small place but arrive in a big city. "She arrived at the station" and "She arrived in Karachi" show the small-point versus large-area rule again, but many phrases are simply customs of English. The only way to master them is to collect them: keep a notebook page headed "Preposition phrases" and add every new phrase your teacher or reader gives you, with a full example sentence beside it.

Reading is the fastest way to grow that collection, because fixed phrases appear naturally in stories and lessons. When you meet one, underline the whole phrase, not just the preposition — "good at mathematics" is the unit to learn, not "at" alone. Then use the phrase in a sentence of your own the same day, so it moves from your reading memory into your writing memory. Ten phrases learned this way beat fifty phrases copied from a list and never used. Before a test, read your phrase page aloud twice; hearing the correct combinations is what stops you writing "in Monday" under pressure.

diagram.alt: In, On and At at a Glance
diagram.caption: One picture for place and time: at is a point, on is a surface or day, in is a space or period.

sections.h2: Common Mistakes and a Quick Test
paras: Here are the mistakes examiners see most often, with their corrections. "In Monday" should be "on Monday." "At the morning" should be "in the morning." "On Karachi" should be "in Karachi." "At the table" for a book resting on it should be "on the table." Each error comes from using the wrong picture — a day treated as a space, a morning treated as a point, a city treated as a surface. Run the picture test on every doubtful sentence and most errors vanish before you write them. Also watch for missing prepositions: "I go school" needs to: "I go to school."

Finish with this quick self-test, answering without looking back. Fill in the blanks: "We meet ___ the park ___ Sunday ___ five o'clock." "The cat is ___ the roof ___ the morning." "My birthday is ___ December." The answers are at, on, at; on, in; in. If you got them all, your picture sense is working. If any felt like a guess, return to the cat picture and the point, surface, and space rule. For more English guides, visit the [book collection](/books.html), the [solved notes](/solved.html), and the [blog](/blog/) from the [home page](/).

points: At is a point, on is a surface, and in is an enclosed space.
For time, at takes moments, on takes days and dates, and in takes longer periods.
Learn fixed phrases as whole units, such as in the morning and at night.
The same building can take at or in depending on how you picture it.
Picture each sentence before choosing the preposition.

faqs.q: Why do we say "on Monday" but "in April"?
faqs.a: On takes days and dates, while in takes longer periods such as months, years, and seasons. Monday is a single day, so it takes on; April is a whole month, so it takes in.

faqs.q: Is it "at school" or "in school"?
faqs.a: Both are possible with different meanings. "At school" treats school as a point where you are, while "in the classroom" treats the room as an enclosed space. The preposition follows how you picture the place.

faqs.q: Why is "at night" correct but "in the morning"?
faqs.a: These are fixed phrases of English custom, not logic. Night takes at, while morning, afternoon, and evening take in. Learn them as phrases and they stop causing errors.

faqs.q: Do we say "arrive at" or "arrive in"?
faqs.a: Arrive at takes a small, specific place, as in "arrive at the station", while arrive in takes a large area, as in "arrive in Karachi". The size rule decides.

faqs.q: How can I stop mixing up in, on, and at?
faqs.a: Use the picture test: point means at, surface means on, and enclosed space means in. Practise by describing your room and your week with all three, and keep a notebook page of fixed phrases you meet in reading.

title: Class 7 Articles: A, An and The Rules That Stick
desc: Learn Class 7 articles a, an and the with a simple rule: first mention versus known things, plus vowel sounds, no-article cases and short drills.
intro: A, an, and the are the smallest words in English and some of the most tested, because a missing or wrong article makes a sentence feel off even when every other word is right. The whole system rests on one idea: a and an introduce something new or any one of a kind, while the points to something already known or the only one of its kind. Add one sound rule for choosing between a and an, and a short list of no-article cases, and you have the complete Class 7 article system. This guide explains each rule with short drills you can do in your notebook tonight.

sections.h2: A and An: First Mention of Something New
paras: Use a or an when you mention something for the first time, or when you mean any one of a kind rather than a particular one. "I saw a dog in the street" introduces a dog the reader has not met before. "She wants to be a teacher" means any teacher, not one specific teacher. "He bought an umbrella" introduces one umbrella out of many. In each case, the reader cannot yet point to which one you mean, and that newness is exactly what a and an signal. Once the thing has been introduced, you switch to the, as the next section explains.

The choice between a and an depends on sound, not spelling. Use an before a vowel sound: "an apple", "an egg", "an hour" — hour starts with the letter h but its first sound is a vowel, so it takes an. Use a before a consonant sound: "a book", "a university" — university starts with the letter u but its first sound is the consonant y, so it takes a. Say the word aloud and listen to its first sound; that sound decides. Practise with a list of tricky words — hour, honest, university, European, one — and the sound rule will replace the spelling guess that causes most errors.

sections.h2: The: Known Things and Only Ones
paras: Use the when the reader already knows which thing you mean. The most common way a thing becomes known is that you mentioned it before: "I saw a dog in the street. The dog was chasing a cat." The first mention takes a, and every later mention takes the, because now both writer and reader are thinking of the same dog. The also points to things known from the situation: "Please close the door" works because there is one obvious door in the room, and "The teacher asked us to sit down" works because the class knows which teacher is meant.

The also goes with things that are the only one of their kind: the sun, the moon, the earth, the sky. There is only one sun in our sky, so it is always the sun, never a sun, in ordinary writing. The same logic covers superlatives and firsts: "the best student", "the tallest boy", "the first chapter" — each one points to a single, identified thing. A useful test is to ask: can my reader point to exactly which one I mean? If yes, use the. If the reader would ask "which one?", you probably need a or an, or no article at all.

sections.h2: When to Use No Article
paras: Some nouns take no article at all, and this is where many pupils add a or the by mistake. General plural and uncountable nouns take no article when you mean them in general: "Dogs are loyal animals" speaks about dogs in general, not particular dogs, so it needs no article. "Water is precious" and "Honesty is the best policy" work the same way. School subjects, languages, and most sports also take no article: "She studies mathematics", "He speaks Sindhi", "They play cricket." Meals follow the same pattern in general statements: "We eat breakfast at seven."

Names of most places take no article too: "She lives in Karachi", "He visited Pakistan", "We went to Murree." Exceptions with the include rivers, seas, and groups of islands — the Indus, the Arabian Sea — and country names that are plural or contain a common noun, such as the United States. Do not add the to a person's name or to a single mountain: "Ali", "Mount Everest". When you are unsure, ask whether you mean the thing in general or one particular thing. General meaning usually means no article, while particular meaning usually means the.

sections.h2: Short Drills That Fix the Rules
paras: Drill one: first mention versus known things. Read this paragraph and fill in the articles: "Ali found ___ old key in ___ garden. ___ key opened ___ small box." The answers are an, the, The, a — an old key is a first mention, the garden is known from the situation, The key is now known, and a small box is newly introduced.
