desc: BSEK raised the Class 9 pass mark from 33% to 40% in 2026. Learn what ungraded means, how the new rule works, and what it means for Class 10 from 2027.
kw: BSEK 40 percent pass rule 2026 Class 9 science ungraded
intro: The Board of Secondary Education Karachi changed the rules of the game for Class 9 students in 2026, and many families only discovered the change when the result arrived. From the 2026 annual examinations, the pass threshold for Class 9 was raised from 33% to 40%, which means a paper scored below 40% is now recorded as ungraded rather than passed. The Board of Secondary Education Karachi announced the Class 9 Science Group result on 28 October 2026, and the new rule shaped that result in ways students and parents need to understand clearly. This guide explains exactly what changed, what ungraded means for your mark sheet, how the rule differs from the old 33% system, and what happens when Class 10 comes under the same scheme from 2027.

sections.h2: From 33% to 40%: What Actually Changed
paras: For years, Sindh board students grew up with a simple number in their heads: 33% was the pass mark. A student who scored 35% in a paper passed it, and a student who scored 30% failed it, and everyone understood where the line stood. From the 2026 annual examinations, that line moved for Class 9. The pass threshold is now 40%, so a paper must be scored at 40% or above to count as passed, and anything below 40% is recorded as ungraded. This is not a small administrative adjustment; it changes the outcome for every student whose marks fall in the 33% to 39% band, because papers that would have passed under the old rule now stand open and must be cleared.

The change applies to Class 9 from the 2026 annual examinations, and Class 10 follows from 2027, so current Class 9 students will meet the same standard again next year. That timing matters for planning, because it means there is no point in treating 40% as a one-year hurdle to scrape past and forget. Students who build study habits that aim comfortably above 40% this year will carry that margin into Class 10, while students who aim only at the borderline risk falling below it again when a paper turns out harder than expected. The sensible response is to treat 40% as the floor and to aim for a clear pass in every paper, using the [book collection](/books.html) and [solved notes](/solved.html) to strengthen weak chapters rather than relying on guesswork.

sections.h2: What Ungraded Really Means on Your Mark Sheet
paras: The word ungraded causes confusion because it sounds softer than failed, but students should understand it precisely. Under the new grading scheme, a paper in which a student scores below 40% is marked ungraded, which means the student is unsuccessful in that paper and has not passed it. It does not mean the paper is ignored, and it does not mean the marks disappear; it means the paper remains open and the student reappears in it subject to eligibility, following the board's official process. Parents sometimes read ungraded as a partial credit or a near pass, but the practical meaning is straightforward: that paper still needs to be cleared before the student's record for the class is complete.

Ungraded also changes how a student should read the rest of the mark sheet. A student who passed some papers and has one or two ungraded papers is in a different position from a student who failed everything, and the plan for each case is different. The first step is always to list every paper, mark each one as passed or ungraded, and note how far below 40% each ungraded paper fell, because a gap of two marks needs a different revision plan from a gap of twenty marks. Students should check their result on the board's official website and keep a printed or saved copy of the mark sheet, since every later step, from reappearance to admission, will ask for exactly what that sheet shows.

diagram.caption: How the same marks are treated under the old and new Class 9 pass thresholds.

sections.h2: How the New Rule Shaped the 28 October 2026 Result
paras: The Class 9 Science Group result announced on 28 October 2026 gives the first full picture of the new rule in action. According to the figures shared by Controller of Examinations Ahmed Khan Chhutto, 180,054 students registered and 177,923 appeared, while 123,757 passed all papers and 53,849 failed. The overall pass percentage was 69.56%, compared with 78.26% in 2025, when 137,350 of 175,511 students who appeared passed all papers. That is a fall of about 8.7 percentage points, and it is tempting to blame the new threshold alone, but the board has published no single official reason for the fall, and this guide does not present one cause as fact. Several factors can move a pass rate, and students should be careful about explanations circulating without an official source.

What can be said safely is that the higher threshold mechanically changes outcomes for students in the 33% to 39% band, and that the large partial-pass groups in the 2026 figures show how many students were affected at the margins. The board reported 21,999 students passing six papers, 11,006 passing five, 7,431 passing four, 4,409 passing three, 3,101 passing two and 2,439 passing one paper, which together describe a very large group of students with open papers. Chairman Professor Musharraf Ali Rajput congratulated students who passed all papers and said transparency remained among the board's top priorities, and the result was available on the board's official website from 5:30 PM on 28 October 2026. For students, the lesson is practical rather than statistical: read your own mark sheet against the 40% line, not against last year's headlines.

sections.h2: What Class 9 Students Should Do Now
paras: The first task after the result is a careful, paper-by-paper review. Take your mark sheet and write down every paper with its marks, marking each one passed or ungraded against the 40% threshold, and calculate the gap for each ungraded paper. Papers missed by a few marks need focused revision of the chapters where marks were lost, while papers with a wide gap need a fresh study plan built from the textbook. Keep your admit card, mark sheet and registration details safe, because the reappearance process will require them, and watch the board's official website for the next official notice rather than trusting dates shared on social media, since no reappearance date for these papers was stated in the 28 October announcement.

The second task is to set a revision target with a margin of safety. Aiming for exactly 40% leaves no room for a hard paper, an off day, or a strict marking scheme, so aim for a comfortable pass well above the line in every open paper. Work from your Sindh Textbook Board book, use solved exercises to check your method, and test yourself under timed conditions so that exam pressure does not eat into your margin. If your school offers extra classes for students clearing papers, attend them and ask teachers which chapters carried the most marks. The [blog](/blog/) carries study guides for revising science subjects chapter by chapter, and building that margin now also prepares you for Class 10, where the same 40% standard will apply from 2027.

sections.h2: Class 10 From 2027: Preparing Under the Same Standard
paras: Class 10 comes under the new grading scheme from 2027, which means the current Class 9 cohort will face the 40% threshold again in their matric year. This is genuinely useful information, because it turns this year's result into a rehearsal rather than a one-off event. Students who learn now how to revise to a comfortable pass, how to read a mark sheet paper by paper, and how to close a gap in a weak subject will use exactly those skills next year, when the stakes are higher because Class 10 results feed into college admission. There is no separate trick for Class 10 under the new rule; the same habits of textbook-based revision, timed practice and honest gap measurement apply, only with more syllabus to cover.

Parents can help by treating the threshold as a planning tool rather than a source of panic. Ask your child to show you the mark sheet, go through the open papers together, and agree on a weekly revision timetable that protects time for both Class 10 schoolwork and the open Class 9 papers. Encourage your child to talk to subject teachers about the chapters that cost the most marks, and avoid agents or unofficial channels that promise shortcuts around the board's process. The board's official website remains the only reliable source for notices about reappearance, fees and dates, and the [about page](/about.html) of this site explains how our study guides are organised for Sindh board students working under the new grading scheme.

points: Class 9 pass threshold rose from 33% to 40% from the 2026 annual examinations.
Scoring below 40% in a paper means ungraded, not passed, and the paper remains open.
Class 10 comes under the same new grading scheme from 2027.
The 2026 Science Group pass rate was 69.56%, down from 78.26% in 2025, with no single official reason published.
Aim comfortably above 40% in every paper so a hard paper does not push you below the line again.

faqs.q: What is the new pass mark for BSEK Class 9 in 2026?
faqs.a: The pass threshold for Class 9 from the 2026 annual examinations is 40%. A paper scored below 40% is recorded as ungraded rather than passed. This replaces the old 33% threshold for Class 9.

faqs.q: I scored 35% in one paper. Did I pass it?
faqs.a: No. Under the new rule, 35% is below the 40% threshold, so the paper is marked ungraded and remains open. You will need to reappear in that paper subject to eligibility, following the board's official notice on its website.

faqs.q: Does the 40% rule apply to Class 10 as well?
faqs.a: Class 10 comes under the new grading scheme from 2027. Current Class 9 students will therefore meet the same 40% standard in their matric year, which is why building a margin above 40% now is so important.

faqs.q: Why did the Class 9 Science pass rate fall in 2026?
faqs.a: The overall pass percentage was 69.56% in 2026, compared with 78.26% in 2025, a fall of about 8.7 percentage points. The board has published no single official reason for the fall, so no single cause should be presented as fact. The higher threshold does change outcomes for students in the 33% to 39% band.

faqs.q: Where do I check official notices about reappearing in ungraded papers?
faqs.a: On the Board of Secondary Education Karachi official website, bsek.edu.pk, and your school notice board. No reappearance date for these papers was stated in the 28 October 2026 announcement, so treat dates circulating on social media as unverified.

title: BSEK 9th Science: Failed Papers? What to Do Next After the 2026 Result
desc: 53,849 students failed in the BSEK Class 9 Science result of 28 October 2026. Read what the figures mean, how partial passes work, and the next steps without invented dates.
kw: BSEK 9th science failed papers what next 2026 result
intro: The Board of Secondary Education Karachi announced the Class 9 Science Group result on 28 October 2026, and one figure has worried thousands of families: 53,849 students failed. That number sits alongside a much larger and more hopeful picture, because the board's own breakdown shows tens of thousands of students who passed some papers but not all of them, and each of those students has a different, manageable path forward. This guide explains what the 28 October figures actually mean for a student who failed or passed only some papers, how the new 40% rule affects the result, and what practical steps to take now, without inventing supplementary dates or promises the board has not made.

sections.h2: Reading the 28 October 2026 Figures Honestly
paras: Start with the board's own numbers, shared by Controller of Examinations Ahmed Khan Chhutto. Of 180,054 students who registered, 177,923 appeared and 2,131 were absent. A total of 123,757 students passed all papers, while the remaining appeared students fall into two groups that are often confused: the partial-pass bands and the failed group. The partial-pass bands are 21,999 students passing six papers, 11,006 passing five, 7,431 passing four, 4,409 passing three, 3,101 passing two and 2,439 passing one paper, and separately 53,849 students are recorded as failed. The overall pass percentage was 69.56%, down from 78.26% in 2025, but the board has published no single official reason for that fall, and families should not accept any single explanation presented as fact.

Why does this breakdown matter to you? Because the label on your own mark sheet decides your next step, and the headline figure does not. A student who passed six papers has one or two open papers and a short, focused job ahead, while a student in the failed group has a bigger job that still starts the same way: by listing every paper and its marks. Do not let the size of the failed figure convince you that your case is hopeless, and do not let a partial pass convince you that nothing more is needed. Both situations are common this year, both are dealt with through the board's formal processes, and both improve fastest when the student knows exactly which papers are open and by how many marks each one was missed.

sections.h2: Failed vs Partial Pass: Know Which Group You Are In
paras: The distinction between a partial pass and a failed result is practical, not just a label. A partial pass means you have passed at least one paper and have specific open papers left to clear, so your plan can be built paper by paper, starting with the paper closest to passing. A failed result means no paper was passed or the result is recorded as failed overall, so the plan must be broader: a fresh, full revision of the subjects, usually with the school's guidance on whether to reappear in the papers or repeat the class as the board's rules allow. In both cases the new 40% rule applies, because from the 2026 annual examinations a paper scored below 40% is recorded as ungraded rather than passed, and Class 10 follows the same scheme from 2027.

The first action is identical for both groups: read your official mark sheet, not a summary from a friend or a social media post. Write down each paper, the marks obtained, and whether it is passed or ungraded, and calculate the gap below 40% for each open paper. This list becomes your study plan, because it tells you where to spend time and where not to. A student who failed by narrow margins in several papers needs steady revision across those subjects, while a student with one wide gap needs to rebuild that subject from the textbook. For subject-wise study material, see the [book collection](/books.html) and the [solved notes](/solved.html), and talk to your subject teachers about which chapters carried the most marks in the papers you missed.

diagram.alt: After a Failed or Partial Result: Your Next Steps
diagram.caption: A practical sequence for BSEK Class 9 Science students after the 28 October 2026 result.

sections.h2: What to Do This Week: Practical First Steps
paras: This week, do four concrete things. First, save and print your result from the board's official website, bsek.edu.pk, where the result has been available since 5:30 PM on 28 October 2026, and keep your admit card and registration details with it. Second, make the paper-by-paper list described above and share it with a parent and a teacher, because an adult who sees the exact gaps can help you plan realistically. Third, ask your school what support exists for students clearing papers, such as extra classes or remedial sessions, and whether the school expects you to continue into Class 10 while clearing open papers or to follow another route under the board's rules. Fourth, set a daily study slot for the open papers immediately, even before any official notice arrives, because revision started now is worth far more than revision started in a panic later.

At the same time, avoid the traps that waste this week. Do not pay any agent who promises to change a result or arrange a pass, because the board's process is formal and no unofficial channel can alter a mark sheet. Do not trust supplementary examination dates, fee figures or form links shared on social media unless they appear on the board's official website or your school notice board, since no reappearance date for these papers was stated in the 28 October announcement. Do not hide the result from your parents or teachers out of embarrassment; the board's figures show that tens of thousands of students are in the same position this year, and teachers deal with clearing papers every year. A result shared early gets help early, while a result hidden until the next examination becomes a crisis.

sections.h2: Building a Revision Plan That Actually Closes the Gaps
paras: A good revision plan for failed or ungraded papers starts from the textbook, not from short notes or guess papers. For each open paper, list the chapters, mark the ones where you lost the most marks, and work through them in order of marks weight, using solved exercises to check that your method is correct. Study in short, daily sessions rather than rare marathon sessions, and test yourself after each chapter with questions answered under timed conditions, because the examination rewards students who can produce answers under pressure, not students who have merely read the chapter. Keep a weekly checklist of chapters completed and practice tests taken, and review it every weekend so that slippage shows up while there is still time to correct it.

Balance is the hardest part of this plan, because Class 10 schoolwork continues at the same time for most students. Protect Class 10 school hours and homework time, and give the open Class 9 papers one or two focused hours a day, starting with the paper closest to passing so that an early success builds momentum. Science subjects overlap heavily between Class 9 and Class 10, so revising a Class 9 physics or chemistry chapter often strengthens the Class 10 chapter built on it, and that overlap should be used deliberately. If the number of open papers is large, be honest about the load: prioritise the papers closest to passing, talk to teachers about a realistic sequence, and remember that clearing papers properly, even if it takes longer, is far better than facing the next examination unprepared.

sections.h2: Staying Steady: Results, Rumours and the Next Examination
paras: A failed or partial result is emotionally hard, and students should be honest about that instead of pretending it does not matter. It is normal to feel disappointed, especially when classmates passed everything, but the board's figures prove that this year's result was difficult for a very large number of students, and a single examination does not fix a student's ability or future. Chairman Professor Musharraf Ali Rajput congratulated students who passed all papers and said transparency remained among the board's top priorities, and the fair way to read that message is that the system is meant to be navigable: open papers can be cleared through the board's own process, and students who follow that process do move forward. Comparing yourself with toppers helps no one; comparing today's marks with your own next attempt is the comparison that matters.

The steady approach is to keep two habits running until the next opportunity arrives: daily revision of the open papers, and weekly checks of the board's official website and your school notice board for the reappearance notice. When that notice appears, read it fully, noting eligibility, fee, last date and examination centre instructions, and complete the process through your school or the board's official channel as the notice directs. Until then, treat every unofficial date, fee claim or shortcut offer as unverified, keep your documents safe, and keep studying. The [blog](/blog/) carries further study guides for Sindh board students, and the [contact page](/contact.html) explains how to reach this site with questions about study material.

points: 53,849 students failed in the BSEK Class 9 Science result announced on 28 October 2026.
Tens of thousands more passed only some papers, from 21,999 passing six papers down to 2,439 passing one.
Below 40% in a paper means ungraded under the new rule, not passed.
List every open paper and its gap below 40% before making any plan.
Watch bsek.edu.pk for the official reappearance notice; no date was stated in the 28 October announcement.

faqs.q: How many students failed the BSEK Class 9 Science result 2026?
faqs.a: According to the figures shared by Controller of Examinations Ahmed Khan Chhutto, 53,849 students failed out of 177,923 who appeared. Separately, large numbers of students passed only some papers, including 21,999 who passed six papers and 11,006 who passed five.

faqs.q: I passed some papers but not all. What should I do first?
faqs.a: Read your official mark sheet and list every paper as passed or ungraded against the 40% threshold, noting how far below 40% each open paper fell. Share that list with a parent and a teacher, then start daily revision of the open papers while watching bsek.edu.pk for the board's official reappearance notice.

faqs.q: Does a paper scored at 35% count as passed?
faqs.a: No. From the 2026 annual examinations, Class 9 papers require 40% to pass, and a paper scored below 40% is recorded as ungraded. The old 33% threshold no longer applies to Class 9.

faqs.q: When will the supplementary or reappearance exams be held?
faqs.a: No reappearance date for these papers was stated in the board's 28 October 2026 announcement. Check the board's official website, bsek.edu.pk, and your school notice board for the official notice, and treat dates circulating on social media as unverified.

faqs.q: Can I continue into Class 10 while clearing Class 9 papers?
faqs.a: Most students do continue Class 10 schoolwork while clearing open papers, giving Class 10 its school hours and protecting one or two focused hours a day for the open papers. Ask your school about its arrangement for your case, since the school can advise on the route the board's rules allow for your result.

title: BIEK Commerce and Arts Part-I Result 2026: How to Read Your Result
desc: BIEK announced HSC Part-I results for Commerce, Arts and other remaining groups on 26 October 2026. Learn how to read your result, group figures and the ungraded rule.
kw: BIEK commerce arts part 1 result 2026 guide
intro: The Board of Intermediate Education Karachi completed its HSC Part-I Annual Examination 2026 results on Monday, 26 October 2026, when it announced the remaining groups on the instructions of Chairman Faqir Muhammad Lakho, with Controller Zarina Rashid overseeing the release. The groups announced that day were Science Pre-Medical, Science General, Commerce in both Regular and Private categories, Humanities and Arts in both Regular and Private categories, Special Candidates in Arts Regular, and Home Economics, while Pre-Engineering had already been announced on 2 October 2026. This guide focuses on the Commerce and Arts students among that release: what the board's figures show, how to read your own result paper by paper, and what the new ungraded rule means if any paper falls below 40%.

sections.h2: What Was Announced on 26 October 2026
paras: The 26 October announcement completed the HSC Part-I picture for 2026, because it covered every remaining group after Pre-Engineering had already been announced on 2 October 2026. For Commerce and Arts students, the important point is that both Regular and Private categories were included, so private candidates should read this guide alongside regular students rather than assuming it covers only college students. The results were published on the board's official website, www.biek.edu.pk, and on the official BIEK Android app, and students should check their result through those official channels rather than through screenshots or unofficial result pages, which can carry errors or outdated data. Keep a saved or printed copy of your result, because every later step, from scrutiny to reappearance, will ask for exactly what it shows.

Students should also note what this announcement was not. It was the HSC Part-I result, meaning Class XI or first year, and it should not be confused with Part-II results or with any supplementary examination. The announcement itself has already been covered by this site's result post, so this guide is written as a reading and next-steps guide rather than another announcement: it helps you understand the figures, interpret your own mark sheet, and decide what to do next. If you are a Science Pre-Medical or Science General student, the same 26 October release covers you too, but the figures and subject combinations in this guide focus on Commerce and Arts, with Science General covered in a companion guide.

sections.h2: Commerce Regular Figures: What the Numbers Show
paras: For Commerce Regular, the board's release gives a complete set of figures that students can use to understand their group. A total of 23,549 students registered, 22,693 appeared, and 9,332 passed all seven papers. That means a large share of Commerce Regular students did not pass all seven papers, and many of them passed some papers while leaving others open, which is a normal and manageable outcome under the board's system. The Commerce course has seven papers rather than six, so passing all seven is a bigger task than in a six-paper group, and students should judge their own result paper by paper instead of comparing themselves with students in groups that have fewer papers or different subjects.

If you are a Commerce student, your first job is to read your own mark sheet against the 40% line for each of the seven papers. List the papers you passed, list the papers marked ungraded, and note how far below 40% each ungraded paper fell, because that gap decides your revision plan. A paper missed by a few marks needs targeted revision of weak chapters, while a paper with a wide gap needs a fresh study plan from the textbook. Commerce subjects such as accounting and business mathematics reward regular practice, so daily worked examples matter more than last-minute reading. For study material matched to your subjects, browse the [book collection](/books.html) and the [solved notes](/solved.html), and ask your college teachers which chapters carried the most marks in the papers you missed.

sections.h2: Arts and Humanities: What We Know From the Release
paras: Humanities and Arts students in both Regular and Private categories were part of the 26 October announcement, and the release also gives a small, complete set of figures for Special Candidates in Arts Regular: 99 registered, 97 appeared, and 58 passed all six papers. Those figures are useful because they show the same pattern as the larger groups: a substantial share of students passed all papers, and the rest have open papers to deal with, which is a normal outcome rather than a disaster. Students in the general Arts and Humanities groups should read their own mark sheets in exactly the same way, paper by paper against the 40% line, rather than judging themselves by group totals that were not published in the release this guide is based on.

Arts students sometimes feel their result matters less than a science result, but that is a mistake, because Part-I papers feed directly into Part-II and into the final intermediate certificate. An ungraded paper left unattended in Part-I becomes a problem carried into the second year, while an ungraded paper dealt with promptly through revision and the board's formal process becomes a closed chapter. Arts subjects reward regular writing practice, so students with open papers should write answers daily, not merely read notes, and should ask teachers to mark a sample answer so that weak points are visible. Keep your result, admit card and registration details safe, and watch the board's official website for any notice about reappearance or scrutiny rather than trusting social media claims.

sections.h2: The Ungraded Rule: What Below 40% Means for You
paras: The new grading system, decided by the Inter Board Committee of Chairmen together with the Sindh Universities and Boards Department, changes what a low mark means. Under this system, scoring below 40% in any paper means the paper is ungraded, which means the candidate is unsuccessful in that paper and reappears in it subject to eligibility. This replaces the older understanding in which 33% could pass a paper, and it applies across the groups announced on 26 October, including Commerce and Arts. Students should therefore read every paper on their mark sheet against the 40% line, and should not assume that a paper scored in the thirties is passed because it would have passed under an older scheme.

The practical consequence is that a student with one or two ungraded papers has a clear, limited job: revise those papers, aim comfortably above 40%, and reappear when the board's process allows. A student with several ungraded papers has a bigger job and should talk to college teachers about a realistic sequence, prioritising the papers closest to passing. In both cases, the board's official website is the only reliable source for notices about reappearance, eligibility and fees, and no reappearance date should be treated as confirmed unless it appears there. The [blog](/blog/) carries further guides for intermediate students, including how to revise commerce and arts subjects chapter by chapter.

sections.h2: Next Steps: Scrutiny, Revision and Second Year Planning
paras: If you believe a paper has been marked incorrectly, the board offers scrutiny, and the fee reported from the board's scrutiny form is Rs 1,000 per paper. No scrutiny deadline is stated in the material this guide is based on, so do not invent or trust an unofficial deadline; check the board's official website and your college notice board for the current scrutiny notice and its last date, and apply only through the official channel. Scrutiny is worth considering when your marks in a paper are far below what your class performance suggested, but it is not a substitute for revision, and students should revise the paper in parallel rather than waiting for a scrutiny outcome before opening the book.

Alongside any scrutiny decision, set up a revision routine for every open paper and protect time for second-year study as well, because Part-II work begins whether or not Part-I papers are fully cleared. Give Part-II its college hours and homework time, and protect a focused daily slot for the open Part-I papers, starting with the paper closest to passing so that an early success builds momentum. Tell your teachers which papers are open, because they can point you to the right chapters and practice material, and keep a weekly checklist of chapters revised and practice answers written. The [about page](/about.html) explains how this site's study guides are organised for Sindh board students.

title: BIEK Science General Part-I Result 2026 Explained: Figures, OMR and What Comes Next
desc: Science General Part-I 2026: 30,991 registered, 30,386 appeared, 15,036 passed all six papers. Learn what the figures mean, how E-assessment worked, and your next steps.
kw: BIEK science general part 1 result 2026 explained
intro: Science General is one of the largest groups in Karachi's intermediate system, and its HSC Part-I Annual Examination 2026 result arrived with the remaining groups on Monday, 26 October 2026, announced on the instructions of Board of Intermediate Education Karachi Chairman Faqir Muhammad Lakho, with Controller Zarina Rashid overseeing the release. The board's figures for the group are precise: 30,991 students registered, 30,386 appeared, and 15,036 passed all six papers. This guide explains what those figures mean for an individual student, how the science groups' E-assessment and OMR marking worked, what passing all six papers actually requires under the new 40% rule, and what students with open papers should do next. Results are available on the board's official website and its official Android app.

sections.h2: Science General Figures: Reading the Group Result
paras: The three numbers for Science General tell a story that every student in the group should understand. Of 30,991 registered students, 30,386 appeared, which means about six hundred registered students did not sit the examination, and 15,036 of those who appeared passed all six papers. Put simply, just under half of the students who appeared cleared every paper, while just over half have at least one open paper, whether that means a single ungraded paper or several. That is not a reason for panic, because intermediate results routinely leave a large group with open papers, but it is a reason for honest self-assessment: if you have open papers, you are in the majority group, not an exception, and the board's formal processes exist precisely for your situation.

The comparison that matters most is not with other groups but with your own mark sheet. Science General students take six papers, and passing all six means clearing every one of them at or above the 40% threshold, because under the new grading system any paper below 40% is recorded as ungraded. A student who passed five papers and missed one by a few marks is in a very different position from a student who passed two papers, and the board's group figures cannot tell you which one you are. Read your own result paper by paper, list the passed and ungraded papers, and measure the gap below 40% for each open paper, because that list becomes your revision plan. For subject-wise study material, see the [book collection](/books.html) and the [solved notes](/solved.html).

sections.h2: E-Assessment and OMR: How Science Papers Were Marked
paras: One distinctive feature of the science groups' assessment in 2026 was the use of E-Assessment through OMR sheets together with E-Marking for the science-group optional subjects. In plain terms, the objective parts of those papers were answered on machine-readable OMR sheets and marked electronically, which is designed to make marking faster and more consistent than hand-marking thousands of objective answers. For students, the practical meaning is that the objective section rewards careful sheet-filling as much as subject knowledge: a correctly known answer marked in the wrong bubble, or a half-filled bubble, can cost marks that knowledge alone would have earned, so students preparing for the next attempt should practise OMR-style answering as part of their revision.

E-Marking also changes how students should think about scrutiny and rechecking. Because the objective marking is electronic, a scrutiny request is more likely to be useful when there is a clear discrepancy, such as marks far below class performance or a suspected error in the subjective section, than when a student simply hopes for a few extra marks. The scrutiny fee reported from the board's scrutiny form is Rs 1,000 per paper, and no scrutiny deadline is stated in the material this guide is based on, so students should check the board's official website for the current notice. Whether or not you apply for scrutiny, revise the open paper in parallel, because waiting for a scrutiny outcome before opening the book wastes the most valuable resource you have, which is time.

diagram.caption: The order in which a Science General student should act after the 26 October 2026 result.

sections.h2: What Passing All Six Papers Really Means
paras: Passing all six papers sounds simple, but under the new grading system it has a precise meaning that students should understand. It means scoring at or above 40% in every one of the six papers, with no paper left ungraded, because a single paper below 40% breaks the full pass even if the other five are strong. This is why the 15,036 figure matters: those are the students who cleared every paper, while every other appeared student has at least one paper still open. Students sometimes add up their total marks and assume a high total compensates for a weak paper, but the system works paper by paper, and a strong performance in one subject does not rescue an ungraded paper in another.

For students who passed all six, the message is straightforward: congratulations, and carry the same standard into Part-II, where the same 40% logic applies. For students with open papers, the message is equally clear: your job is defined by the list of open papers, not by your total, and it should be tackled paper by paper, starting with the paper closest to 40%. Work from the textbook, practise objective questions in OMR style where relevant, and write subjective answers under timed conditions, because both halves of a science paper need practice. The [blog](/blog/) carries study guides for intermediate science subjects, and your college teachers can identify which chapters carried the most marks in the papers you missed.

sections.h2: If You Have Open Papers: A Practical Plan
paras: Begin by making the paper-by-paper list and sharing it with a parent and a teacher, because adults who see the exact gaps can help you plan realistically and can tell you what support your college offers, such as extra classes or remedial sessions. Then set a daily revision slot for the open papers alongside your Part-II study, protecting Part-II college hours while giving the open papers focused time each day. Start with the paper closest to passing so that an early success builds momentum, and use the overlap between Part-I and Part-II science chapters deliberately, since revising a Part-I concept often strengthens the Part-II chapter built on it. Keep a weekly checklist of chapters revised and practice tests completed, and review it every weekend.

Avoid the two most common mistakes. The first is trusting unofficial dates, fee claims or agents who promise shortcuts; the board's official website, www.biek.edu.pk, and your college notice board are the only reliable sources for reappearance and scrutiny notices, and no reappearance date should be treated as confirmed unless it appears there. The second is stopping study while waiting for a notice, which turns a small gap into a forgotten subject by the time the examination arrives. Keep your result, admit card and registration details safe, because the reappearance process will require them, and treat every claim about dates or fees that does not come from the board as unverified until you have checked it yourself.

sections.h2: Science General in Context: The Full 26 October Release
paras: Science General was announced alongside Science Pre-Medical, Commerce in Regular and Private categories, Humanities and Arts in Regular and Private categories, Special Candidates in Arts Regular, and Home Economics, completing the HSC Part-I results after Pre-Engineering had already been announced on 2 October 2026. For comparison, Pre-Medical reported 25,157 registered, 24,544 appeared and 11,966 passing all six papers, while Commerce Regular reported 23,549 registered, 22,693 appeared and 9,332 passing all seven papers, and Special Candidates in Arts Regular reported 99 registered, 97 appeared and 58 passing all six. These comparisons are useful only in a general sense, because each group has different subjects and, in Commerce's case, a different number of papers, so students should not judge their own result by another group's pass rate.

What the full release does show is that the new grading system now runs across the intermediate groups, with the same 40% logic and the same ungraded outcome for any paper below that line. Science General students should therefore treat this year's result as the baseline for how the system works, not as an exception, and should build study habits that aim comfortably above 40% in every paper rather than at the borderline. That margin protects against a hard paper, an off day, or a strict marking scheme, and it carries directly into Part-II. The [about page](/about.html) explains how this site's study guides are organised, and the [contact page](/contact.html) explains how to reach us with questions about study material.

faqs.q: How many Science General students passed all six papers in 2026?
faqs.a: According to the board's release, 15,036 students passed all six papers out of 30,386 who appeared, from 30,991 registered. Just over half of the students who appeared therefore have at least one open paper, which is a normal outcome with a formal process for clearing it.

faqs.q: What is E-Assessment and OMR marking?
faqs.a: For the science-group optional subjects, objective answers were given on machine-readable OMR sheets and marked electronically, together with E-Marking. This makes objective marking faster and more consistent, and it means students should practise careful OMR sheet-filling alongside subject revision.

faqs.q: I passed five papers but one is ungraded. Have I passed Part-I?

faqs.q: Does a high total compensate for one weak paper?
faqs.a: No. The system works paper by paper, so a strong performance in one subject does not rescue an ungraded paper in another. Each paper must individually reach the 40% threshold to count as passed.

faqs.a: On the board's official website, www.biek.edu.pk, and the official BIEK Android app, plus your college notice board. Treat dates, fees or procedures from any other source as unverified until you have confirmed them officially.

title: Punjab Second Annual 12th Class 2026: Subject Dates Guide and Warnings
desc: 12th class second annual papers run 3-16 November 2026. Read the Multan-sheet subject windows for English, Maths, Biology, Computer Science, Chemistry and Physics.
kw: Punjab second annual 12th class subject dates 2026 guide
intro: For 12th class students in Punjab, the second annual examinations are now only days away, with Part-II theory papers running from 3 to 16 November 2026 under the province-wide schedule. Subject-wise planning matters enormously in such a short window, because the gap between two papers decides how much revision each subject gets, and students who know their subject dates can plan backwards from each paper instead of revising blindly. This guide sets out the subject windows from the BISE Multan date sheet, including English Compulsory on 4 November, Mathematics and Biology on 6 November, Computer Science on 10 November, Chemistry on 12 November and Physics on 16 November, with a warning to confirm your own board's sheet.

sections.h2: The Multan Sheet: 12th Class Subject Windows
paras: The BISE Multan date sheet gives 12th class students a concrete sequence to plan around. English Compulsory falls on 4 November, very early in the window, which means English revision must be finished before the examinations begin rather than fitted in afterwards. Mathematics and Biology fall on 6 November, giving students two days after English to switch subjects and revise, while Computer Science follows on 10 November, Chemistry on 12 November, and Physics on 16 November, which is the last day of the Part-II window. That sequence is the backbone of a revision plan: work backwards from each date, giving the earliest papers the most attention now, and letting later papers take a lighter daily slot until their turn approaches.

It is worth noting what this sequence implies about workload. A student taking Mathematics, Chemistry and Physics faces papers on 6, 12 and 16 November, with gaps of six and four days between them, which is workable if revision is already underway but punishing if it starts from scratch. A student taking Biology instead of Mathematics faces Biology on 6 November and then a longer run to Chemistry and Physics, which changes the balance of the plan. Whatever your combination, write your own subject dates on a single page, mark the gaps between papers, and assign revision hours in proportion to both the gap and your weakness in each subject. For subject-wise study help, see the [book collection](/books.html) and the [solved notes](/solved.html).

sections.h2: The Warning That Matters Most: Confirm Your Own Board's Sheet
paras: Every subject date in this guide comes from the BISE Multan date sheet, and that fact must be stated plainly, because Punjab has nine boards and subject-wise dates can differ between them. All nine boards share the 3 November start and the overall Part-II window of 3 to 16 November 2026, but a student under BISE Lahore, Rawalpindi, Gujranwala or any other board cannot safely assume that English falls on 4 November or Physics on 16 November for their board. Using another board's sheet as if it were your own is one of the most expensive mistakes a student can make, because it can mean revising the wrong subject for a paper, or worse, missing a paper entirely through a wrong date.

Confirming your own sheet takes ten minutes and should be done today. Check your board's official website, collect the date sheet from your school or college, and compare it paper by paper with the Multan windows given here, noting every difference on your own revision page. If your board's sheet shows a different date for any subject, your board's sheet governs, full stop, and the Multan dates become irrelevant for you. Save a copy of your own sheet on your phone and keep a printed copy with your roll number slip, so that both are checked together the night before each paper. The [blog](/blog/) carries further examination guides, but no guide can replace your own board's official date sheet.

diagram.caption: Subject dates from the Multan date sheet; confirm your own board's sheet before planning.

sections.h2: Planning Backwards From Each Paper
paras: With the subject dates known, the most effective planning method is to work backwards. Take the first paper, English on 4 November in the Multan sheet, and ask what must be finished by 3 November: essay and precis practice, grammar revision, and at least one timed past paper. Then do the same for 6 November, whether your subject is Mathematics or Biology, assigning the days after English to that subject's heaviest chapters and to timed numerical or diagram practice. Repeat the process for Computer Science on 10 November, Chemistry on 12 November and Physics on 16 November, so that every paper has a defined finish line and no subject is left to chance. This method works because it forces decisions about priority, and priority is exactly what a short examination window demands.

Within each subject's slot, follow a simple pattern: revise the highest-mark chapters first, practise past-paper questions under timed conditions, mark your answers strictly, and spend the remaining time only on the chapters where marks were lost. Do not start new, low-weight chapters in the final days, and do not re-read chapters you already know well, because both habits feel productive while adding few marks. Sleep properly before each paper, travel on a plan made the night before, and arrive at the centre at least thirty minutes early, since morning papers begin at 9:00 AM and evening papers at 2:00 PM, with Friday evening papers at 2:30 PM. A plan followed daily beats a perfect plan followed once.

sections.h2: Subject Tips for the Five Key Papers
paras: English Compulsory rewards practice over reading, so spend the remaining days writing essays, precis and comprehension answers under time limits, and revising grammar rules through examples rather than through rules alone. Mathematics rewards worked examples, so solve past-paper numericals by hand, check each step, and keep a short list of formulas you tend to forget, revising that list every evening. Biology rewards labelled diagrams and precise definitions, so practise drawing and labelling diagrams from memory and writing definitions in the textbook's language, because examiners award marks for accuracy in both. Computer Science rewards logic practice, so trace programs by hand, practise short questions on data and networks, and revise definitions until they can be written without hesitation.

Chemistry rewards balanced equations and numerical practice, so work through reaction types, practise mole and concentration calculations, and revise the chapters that carry the most marks first. Physics rewards numerical method, so practise past-paper numericals with units and significant figures, revise derivations by writing them out rather than reading them, and keep a formula sheet that you test yourself on daily. In every subject, the same principle holds: marks come from answers written under timed conditions, not from hours spent reading. If a chapter is weak, study it from the textbook, attempt its questions, and move on, because the examination rewards coverage of the whole syllabus more than perfection in one chapter.

sections.h2: After the Last Paper: Practicals and Results Thinking
paras: Physics on 16 November closes the Part-II theory window in the Multan sheet, but the examination season is not over, because practical examinations follow from 1 to 11 December 2026 in two batches each day, from 9:00 AM to 12:00 PM and from 1:00 PM to 4:00 PM, with the Friday second batch adjusted to a 2:30 PM start. Students should therefore keep their practical notebooks, apparatus familiarity and viva preparation ready during the theory window, rather than treating practicals as an afterthought once theory ends. Confirm your practical date, batch and centre from your own board's sheet as soon as it is published, and keep your practical record complete and signed, because an incomplete record is a preventable loss of marks.

Once the examinations end, resist the urge to chase rumours about results, marking or expected dates, and instead keep your roll number slip, admit card and date sheet safe until the result process is complete. If you later feel a paper was marked incorrectly, your board will publish a formal rechecking process, and the earlier Part-I result context, where all nine boards announced on 22 October 2026 at 10:00 AM with a rechecking window of about fifteen days, shows how such processes normally work, though the second annual rechecking notice must be checked on its own terms. The [about page](/about.html) explains how this site's guides are organised, and the [contact page](/contact.html) explains how to reach us with questions about study material.

faqs.a: On the BISE Multan date sheet, English Compulsory falls on 4 November 2026. Students under other boards must confirm their own board's sheet, because subject dates can differ between boards even though all boards share the 3 November start.

faqs.a: Mathematics and Biology fall on 6 November, Computer Science on 10 November, Chemistry on 12 November, and Physics on 16 November 2026. These are Multan-sheet dates; always confirm your own board's subject-wise sheet before planning.

faqs.a: Morning papers begin at 9:00 AM and evening papers at 2:00 PM, with Friday evening papers starting at 2:30 PM. Arrive at least thirty minutes early so transport delays do not cost you a paper.

faqs.a: Your own board's sheet, without exception. The Multan dates in this guide are examples from one board's sheet, and your board's official date sheet is the document that governs your papers.

title: Punjab Second Annual 11th Class 2026: After the 12th Papers, Your Turn
desc: 11th class second annual papers run 17-28 November 2026, after the 12th papers. Read the Multan-sheet subject windows, practical dates and a revision plan for the gap.
kw: Punjab second annual 11th class papers 17 November 2026 revision
intro: While 12th class students sit their second annual papers from 3 to 16 November 2026, 11th class students across Punjab have a different challenge: a waiting period that must be used, not wasted. Part-I, or 11th class, theory papers run from 17 to 28 November 2026 under the province-wide schedule, followed by practical examinations from 1 to 11 December 2026, and the gap before the first paper must be used well. This guide sets out the 11th class subject windows from the BISE Multan date sheet, including English Compulsory on 18 November, Computer Science on 23 November, Mathematics and Biology on 25 November, and Physics on 27 November, with a revision plan for the gap and a warning to confirm your own board's sheet.

sections.h2: Your Window: 17 to 28 November, After the 12th Papers
paras: The order of the second annual examinations is deliberate: Part-II papers come first, from 3 to 16 November 2026, and Part-I papers follow from 17 to 28 November 2026, so that centres, invigilators and marking can move from one group to the next in an orderly way. For 11th class students, this order creates both an opportunity and a trap. The opportunity is nearly three weeks of revision time from today, 30 October 2026, before the first paper, which is enough to cover a syllabus properly if it is used daily. The trap is that a long runway feels comfortable, so revision drifts, days slip, and the first paper arrives with chapters still unrevised. Treat the gap as a working period from today, not as a holiday that ends on 16 November, and the window becomes an advantage rather than a risk.

Timings for the Part-I papers follow the same province-wide pattern as Part-II: morning papers begin at 9:00 AM and evening papers at 2:00 PM, with Friday evening papers starting at 2:30 PM. Practical examinations follow from 1 to 11 December 2026 in two batches, from 9:00 AM to 12:00 PM and from 1:00 PM to 4:00 PM, with the Friday second batch adjusted to a 2:30 PM start. Write your own papers, timings and centre details on a single page as soon as your board's sheet is confirmed, and keep that page with your roll number slip, because a plan written down is far harder to drift away from than a plan kept only in your head. For subject-wise study help during the gap, see the [book collection](/books.html) and the [solved notes](/solved.html).

sections.h2: The Multan Sheet: 11th Class Subject Windows
paras: The BISE Multan date sheet gives 11th class students a concrete sequence to plan around. English Compulsory falls on 18 November, the day after the Part-I window opens, which means English revision must be complete before the window begins, not fitted in during it. Computer Science follows on 23 November, giving five days after English to switch subjects, while Mathematics and Biology fall on 25 November, and Physics on 27 November, one day before the window closes on 28 November. That sequence shapes the whole revision plan: English first and finished early, then a focused block for Computer Science, then the science subjects in the final stretch, with the gaps between papers used for the next subject rather than for rest.

As with the 12th class guide, the warning about boards must be stated plainly: these dates come from the Multan sheet, and all nine Punjab boards share the overall windows but can differ on subject-wise dates. A student under any other board must confirm their own board's sheet and follow it wherever it differs from the Multan dates, because your board's sheet is the document that governs your papers. Check your board's official website, collect the sheet from your school or college, and mark every difference on your own revision page before you plan a single day. The [blog](/blog/) carries further examination guides, but no guide can replace your own board's official date sheet.

diagram.caption: Subject dates from the Multan date sheet; confirm your own board's sheet before planning.

sections.h2: Using the Gap: A Revision Plan From 30 October to 17 November
paras: The gap from 30 October to 17 November should be divided into three phases. In the first phase, from now until about 10 November, cover the full syllabus chapter by chapter, working from the textbook, making short notes, and attempting solved exercises to check your method. In the second phase, from about 11 to 16 November, switch to timed past papers, marking your answers strictly and spending the remaining time only on chapters where marks were lost. In the third phase, the examination window itself, revise one subject at a time in the order of your papers, using the gaps between papers for the next subject and keeping each day's work narrow and timed. This structure works because it separates learning from testing, and testing from final polishing, instead of mixing all three into a confused final week.

Within each phase, keep the daily pattern simple and repeatable: a fixed number of study hours, a chapter list for the day, timed practice, and a short evening review of what was actually completed. Track completion on paper, not in your head, because a checklist reveals slippage while there is still time to correct it, while memory hides it until the paper arrives. English deserves early attention, since it falls on 18 November and cannot be crammed in a single day, while Mathematics, Biology and Physics reward daily numerical and diagram practice that should run through the whole gap rather than starting in the final week. Sleep properly throughout, because a tired mind in the examination hall loses more marks than a missed chapter.

sections.h2: Subject Tips for the 11th Class Papers
paras: English Compulsory rewards writing practice, so write essays, precis and comprehension answers under time limits through the gap, and revise grammar through examples rather than through rules alone. Computer Science rewards logic and definitions, so trace programs by hand, practise short questions, and revise definitions until they can be written without hesitation. Mathematics rewards worked examples, so solve past-paper numericals by hand, check each step, and keep a short list of formulas you tend to forget, revising that list every evening. Biology rewards labelled diagrams and precise definitions, so practise drawing diagrams from memory and writing definitions in the textbook's language.

Physics rewards numerical method, so practise past-paper numericals with units and significant figures, revise derivations by writing them out rather than reading them, and test yourself on a formula sheet daily. In every subject, marks come from answers written under timed conditions, not from hours spent reading, so the gap should be filled with practice, not with re-reading. If a chapter is weak, study it from the textbook, attempt its questions, and move on, because the examination rewards coverage of the whole syllabus more than perfection in one chapter. Ask your teachers which chapters carried the most marks in past papers, and give those chapters the heaviest weight in your plan.

sections.h2: After Theory: Practicals, and Keeping Documents Safe
paras: Practical examinations follow the theory window, running from 1 to 11 December 2026 in two batches each day, and 11th class students should keep practical preparation running alongside theory revision rather than leaving it until theory ends. Keep your practical notebook complete and signed, revise the experiments for your subjects, and practise viva answers, because practical marks are often the easiest marks to secure and the easiest to lose through an incomplete record. Confirm your practical date, batch and centre from your own board's sheet as soon as it is published, and arrive with the same punctuality as for theory papers, since the batch timings are fixed and late arrival disrupts the whole batch.

Once the examinations end, keep your roll number slip, admit card, date sheet and practical record safe until the result process is complete, and resist chasing rumours about results or marking. If you later feel a paper was marked incorrectly, your board will publish a formal rechecking process, and you should follow that notice on its own terms rather than trusting social media claims. The earlier Part-I result context, where all nine boards announced on 22 October 2026 at 10:00 AM with a rechecking window of about fifteen days, shows how such processes normally work, but each notice must be checked separately. The [about page](/about.html) explains how this site's guides are organised, and the [contact page](/contact.html) explains how to reach us with questions.

points: Part-I theory papers run 17-28 November 2026, after the Part-II window of 3-16 November.
Multan sheet: English 18 November, Computer Science 23 November, Mathematics/Biology 25 November.
Multan sheet: Physics 27 November, near the close of the Part-I window.
Use the gap in three phases: syllabus coverage, timed past papers, then paper-by-paper polishing.
Practicals follow from 1-11 December 2026; keep your practical record complete and signed.

faqs.q: When do 11th class second annual papers start?
faqs.a: Part-I theory papers run from 17 to 28 November 2026, after the Part-II papers of 3 to 16 November 2026. Practical examinations follow from 1 to 11 December 2026 in two batches each day.

faqs.q: What are the Multan-sheet dates for 11th class subjects?
faqs.a: English Compulsory falls on 18 November, Computer Science on 23 November, Mathematics and Biology on 25 November, and Physics on 27 November 2026. These are Multan-sheet dates; confirm your own board's sheet, since subject dates can differ between boards.

faqs.q: How should I use the gap before 17 November?
faqs.a: Divide it into three phases: syllabus coverage from now until about 10 November, timed past papers from about 11 to 16 November, and paper-by-paper polishing during the examination window itself, using the gaps between papers for the next subject.

faqs.q: What time do the papers start?
faqs.a: Morning papers begin at 9:00 AM and evening papers at 2:00 PM, with Friday evening papers starting at 2:30 PM. Practical batches run from 9:00 AM to 12:00 PM and from 1:00 PM to 4:00 PM, with the Friday second batch adjusted to a 2:30 PM start.

faqs.q: My board's sheet differs from the Multan sheet. Which do I follow?
faqs.a: Your own board's sheet, without exception. The Multan dates are examples from one board's sheet, and your board's official date sheet is the document that governs your papers.

title: Arabic Alphabet and Harakat for Beginners
desc: Learn the Arabic alphabet and harakat step by step: letter shapes, sounds, short vowels, and simple reading practice for complete beginners.
kw: Arabic alphabet harakat beginners learn Arabic letters
intro: The Arabic alphabet is the doorway to reading Arabic, and it is also the doorway to reading the Quran with understanding. Arabic has 28 letters, written from right to left, and most letters change shape depending on whether they stand alone, join to the letter before them, or join to the letters on both sides. This sounds difficult at first, but the system is regular, and students who learn a small group of letters at a time usually make fast progress. Harakat are the short vowel marks placed above or below a letter, and they tell the reader which vowel sound to pronounce. In this guide, we explain the alphabet, the letter shapes, and the harakat in simple steps, with a practice method that any beginner can follow at home or in class.

sections.h2: The 28 Letters and the Right-to-Left Direction
paras: Arabic is written and read from right to left, which is the first habit a beginner must build. Start at the right side of the page and move leftwards, and practise by pointing at each letter as you read it. The 28 letters are alif, ba, ta, tha, jeem, ha, kha, dal, dhal, ra, zay, seen, sheen, saad, daad, ta, za, ain, ghain, fa, qaf, kaf, lam, meem, noon, ha, waw, and ya. Do not try to memorise all 28 in one sitting; learn them in groups of four or five, saying each name aloud and writing it several times. When you can name and write one group without hesitation, add the next group.

Many Arabic letters come in pairs that look alike but differ by dots. Ba has one dot below, ta has two dots above, and tha has three dots above, yet all three share the same basic shape. Seen and sheen are another pair, differing only by three dots, and the same pattern repeats with several other letters. This is good news for beginners, because learning one shape often means learning two or three letters at once. Pay close attention to the dots from the very first day, because a misplaced dot changes both the letter and the meaning of the word.
bullets: Learn letters in small groups of four or five, not all 28 at once
Read and write from right to left, pointing at each letter as you read
Watch the dots carefully: ba, ta, and tha share one shape but differ by dots

sections.h2: How Letter Shapes Change When Letters Join
paras: Most Arabic letters join to the letter that follows them, so a letter can look different at the beginning, middle, and end of a word. For example, the letter ba looks like a small boat with a dot below when it stands alone, but when it joins to the next letter it loses its tail and stretches into a connecting stroke. This is normal and regular, and once you learn the four forms of a few common letters, the rest become easy to predict. Practise by writing the same letter in all its forms on one line, and say the form aloud as you write it: isolated, initial, medial, and final.

Six letters do not join to the letter that follows them: alif, dal, dhal, ra, zay, and waw. When one of these letters appears in a word, the next letter must start afresh, which creates a small break inside the word. Beginners often mistake this break for the end of a word, so it is worth learning these six non-joining letters early. A simple memory trick is to call them the letters that refuse to hold hands with the next letter. Once you know them, you will read joined words more confidently, because you will expect the break instead of being surprised by it.

sections.h2: Harakat: The Short Vowels That Guide Pronunciation
paras: Harakat are small marks that show the short vowel sound of a letter. Fatha is a small slant above the letter and gives an short a sound, as in ba. Kasra is a small slant below the letter and gives an short i sound, as in bi. Damma is a small curl above the letter and gives an short u sound, as in bu. These three marks are the foundation of Arabic reading, and a beginner who masters them can sound out most simple words. Practise by taking one letter, such as ba, and reading it with all three harakat in turn: ba, bi, bu, until the sounds come without thinking.

Two more marks complete the beginner's toolkit. Sukun is a small circle above a letter and means that the letter carries no vowel, so it joins its sound to the vowel before it. Tanween doubles the fatha, kasra, or damma and adds an n sound at the end, giving an, in, or un. Shadda, which looks like a small w shape, means the letter is doubled and pronounced with extra strength. You do not need to master all of these in the first week, but you should recognise them when you see them. Reading practice with harakat marked, as in school textbooks and beginners' Quran copies, makes all of these marks familiar step by step.

diagram.alt: Reading an Arabic Letter in Four Steps
diagram.caption: Name the letter, note its shape, add the harakat, then blend the sound.

sections.h2: Long Vowels and the Letters Alif, Waw, and Ya
paras: After the short vowels, the next step is the long vowels, which stretch a sound for about twice as long. Alif after a fatha stretches the a sound, waw after a damma stretches the u sound, and ya after a kasra stretches the i sound. For example, ba with fatha and alif becomes baa, a longer sound that is easy to hear when a teacher reads it aloud. The difference between short and long vowels matters for meaning, so listen carefully when your teacher reads and copy the length of each vowel. Reading aloud every day, even for ten minutes, trains your ear faster than silent reading alone.

A common beginner mistake is to rush past long vowels and pronounce them as short vowels, which makes words hard to recognise. Another mistake is to add a long vowel where none is written, which changes the word. The cure for both mistakes is slow, loud reading with a finger under each word. Read the word letter by letter first, then read it again as a whole word, and finally read the whole sentence smoothly. This three-pass method feels slow at first, but it builds accuracy, and accuracy is what turns a struggling reader into a confident one within a few weeks.

sections.h2: A Simple Daily Practice Plan for Beginners
paras: A short daily routine beats a long weekly session, because Arabic reading is a skill that grows with repetition. Spend five minutes writing the letter group you are learning, five minutes reading words that use those letters, and five minutes listening to a teacher or a reliable recording and repeating after it. Keep a small notebook in which you copy five new words each day with their harakat and meanings, and review yesterday's words before adding new ones. If you miss a day, simply resume the next day without trying to double the work, because steady practice always beats hurried catch-up.

Use the resources around you to stay on track. Your class textbook and your teacher's pronunciation are your best guides, and solved notes can help you check your understanding of a lesson. For extra reading material and revision help, explore the collection on [Solved Notes](/solved.html), browse the full book list on [Books](/books.html), and visit the article index on [Blog](/blog/) for more study guides. Remember that every fluent Arabic reader once struggled with the first letters, so patience and daily practice will carry you further than any shortcut.

points: Arabic has 28 letters, written and read from right to left.
Most letters change shape when they join, but six letters never join forwards.
Fatha, kasra, and damma give the short a, i, and u sounds.
Dots change the letter, so ba, ta, and tha must be told apart carefully.
Fifteen minutes of daily reading, writing, and listening beats occasional long sessions.

faqs.q: How many letters are in the Arabic alphabet?
faqs.a: The Arabic alphabet has 28 letters, from alif to ya. Beginners should learn them in small groups of four or five, saying each name aloud and writing it several times. Learning the groups in order, with daily review, makes the full alphabet manageable within a few weeks.

faqs.q: What are harakat in Arabic?
faqs.a: Harakat are short vowel marks placed above or below a letter. Fatha gives an a sound, kasra gives an i sound, and damma gives an u sound, while sukun marks a vowelless letter and tanween adds an n sound. These marks guide pronunciation, especially in textbooks and beginners' reading material.

faqs.q: Why do Arabic letters look different inside words?
faqs.a: Most Arabic letters join to the following letter, so their shape changes at the beginning, middle, and end of a word. The basic shape stays recognisable, but tails are dropped and connecting strokes are added. Learning the four forms of a few common letters makes the pattern predictable across the whole alphabet.

faqs.q: Which Arabic letters do not join to the next letter?
faqs.a: Six letters do not join forwards: alif, dal, dhal, ra, zay, and waw. When one of these appears in a word, the next letter starts afresh, creating a small break inside the word. Knowing these six letters early prevents the common mistake of treating that break as the end of a word.

faqs.q: How long does it take a beginner to read Arabic words?
faqs.a: With fifteen minutes of daily practice, most beginners can sound out simple marked words within a few weeks. Progress depends on regular reading aloud, writing the letters, and listening to correct pronunciation. Slow and accurate reading at first is better than fast guessing, because accuracy builds the confidence that later brings speed.

title: Arabic Greetings and Daily Phrases
desc: Learn Arabic greetings and daily phrases with correct pronunciation and manners: salam, replies, thanks, and polite classroom expressions.
kw: Arabic greetings daily phrases salam learn Arabic speaking
intro: Greetings are the friendliest way to begin learning spoken Arabic, because they are short, useful, and used every single day. A student who can greet, thank, apologise, and ask politely in Arabic has already taken a real step into the language, and has also learnt something about Arab manners and Islamic etiquette. The most important greeting is Assalamu Alaikum, peace be upon you, and its reply is Wa Alaikum Assalam, and upon you be peace. In this guide, we explain the common greetings and daily phrases, how to pronounce them, when to use each one, and how to practise them until they come naturally in conversation.

sections.h2: Assalamu Alaikum and Its Reply
paras: Assalamu Alaikum is the Islamic greeting, and it means peace be upon you. It is used when meeting someone, entering a room, starting a phone call, or greeting a teacher or elder. The reply, Wa Alaikum Assalam, returns the same wish of peace to the speaker, and a fuller reply adds Wa Rahmatullahi Wa Barakatuh, and the mercy of Allah and His blessings. Muslims are encouraged to greet warmly and to reply with an equal or better greeting, so learning both the greeting and the reply together is the correct approach. Practise them as a pair, not as separate words, so that the reply comes automatically when you hear the greeting.

Pronunciation matters, so break the greeting into parts and practise slowly: As-sa-la-mu A-lai-kum. Listen to your teacher's pronunciation and copy the sounds, especially the long vowel in salam and the clear k sound at the end. A common mistake is to rush the greeting into a mumbled single word, which loses both clarity and courtesy. Speak it clearly, with a smile, and look at the person you are greeting, because a greeting is a social act as much as a language exercise. When you greet your teacher or classmates in Arabic each morning, you turn a lesson into a daily habit.

sections.h2: Morning, Evening, and Parting Greetings
paras: Arabic also has time-based greetings that students will hear in conversations, stories, and lessons. Sabah Al-Khair means good morning, and its reply is Sabah An-Noor, morning of light. Masa Al-Khair means good evening, with the reply Masa An-Noor. These greetings are polite and common, but Assalamu Alaikum remains the greeting Muslims use most, and it can be used at any time of day. Knowing both kinds helps students understand dialogues in their textbook, because a character might greet with Sabah Al-Khair in a morning scene and reply with Sabah An-Noor.

For parting, Ma'a Salama means with safety, or goodbye, and it is a kind wish for a safe journey. Another useful parting phrase is Ila Al-Liqa, until we meet again, which suits classmates and friends. When leaving a teacher, students often combine politeness with gratitude, saying thank you before Ma'a Salama. Learning greetings in pairs, greeting and reply, morning and evening, meeting and parting, gives students a complete small toolkit that covers almost every everyday situation they will meet in class or at home.
bullets: Sabah Al-Khair means good morning; reply with Sabah An-Noor
Masa Al-Khair means good evening; reply with Masa An-Noor
Ma'a Salama means goodbye, literally with safety

sections.h2: Polite Phrases: Thanks, Apology, and Permission
paras: Polite phrases make a beginner sound respectful, and they are used constantly in Arabic-speaking settings. Shukran means thank you, and Jazak Allahu Khairan, may Allah reward you with good, is a warmer Islamic way to thank someone. The reply to thanks is Afwan, which means you are welcome. When you need to apologise, say Afwan can also mean pardon, but the clearer apology is Ana Asif, I am sorry, for a boy, and Ana Asifa for a girl. These small gender differences appear throughout Arabic, and noticing them early helps students speak correctly rather than repeating one form for everyone.

Asking permission politely is another essential skill. Min Fadlik means please, said to a boy or man, and Min Fadlik is the same phrase addressed to a girl or woman, with a different ending sound. To ask a question, you can begin with Hal, which turns a statement into a yes-or-no question, as in Hal tafham, do you understand? Learning these polite frames first means that even a beginner with a small vocabulary can ask, thank, and apologise gracefully. Manners and language grow together, and teachers notice both when a student speaks politely in Arabic.

sections.h2: Classroom Phrases Every Student Should Know
paras: Classroom Arabic is immediately useful, because students can use it in every lesson. Ana fahimt means I understood, and Ana lam afham means I did not understand, and both are better than silence when a lesson is unclear. A student who wants the teacher to repeat can say A'id min fadlik, please repeat. To ask the meaning of a word, say Ma ma'na hadhihi al-kalima, what is the meaning of this word? These four sentences alone can transform a student's participation, because they let the student ask for help in the language being learnt, which is exactly how language learning works best.

Other classroom phrases include Iftah al-kitab, open the book, and Ighliq al-kitab, close the book, which teachers use as instructions. Students answering a question might begin with Na'am, yes, or La, no, before giving their answer. Practise classroom phrases by role-playing with a partner: one student plays the teacher giving instructions, and the other responds and asks questions. After a few rounds, swap roles. This kind of paired speaking practice is more effective than memorising a list silently, because speaking aloud builds the mouth memory that silent study cannot give.

diagram.alt: A Polite Arabic Conversation in Five Steps
diagram.caption: Follow this order to greet, ask, thank, and part politely.

sections.h2: Practising Phrases Until They Become Natural
paras: The secret to speaking phrases naturally is to use them in real moments, not only in study time. Greet your family with Assalamu Alaikum in the morning, thank your mother with Jazak Allahu Khairan after a meal, and say Ma'a Salama when a guest leaves. Each real use strengthens the phrase far more than ten silent repetitions from a list. Keep a small phrase diary in which you write one new phrase each day with its meaning and a sentence showing when you used it. At the end of the week, read the diary aloud and check which phrases you now use without thinking.

Pair practice also helps a great deal. Find a classmate and agree to greet each other in Arabic every day for a week, then add one new phrase each week, such as a thanks, an apology, or a classroom question. Mistakes are part of the process, and a good partner corrects gently and keeps the conversation going. For more study guides and revision material, visit [Solved Notes](/solved.html), browse [Books](/books.html) for your class, and explore the article index on [Blog](/blog/). Speaking a language is a habit, and habits are built one greeting at a time.

points: Assalamu Alaikum means peace be upon you; reply with Wa Alaikum Assalam.
Sabah Al-Khair and Masa Al-Khair cover morning and evening greetings.
Shukran and Jazak Allahu Khairan are two ways to say thank you.
Classroom phrases like Ana fahimt help students ask for help in Arabic.
Daily real use turns memorised phrases into natural speech.

faqs.q: What does Assalamu Alaikum mean, and how do I reply?
faqs.a: Assalamu Alaikum means peace be upon you, and the reply is Wa Alaikum Assalam, and upon you be peace.
